div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Baptist Church, Colborne-street.

"Our Mount of Vision" was the subject of the Rev.H. Dunnico's evening sermon on Sunday last, when he took for his text words from the epistle to the Hebrews chap. 8, v. 5, "See, saith He, that thou makest all things according to the pattern showed to thee in the mount." After a brief study of the life and character of Moses, the preacher pointed out that every man had his Mount of Vision, and that faithfulness to that vision entailed, as in the case of Moses, coming down and living in obedience to it on the plain. The great difficulty with most of us was that our visions and our tasks were so unrelated to each other. Many people on this account despised visions,but visions were essential to effective and successful work. Without tasks they were worth- less, but also tasks without visions were of very little use. St. Francis d'Assisi, William Carey, William Wilberforce, William Booth and others were all noble examples of men who had worked out the vision God had shown them. Faithful obedience to what we had seen ever led to a larger and better vision.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.ik, Soci3ty.—Ma3tiag Conducted
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.ik, Soci3ty.—Ma3tiag Conducted
by Ladies.

The open meeting in connection with the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society on Sunday was unique in its character, owing to the fact that ladies were entirely responsible for the conduct of the meeting. There was a lady in the chair, a lady speaker, a lady reader, and a lady also offered prayer. The proceedings were presided over by Mrs. Yonge (wife of the President) who based an interesting address on the text "Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy." She was aware, she said, that many people were prevented from very good reasons from attending a plate of worship on Sundav, but she could not understand why so many chose the hours appointed for public worship as the most suitable for a walk, when they had so many other hours of the day at liberty.—To mothers who could not attend places of worship she would enjoin them to have private worship at home, with the children around them.—Mrs. Moores delivered an address in which she corn- pared life to a voyage on the ocean. She asked them not only to praise God and trust Gdd but to let their life be characterised by earnestness and steadfastness. Miss Beswick read the scripture lesson and Miss V. Taylor offered prayer.—A violin solo was very efficiently contributed by Master T. Barton, and Master Pierce, who presided at the organ, also played an organ solo. A collection was taken on behalf of the society's funds.

div.head: MUSH INTEREST AWAKENED.
div.p: MUSH INTEREST AWAKENED.

Much interest has been awakened in the neighbour- hod ofSheepwash, Devon, by the tale of suffering, end- ingin a happy recovery,related by Mr. J. Sleffield,!of Ivy Cottage. Mr. Sle:Reld gives the following account of the matter "Affected by a series of disappointments and losses, my general health gave way; my liver, heart, and kidneys were affected. While in this weak condition I contracted Influenza. "I was so ill and weak I had the greatest difaculty in turning round in bed. I had great pain in my back and head. My heart used to palpitate violently and I suffered from extreme weakness. In the morning when I got up and looked in the glass I found my hands and face very much swollen. I was afraid I was going to have an attack of Dropsy. "This was the state of my health when I happened to read in the paper the testimony of several persons whose painful experiencas were similar to my own, and who had been cured by Dodd's Kidney Pills. I resolved to give them a trial. "I begin to take then.and after tvo doses felt much better. I kept on getting better every day. Tae nains in my back grew less and ceasal; so did the swelling. I can now safely say that Dold's Kidney Pills have restored me to health."

div.head: LICENSING BILL Resolution Passed at Wycliffe Church.
div.p: THE LICENSING BILL Resolution Passed at Wycliffe Church.

At the conclusion of the service at Wycliffe Congre- gational Church, Bewsey-street, on Sunday evening, the Rev. John Yonge asked the congregation to remain seated for a few minutes whilst he brought forward a matter a importance. The mattet was one, he said, in which the congregation took an interest. A short time ago they sent a petition to the House of Common.s against the Government Licensing Bill. Those who followed the newspapers would know that to all appear- ance the Government's licensing bill in its most un- desirable provisions would pass the House of Commons. It would then in the ordinary course go to the House Of Lords, where it was expected to reached in the course of a few days. He (Mr. Yonge) had received a letter from the United Kingdom Alliance, advising as to what course of action should be pursued. When the Bill reached the House of Lords, Lord Peel and the Archbishop of Canterbury would make a strenuous effort to get a time limit inserted. Petit one to the House of Lords were of very little value but it was suggested that it would be a good thing, to pass a resolution in favour of a time limit, and for ward it to the following members otf the House of Lords: the Earl of Crawford, the Earl OT Derby, the Earl of Lathom, Lord Newton, Lord Stalbridge, the Duke of Westminster, the Archbishop of Canterbury, Viscount Peel, and the Earl of Sefton. By this means it was hoped to strengthen the bands of the friends of temperance. The resolution which he now proposed was as follows : " That this meeting of the members of the church and congregation worshipping in Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington, held on Sunday evening, July 24th is of,opinion that the Government Licensing Bill, by conferring upon brewers and licence holders a freehold property in what, for centuries past, has been simply an annual permission to sell, is erecting a tremendous barrier against all future temperance reform. It hopes, therefore, that the House of Lords will insert a time limit by the action of which the nation may be able to resume its power of dealing with the traffic in intoxi- cating liquors as it may deem necessary and desirable in the interests of public health and morality." The congregation signified their approval of the reso- lution by a show of hands.

Exciting Scene on the Ship Canal. John Finney, of Workington, fireman on the steam- ship Nellie, of London, discharging grain from the Black Sea at Runcorn lay-bye, made a determined attempt to commit suicide on Sunday evening. Finney was foiled in one attempt to jump into the Canal, but afterwards escaped from two shipmates and leaped into the water. He was almost dead when rescued. Ex-Constable Crowder and Constables Davies and Oakes resuscitated him after an hour's hard work.
G.W. R

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

A Popular Princess.—Princess Victoriaof Schleswig- Holstein has made an excelleet recovery from the effects of her operation for, appendicitis, and proposes in the autumn to accompany her mother, Princess Christian, to South Africa, with the purpose of visiting Prince Christian Victor's grave. It was in his memory that the Memorial Home was erected at Windsor,where Princess Victoria has been staying as a patient. Few people know more about hospital arrangements than Princess Christian and her daughter, and they are sure to take great interest in these matters in the various South African Colonies. Princess Victoria is of an active , and very lovable disposition,always managing to occupy ' her time with some or other useful work, and she is much appreciated among the poor in the neighbour- hood of. Cumberland Lodge. She is the one and only member of the Royal Family to extend her love of animals to cats, and has taken several prizes at the leading cat shows. Some Newly Announced Engagements.—Several in- teresting, end-of-the-season engagements have been announced, including that of Miss Dorothy Vivian, one of the twin daughters of Lady Vivian who have been maids of honour to the Queen since the accession of King Edward VII. Her fiance is Mr. Sandys, of the Life Guards. Another interesting engagement is that of Lady Ulrica Duncombe, the youngest of the four beautiful daughters of the Earl and Countess of Fever- sham, who is also to marry a soldier, the Hon. Everard Baring, of the 10th I-lussars. Some five years ago Lady Ulrica was engaged "to Dr. Winnington Ingram, the present Bishop of London, but the match was broken off owing to the opposition of Lady Ulrica's family,and the Bishop is still unmarried. Since the death of her eldest sister, the Duchess of Leinster, Lady Ulrica has devoted much of her time to the care of her orphan nephew, the young Duke of Leinster. Her other sisters are the wives of Sir Edgar Vincent, and Sir Richard Graham, Birt. The Ghost of a Dog.—Those persons who believe in the auguries and forebodings of dreams, will no doubt readily agree with Mr. Rider Haggard that what is called telepathy can exist not only between two human beings, but also between a dog and his master. Mr. Haggard dreamed that a favourite retriever dog was appealing to him in distress, and though not ascertained until some days afterwiirds, it would appear that a few hours previous to the dream, the dog was run over, and killed by a passing train. Was it then what one is forced to call the ghost of the dog,or the moanings of its spirit that inspired the dream? Perhaps the Psychical Research Society will have something to say about it, but the sceptical will no doubt regard it as simply a remarkable coincidence, the more readily because it is not an uncommon experience among the elderly to have one or two dreams in the course of a lifetime, which afterwards appear to have been of a prophetic character. The Craze for Cures.—ln the search for health, fashionab!e Society seems to be more and more resort- ing to fads and crazes. Instead of exploring fresh fields and pastures new,the holidays are spent in working hard at some or other cure recommended by the doctors as the latest and best of all remedies for nervous break- down. In America the music cure has been taken up. with enthusiasm, and there are good grounds for believ- ing that 'this treatment is really beneficial for those suffering from mental overstrain or fatigue. Various kinds of music are provided for the different classes of patients at these sanatoria, and in addition, medicated air is supplied to represent the atmospheric conditions, supposed to be good for certain diseases. The air is so treated as to reproduce the virtues of various climates,' and this saves the patient the trouble of making a long journey to distant parts of the world. The old- fashioned way of wooing Nature's restorative has apparently betome too slow for Society, but whether all the so-called' cures and artificial arrangements are as good, may perhaps be doubted. Uncared for Cats.—Some humane people have been impresting upon householders that when they go away for their summer holidays they should make some pro- vision for the cat. One cannot help reflecting on this subject that the aggregate of suffering occasioned to cats which are left at home during the holidays, does not compare with that of the cats which are altogether homeless, but that is a point which receives very little attention, and it seems to be of no use to refer to it. Like the boiling of fish alive, it is one of those things which people take for granted. But at the same time two wrongs do not make a right, and it is well that attention should be drawn to the cruelty of leaving cats to starve while the owners go to the country, or the seaside. If no arrangement can be made for feed- ing the animal, it would be preferable to send it to the Temporary Home for Dogs, Battersea, where—unless anybody will buy it—for a fee of is. it will be pain- lessly d i estroyed n the lethal chamber. Furs Require Attention.—At no time of the year do furs require more careful attention than just now when the moth is so much about doing its deadly work. There are some furs, such as sealskin, which the moth does not fancy, because of the dye used in the dressing, but all alike should be carefully gone over, hung on a line in the sun, and. gently beaten upside down with a cane. It is not safe to trust to campher, carbon, or any of the moth powders. Of course those who possess costly furs and send them away to be kept in cold chambers, need never worry about the moth, but with only drawers or cupboards to depend upon, every precaution is neces- sary at this time of the year. Hanging out, and beating furs may involve a good deal of trouble, but it is the only way to make sure of keeping them free from the moth grubs. The Muslin Year.—This .has distinctly been a muslin .year, not only for "grown lips "but also for the little folks. Nothing is prettier and froher looking, for tiny girls than the clear white book muslin, now so much ' in request by dressmakers, for their juvenile customers, but the amount of work and trimming, put into these little garments is growing excessive, like the charges ' made for them. Pink or blue ribbons adorn nearly all the little white muslin frocks and.paletots, the idea of keeping small children entirely in white, being appar- ently among those past and gone. Juvenile Headgear.—The cottage bonnet, made of coarse straw, finished inside with a quilling of muslin and lace, and boasting the inevitable pair of soft ribbon strings, is a favour:te choice for little girls, so also is the leghorn of the old-fashioned type, simply trimmed with a wreath of daisies, forget-me-nets, or other simple childish looking flowers. But of all the shapes now in evidence for small girls, the mushroom variety is, generally speaking,the most becoming that can crown a pretty head. Moreover the children like it, because it is so comfortable. The huge floppy, frilly hats have disappeared and a neater and more-in-proportion style of headgear now prevails for the little folks. MADGE.

BETTING AT EARLESTOWN. At the Newton Police Court, on Thursday, Matthew Seton, a bookmaker, with 11 previous convictions, was fined .C 5 and costs for betting in two cases. Frank Dale, Edward Dale, and John Conroy, were each fined £5 and costs for betting in Earle-street, Earlestown. For aiding and abetting bookmakers, John Williams was fined 20s. and costs, George Johnson 20s. and costs, Owen Morris 40s. and costs, and Robert Salisbury 40s. and costs. For street betting, John Williams, Charles Taylor, and George Johnson, were each mulcted in 40s. and costs. The cases against Thomas Hughes and James Lee were dismissed.

div.head: Examiner Saturday, July 30 1904.
div.p: The Examiner Saturday, July 30 1904.
FIASHIORIS OF TO-DAY.

Much of our immediate spare time is taken ip in determining the fate of the oddments of ;ilk lace and muslin secured by us at the -ecent sales. Muslins there were, too, of the Latest designs, and these were really marked down to ridiculously low prices, thereby re- joicing tke hearts of those who had delayed purchasing these dainty toilettes till July had arrived with its period of sales. Summer is nowadays never at its prime till after the longest day is over, and there were few days in June when one felt that a muslin frock was really necessary to one's well benig. There- fore there is little difficulty in evolving dainty gowns and blouses out of this season's bar- gains trimmed with one or more pieces of the pretty laces that were also " thrown away." Spotted muslins seem greatly in demand, and as this season's vogue is generally defunct before another ckawns it is wise to get as much

div.head: MUSLIN GOWN.
div.p: A MUSLIN GOWN.

wear as possible out of any material in which the pattern is at all pronounced. Large lozenge shaped designs in different pretty colours on a white or string coloured ground makes up into fascinating garments and look particularly nice when finished at the waist by one of the new ribbon belts which have an impertinent-looking bow half way up the back of the wearer and long knotted ends depend- ing quite half way down the back of the skirt. Chine ribbon is floral blurred designs were to be picked up at the sales for almost nothing, and could not be used in any nicer fashion than when transformed into a pretty belt of this style.

The pretty muslin frock which forms the subject of my first sketch is of soft, clear cream muslin trimmed with ecru lace and is finished by a waist band, such as I have described, of pink chine ribbon covered with a blurred design of roses of a dull red hue. The hat is trimmed with a wreath composed of clusters of tiny crimson banksea roses, while a soft lace veil forms the fall at the back. The dress is a very simply made one, the skirt being slightly gauged round the hips. and trimmed at the lower edge by a shaped flounce edged with lace. The sleeves fall in a very full lace' edged flounce, while the bloused
A PRETTY HAT.
bodice boasts a cape-like collar of ecru lace

matching in design that used in the irt. White alpaca makes up into the most delight- ful gowns sparingly trimmed with black and white striped linen land pearl buttons. Worn with a bright red leather belt and a hat and sunshade of the same bright tint a most effective toilette is arrived at. The lace veil worn flowing down the back is a mode which has found great and very general favour in the eyes of nearly all women, but a little variety from this is evinced in the pretty hat shown in my second illustration which has its high crown enveloped in soft folds of chiffon, while the same becoming material forms the soft strings which are brought loosely round from the back to the front, where they are knotted in a large full bow. A trail of pink roses with buds and leaves crosses the curved brim, for the hat needs little trimming as it depends for success on shape alone. The brim is again bent downwards at the back where it fits the head closely. The high jam pot crown is a mode which is very popular this year and proves becoming to most faces. These hats are seen worn with morning frocks of muslin or linen trimmed only by a band of soft hued ribbon enoircling the crown, while a large

div.head: LINEN OUTFIT.
div.p: LINEN OUTFIT.

bunch of cabbage roses is arranged a little to one side of the front. In rustic straw they look very well, and are also charming in fine chip trimmed with delicate lace and an abun- dance of flowers. Others again are made with a lower and wider crown which is surrounded either by a ruche of silk or satin or by a stiff wreath of roses. For morning wear the silk niche looks very smart, while the flowers are better suited to afternoon wear.

My last sketch gives a very nice outfit suited for a little girl's wear at the seaside. The hat, coat, and skirt are all of pink linen, the only trimming being a little open work Swiss embroidery; and a large chou of white silk placed at one side of the wide crown of the hat. It is a simple dress and very cool wear as neither the coat nor skirt needbe lined. It is also 'easily washed and dressed as there is nothing in the very least elaborate about it. There are many styles of dress for little girls this year which vary from the frock which depends in soft folds from the tucked or lace inserted yoke to the long-waisted French style, where the fulness is caught in by a smart sash a little below the waist, a series of full frills standing out and forming an exceed- ingly abbreviated little skirt. This is cer- tainly a pretty mode for a dressy frock and looks very smart on a little child, but is only absurd when worn by a girl over five years of age. The coat and skirt style is, however, suited to all ages and is therefore likely to outlive the more fleeting modes.

div.head: (Copyright.) HE OLD FASHION-AND THE NEW.
div.p: (Copyright.) HE OLD FASHION-AND THE NEW.
By EVELYN EVERETT GREEN, Author of "Monica," "Arnold Inglehurat the Preacher," "Over the Sea Wall," &c.

She was just a sweet-faced, country-bred girl, : brought up in the old-fashioned ways. She had ' : 3.ever ridden a bicycle, or dreamt of emancipation from the old-faghioned tradit;ons of her home. She ! had seldom travelled by rail, and had only once ' heen in London. She was the only child of her ; tW her —a real old-fashioned country squire—and ' nce the death of her mother, three years ago, she had been more than ever the companion and friend : of her father. She knew every man, woman and child upon he estate, and, indeed, within, a radius of ten miles or more. Everybody loved "Miss Dulcie," as Oley had always called her. She visited the cottages, ott in the Sunday-school, made warm clothes h, be distributed in the winter months, and doled out soup and kitchen physic in times of sickness tad emergency. And she was perfectly happy. It . Lad never occurred to Dulcie Carlingford that her life was dull and tame, that women were meant to ; :lave "vocations" which took them away from the !,phere in which they were born; and she did : pot even know what was meant by the "New IVoman," of which the newspapers sometimes . wrote.

Dulcie read the political articles to her father of in evening, and was by no means ignorant of what pissed in the world without; but of modern literature and modern social upheaval she knew next to nothing. She read things on the subject without being able to understand thorn; and her father would stop her with a quick word, and bid her not trouble her bead over such balderdash. So Dulcie thought that the world was a bright and happy place, and that if people would only be lood they would be happy too. She hoped that they were growing better and happier, and she liked to feel that she was able to carry sunshine about with her in the little corner where her own Jot had been placed. She was riding home now from an errand of ; mercy to some distant corner of the parish. Dulcie's one emancipation had been the permission to ride unattended about the familiar lanes within five-mile radius of her own home. She was not 7;,ear as late home as this; but she had been -.'etaitied by the necessity of riding round by the doctor's house on her return. She made a pretty picture in the gathering twilight; her fair face framed in its wealth of golden hair, her neat, closely-fitting habit showing off the slight and rounded figure, the graceful seat betokening perfect horsemanship, the little gaunt leted hand controlling the mettlesome creature with perfect ease. ' The horse was a fine specimen of an old-fashioned stock, of which the Squire was justly proud; wide- chested, deep in the shoulder, with fine strong hind-quarters, rather short legs, but fine long pasterns. Upon a horse like that Dulcie felt perfectly safe. Jack could he trusted to talcs care of his mistress, and, moreover, she was attended by several dogs, all of them devoted to her : service. Woe betide the man, indeed, who offered to molest her now! I She was drawing rein, for the road took a down- i ward trend and there was the gate into their own park. It was a side gate, and there was no lodge to it; but Jack understood how to stand so as to let his rider open it easily. But as Dulcie rode up she saw something standing there in the dim light beneath the trees; and she paused in perplexity, whilst Jack snorted with a sort of fear, and the dogs rushed forward, barking loudly. "Why," breathed Dulcie to herself in a state of considerable excitement, "it must be a motor-car! clh, how I have wanted to see one! What would papa say if he were here ! " For now that she could see more clearly she perceived that this thing was a little carriage on four cycle wheels, with no horse in front of it. Behind stood its owner, turning a wheel round and round; but the noise inade by the dogs caused him to turn round quickly: and when he perceivel Dulcie, only a dozen yards off, he took off his hat and came forward, saying in a courteous tone, and with an unmistakable gentleman's voice : "Am I frightening your horse? Shall I lead him past? " "Oh, thank you," said Dulcie; "but he is not frightened, only surprised. I thought motor-cars always made a noise ? " "I wish mine would make a noise,' answered the stranger, smiling; "but there is something wrong. I think the ignition tube is broken. It has been driving badly and missing fire for some time. I hoped to get it as far as the next village; but it came to a dead stop a few minutes ago, and I can't get it to go asyhow." "Can you mend the tube ? " asked Dulcie with interes'. Old-fashioned es she was, and not natur- ally prone to speak with strangers on the road, she ; was too old-fashioned to pass by any person in difficulties at her own gate. She knew that her father would never do such a thing himself, and she was his own daughter. "No; but I always carry a spare one, which I could put in. Only I must wait till the thing is a little cooler before I can make the change, and then it will be too dark for me to drive without lights, and, stupidly enough, I forgot to put fresh candles in my lamps before I started in the morn- ing. Could you tell me whether there is any shed near at hand down this hill where I might put the car for the night? I should see to it better by daylight to-morrow. I an touring about, and could sleep at the village inn; only I should prefer to see the car under cover if possible. I can push it downhill easily enough ; but it would be too heavy to take it uphill like that." "Then," said Dulcie quickly, "if you will open that gate and push it 'a little way down the drive there, it will take you straielit into our stable- yard, and I will ride on and tell the coachman to see it properly housed. My falher will be so much interested to see a motor-car. He cites not believe in thcar one bit. We are very old-fashioned people here. But he will like to see one very much; and it shall be well taken care of." "You are exceedingly kind," said the young Iman, as he hastened to open the gate for her. "It is too good an offer to refuse; but I did not mean I to take advantage of your kindness like this." I "It, is downhill the whole way," said Dulcie, I smiling as she rode past; and putting her horse to a gentle trot, she rode along the road, and after perhaps a quarter of a mile of easy riding she passed through the big gates into the stable-yard. "0 papa, are you trere ? I am so glad!" 'MY darling,- I thought you were rather late out, "fIMO to ask if You had not got home. Is any- innw the matter?"' "Not with me, papa, or with Jack; but just think of:it!—a gentleman with a motor-car was standing by the spinney gate; and something was the matter, and he could not get on: So I asked him to push the car down here; he can run it downhill quite easily. I thought you would like to see it; and I could not go in and leave him in troul le, could I, papa? " "No, no, my dear; certainly not! Bless my soul! a motor-car in my stable-yard! Who would have thought it? Come, we will go and meet him. I always knew they would be no good. Give me a horse and an old-fashioned carriage. Motor-cars indeed!" Dulcie lartelled. She 'sad alighted from her horset and was eager to go forward to meet the stranOr. -They started off up the road, and almost immediately she exclsimed : -0 papa! here he conies! Ire must have mended it after all! See, he is ridine along in it ! How nicely it gees ; and it makes no noise at all!" The car, irvieed, was now rolling smoothly along the road ; but ns a matter of fact it was tiayelling only by its own momentum clown the gentle decline. The motor arns not seerking. Father and daughter watched with much interest as it glidel past them, and brought up neatly in the great yard, where the stablemen crowded out to look at it. The came forward, cap in hand, and was pre- ns Squire Carlingford. _ollie's, lingered a little to hear the first words exchanged, and then slipped indoors, feeling that Perhaps her father would net care for her to re' airs longer. She was much interested in the whole incident, fled she told her maid all about , it as her habit was removed and exchanged for a pretty tea-gown. And it was the girl lrho suddenly exclaimed : ; "Bus to-morrow' s Simm,l my, ma •am I The master su gentleman to mend his sea ont r wons't,inliiikne 9, •m% y.,1 Pulcie had not thought of that ; hilt she saw the d;f11-ulty at once. Sunday at Carlingford Manor was kept as a day of rest for man and beast. The carriage never went out unless oil a real emergency; and it would certainlv fusainst the Sauire's cramn

for any sort of work to be carried on on his Premises on Sunday. "Well, we shall see," said Dulcie, as she prw rtred to go down.. I should have liked to see him mend it and go o in it; but I could not if he did it on Sunday. Para would not like it. I do not think I should quite like it myself." When Dulcie got down to the hall, where the cosy -afternoon tea was always taken, there was the stranger in animated talk with her father; and as she came down to them the Squire said:

"Dukin, my dear, Mr. Talbot will remain oI1? guest until Monday. Ills father and I were old frietr's at Oxford. Will you tell. Mrs. Dobbs bi have a bedroom got ready, and the luggage taken. up ?--it has been brought in from the yard." Dulcie was very please,i, and her eyes s! -sari it. She gave th- gentlomen their tea, and ;1-
a groat deal to Mr. Talbot about his ruotor-ca, and laughed to hear the little passages of arm, between hint and her father.

Mr. Talbot, however, was an ardent lover or horses, and was by n 6 means dispcsed to overre- his "new thy," as he called the car. He Wh' wishful to test • their capacities, as he said ; but his opinion was that it would be a long while before there would he any very great demand tor them. There were so many I hini:s that might go wrong, and the strvin upon them was great.

the same time, when everything is goin,r right, the power of flying along a good empty road on a down grade at perhaps twenty miles an hour is a great delight, Miss Carling,ford. It is not often one can get a road where it is practiemble to put on such a pace; but when you do—well, it is a very delightful experience. Dulcie's cheeks glowed ; she felt she would like to experience it for herself ; but she did not say so, for she felt sure her father would vow that thing would explode and make an end of her, latt she had grown up with a loyal belief in all her father's pet theories. . Very soon she forgot all about the motor-car in the plefrure of entertaining its owner. Rupert Talbot was a singularly attractive man, simple- minded, open-hearted, without vanity and without self-sufficiency. He was not handsome, hut his brown face with its irregular features was full of intelligence and genial humour. He was very young--certainly he would never see five-aud• thirty again—hut he bore himself with elasticity and ease. He bad travelled much and read much; and to listen to him was a keen pleasure to Dulcie. The Squire enjoyed his coe,pany likewise, and the fact of knowing something of his family made a bond at once, which was speelly strengthened. In fact, before the Sunday had ended, it had been settled that Rupert should stay on for a few more days; and Dulcie felt her heart give a sudden bound as she heard of this arrangement. The hounds were to meet upon the Monday, and Rupert was provided with a mount. He laughed at the idea of wasting time over the muter-car when there was hunting in prospect. Dulcie had bunted at her father's side ever since she had h.ain a tiny little maid upon a pony, with a mane of hair flowing behind her. She rode by his side to- day, never afraid to face what he faced, knowing herself perfectly safe with him ; and to-day all the safer that she had Another cavalier as well, in the person of Rupert. His flue horsemanship and eager pleasure in the run delighted the Squire's heart, whilst Dulcie felt as though she had never enjoyed a day's hunting so much in all her life. _ _

In „the evening her father dozed Ozer the fire, whilst she and their guest spent their time over the plain) together. They were both extremely fond of music, and it was always a delight to Dulcie to find somebody who shared her enthusiasm fo' Mozart, Pergolesi and Purcell. Of the modern school of music she knew little, but the oh masters of harmony were like living friends to her. Next day nothing would serve the Squire but that Rupert should have a day amongst his pheasafits. The motor-car again stood neglectetl Dulcie brought lunch to the sportsmen at an appointed time and place; and found that the straight shooting of their new friend had pleased the Squire as much as his fine handling of a horse had done the previous day. "You are one of the old-fashioned sort after all, Talbot," he said, "even though you drive a motor- car!" _

"The old fashion 3 have a great attraction tr me, sir,". answered the young man with a quick, half-unconscious glance towards Dulcie ; and the father's keen eyls saw that glance. For a Moment a quick thrill of pain shot through his heart. To be sure, he had always looked forward to seeing Dulcie suitably married one day, and holding a child of hers upon his knee; but he had never before had occasion to feel that the wrench of parting with his treasure !right be near. Hitherto his little maid had been fancy-free and his very own.

_ _ That evening, as he sat in his big cl.air beside the fire with half-closed eyes, he watched the pair at the piano, and found that sleep did not come to him as usual. He went to bed with his mind preoccupied, and he was more silent than usual at breakfast the next morning. But Dulcie had somebody else to talk to, and did not appear to ,notice this. Her father often had letters that engrossed him on "Board-lay " ; and the carriage always came for him very soon after the close of breakfast.

She put him into his coat and saw him off as usual ; and then with a laughing look she turned to Rupert and cried: • "He will be away all the morning; now can't we go arid see the motor-ear? Do you think he would mind if I had a ride in it?" It was very interesting to Dulcie to see the car brought out, and watch their guest take out the ignition tube and examine it. "Just as I thought," he said; "the porcelain ts cracked. It does happen so sometimes, after beinn• in use a good while. Then there is' a leak, and you get no compression, and cannot drive. I will have the new one in in a lifreY ; and you shall have a new experience, Miss Carlingford. Your roads roaind here are capital; and if we don't frighten your old-fashioned horses .0U shall spin along in 'fine style." Dulcie quite clapped her hands at the thought. She watched the insertiiin of the new tube and the connecting up of the electric wires; and felt quite learned when the course of the current was explained to her, and she had switched the. spark on two or three times, and heard it buzz and crackle, and had been shewn where and how it fired the vapour of the oil through the ignition tube. Then she watched Mr. Talbot do a few mysteriout things with an index handle in front, after whia he turned his wheel again, she switched on thc spark, and the motor went off, with a series of puffs and explosions which seemed to betoken a van, amount of latent energy. "Now, Miss Carlingford, will you take your seat ?—the vibration will be much less as soon as we put it into motion." And Dulcie got up into the ear beside him, whilst the coachman tucked a rug about her, smiling to think of his young lady going out on a motor-car, and asking respectfully if the owner was sure that it would not "bust up.'" "Quite sure," answered Rupert, laughing. "The worst that can happen will be that it will stop, but I don't anticipate any such casualty. Now, Miss Carlingford, are you ready? Now, you see this handle; I turn it so, and that throws on the driving band of the slow speed. There—we have started now, and as soon as we have a little pace on I throw off this band and throw on the fast speed, and then you will feel how we can travel! " A light, tremulous laugh broke from Dulcie's: lips as the little carriage began to 'move, and when, after travelling at a quiet rate for a short distance, the change of the handles was made, and she felt the car gathering momentum, and spring- ing forward with a peculiarly bounding, elastic movement, the laugh lost its tremour and became one of pure delight. '°ooo Mr. Talbot! it feels like to., live thing und— one ! It's not a bit dull and dead and mechanical- It's almost like a horse cantering—only so mac.' smoother and faster! What a pace we do got 0. it is a delightful movement! I wish papa cot;;1, see me now! I wonder if it was good of ap' go without asking leave ?—but I was so aftv'' would say no. Ho always thinks new-fastikaseme things will come to grief.' It was delightful to Rupert to hear this grown maiden of two-and-twenty summers speak in this way of the relations between herself and her fatly r. Her simple, old-fashioned obedience and childlike docility and affection were like the scent of prim- roses and lavender, fragrant, delicate, old-world. The whole atmosphere Of this place bad penetrated him with a sense of content and well-being. Alight .it be his good hap, when the day of his choice came, to find such a won:an for his wife as Dulcie Carl in gford ! The thought leaped into his head as he drove his motor-car along the wide empty roads at a tine dashing pace, and watched the fair face of the eager girl beside him. Her simple pleasure, her ehildlike confidence in his skill and knowledge. her constant references to her father, all charmed hien alike. "It is de-Anious ! " she (tried. "I never thought

he movement could he half so pleasant. Of course, there is nothing like horses in one way ; but to along like this aiid never feel that you are tiring your horse—oh, it i, quite delightful!" So they Cashed alotig mile after mile through the level r 4 ads, ila-kiog and stopping sometimes for the sake of nervous horses; but flying on aegain in gallant style so soon as :the obstruction was over. Sometimes they climbed a hill on the slow 'speed, with a considerable amount of Puffing ; then, almost shutting off all g:ts, they would glide down the other side, with a breathless rapidity that brought Dulcie's soft laugh ringing out again and again. She was loth to turn homewards, but time was getting on, and it would never do for her father to get back and hear that she had gone out in the motor-car. He would be certain to think that something had happened. • So round they turned, and set off towards the Manor House; and suddenly, after they had travelled some miles, Dulcie shaded her eyes with her band and looked along the road, exclaiming

"Why, I do declare- there is papa coming driving along after us! Oh ! how he is urging the horFes! Can anything be the matter? That is our ca,rilge coming to meet us. Perhaps he has come t, see how the car travels." _

The motor spinning in one direction and the carriage in another soon came to close quarters. "I think we had better stop," said Dulcie. "The horseA will be frightened; they have never seen such a ,bing before." Rupert threw off the band and brought the carriage to a standstill, letting the motor run gently the while. _ _
"I will get out and speak to your father," he said, "and see if be wants anything. Perhaps he is afraid fer you, and has come to drive you home in his carria(.:e." _ _

"Oh, but please ask if I may not go home in the motor-car. I ran drive in a carriage any day; and this is so dt llghtful!" Rupert laughed and walked rapidly forward to the spot where the carriage had drawn up, at a little distance from the motor-car, the Squire look- ing very red and heated; the groom at the heads of the horses, tiyint,o to soothe their nervousness at the sight and sound of the throbbing vehicle in the road beyond them. upert swung himself up beside the Squira, whose face was a study of conflicting emotions, and who seemed to have been passing through some considerable mental disturbance. Rupert spoke of their morning's pleasuring, and Dulcie's desire to finish her jaunt upon the car ; when the Squire suddenly burst out: "Ti en you are not running away with my little girl ?" "I don't understand you, sir. I have taken her for a spin--" "Yes, yes; I have nothing to say to that. What I heard %%as that you were running away with her for good and all. A neiEthbour of mine declared she saw you, and was certain it was an elopement. I beg your pardon if I have misjudged you. Per- haps 1 am an old fool where my daughter is con- ce:ned ; but what with all these new-fangled wachines, and these new-fashioned ways—what is an old-fashioned father to think? " _ _ _

„._ Rupert suddenly threw back his head and broke into a laugh ; and then as suddenly grew grave a Air. He held out his hand to the Squire. "Sir,” lie said, "I have seen something of the nf w-flishioned ways of the world, as well as the o'd. I don't lay that all of them are bad. Yet the old have a charm for me which the new have never possess: d. And I give you my word of ho flour that when the day conies that I ask &woman to I e my wife I will follow the old-fashioned cus'ona, and ask leave of her father first. On that understanding, will you let me drive your sweet Dulcie home ;gain ? " The Squire gripped the young man's band hard. Not a word more passed between them. Rupert joined Dn'cie on the car, and after a little coaxing they got it past the snorting horses, and were flying along the rial again, whilst the Squire followed in his carriage. "We have left them quite, quite behind!" cried Dulrie, who kept looking Over her shoulder. "Of course, no horses could go this pace ! " she laughed, and Rupert laughed at her spontaneous enjoyment; but after a few more miles, as they were nearing home, she said quite seriously : "Mr. Talbot, do you think you could manage for something to go wrong, so that, papa might overtake us with his horses and pass us? I think it would please him so very Much. He is very proud of Robin Hood and Little John." Rupert laughed at the notion. "I'll tell you what we might do. One of the accumulators is almost empty; if we changed to that the car would go no .ace at all, and perhaps come to a stop altogether. We're driving on I lie new one now; but, if you don't mind getting out. I'll put on the other, and we shall soon be passed." Dulcie laughed gleefully, and got out whilst the cushion under her seat was lifted and the change made. Then they got in again, and she soon felt. the difference. There was a dragging motion; the motor seemed not able to fly along as before. It went unevenly, and her companion explained that it, was missing fire from the exhausted state of the battery. Sometimes the motor threatened to stop altogether; and Dulcie laughed and clapped her hands as presently there hove in sight the carriage drawn by her father's favourite horses; and just before they reached them the spark missed alto • gether, and the motor stopped dead. Rupert laughingly got down, and the Squire drove past them with a flourish of the whip.. "Nothing like the old-fashioned carriages after all!" he cried. "Dulcie, my dear, shall I take you home ? "

In the gay ,-;pringtide there was an old-fashioned wedding from the old Manor House; and Dulcie made the most charming of brides. The only thing which was not old-fashioned about it was that the bric1,...1 pair started for their honeyino,3n trip upon a liltle motor-car. [Tus Elm.]

Councillor I.Nuttall, of Bury, who has used the path for 40 year.- I • • : said the reservoir district was their Blackpool.

div.head: aIiENTS OF THE WEEK.
div.p: aIiENTS OF THE WEEK.
I GREAT BRITIAN AND RUSSIA

• Suddenly last ,week the relations between England and Russia became stretched almost to snapping point, and it was only the com- 'Vete climb down of the latter which saved -what would have 'been a great European war. It was due to the seizure of the P. and 0. 'liner, the "Malacca," in the Red Sea by 'Russian cruisers on the ground that she :was .carrying contraband of war to the Far East. The British flag was torn down and the Russian flag hoisted in its place, a prize crew being put on board with orders to take the " Malacca " to Libau for 'the sitting of a prize court. The British Government did mot hesitate, and an unmistakable message was despatched to St. Petersburg, which gave the Tsar and his Ministers to understand that 'the " Malacca " would not be allowed to reach a Russian port, whatever might, be entailed. Our Ambassador, Sir Charles Hardinge, was instructed directly from home, .and the Cabinet met several times to consult

div.head: SIR CHARLES HARDINGE
div.p: SIR CHARLES HARDINGE

on the situation, and Lord Lansdowne was -summoned in person to Buckingham Palace. The sudden situation was grappled with in the finnest manner, • and it will greatly add to the popularity of Mr. Balfour's Govern- ment that they showed such promptness in a 'question of British prestige. To begin with, 'the presence of the Russian cruisers, " Peters- burg" and "Smolensk," which had passed - through the Dardanelles -recently•as merchant- men, was a distinct breach of the treaty of Paris. In answer, the Mediterranean Squad-' • ron was mobilised under Sir Compton Dorn- -vile. The result after -a day or two of !-uncertainty, was - that all British demands were ceded by the Russians, who again hoisted the British flag on the "Malacca." The incident was short and sharp, but the :result cannot fail to be healthy.

div.head: RELEASE OF MRS. MAYBRICK.
div.p: RELEASE OF MRS. MAYBRICK.

The greatest interest has been shown by he public in the release of Mrs. Maybrick, who fiiteen years ago was sentenced to death for poisoning her husband. The sentence was commuted by Lord Liandaff, then Mr. :Matthews and Flume Secretary, to one of penal servitude for life, which entails fifteen years. pf exem- plary conduct in a convict pri- son. Never be- fore has a case taken such a strong hold on the public ima- gination, and ever since the arrest of Flor- ence Maybrick in May, .1889, the question of her guilt or in- nocence has been hotly de- bated. After the trial at the Liverpool Sum-
61RS.
MAY

mer Assizes of the same year leeling ran very high, and Mr. Justice Ste- phen, who tried the case, was actually stoned as he drove from the Court. Since then there -has been a continuous agitation in England -and'the States for her release, headed by the late Lord Chief Justice, Lord Russell Of Ku- lowan, who, as Sir Charles Russell, had de- fended hr. However, the various) Home Secretaries of the last decade and a half have found no reason to alter the verdict. The great ”oint at issue is the question .whether James Maybrick was ever poisoned at all, and on that hangs the whole matter. Last January Mrs. Maybrick was released from Aylesbury Prison and sent to the Home of the Sisterhood of the Epiphany at Truro, where she passed the few months prior to her release. Last week her official release came, and she was allowed to go free. Avoid- ing Truro, she drove with two lady friends to 'St. Austell, which she left by the 12.14 train. She left the train mysteriously en route for Paddington, and is now on her way to America. The whole of the case is likely to be reopened, and the agitation for a free par- don grows daily.
PIER BURNT DOWN

Southsea's South Parade Pier has been lotally destroyed ' by fire, the result it is stated of a carelessly thrown match. Hap- pily no lives were lost, nor was anybody hurt. A concert was in progress when the alarm was raised, but luckily the audience was a small one and was able to escape Without a panic occurring. Crowds of yisi- • tors were idling dreamily on the beach when .attention was attracted to a little cloud of smoke on the east side of the pier, which in 'a few minutes, fanned by a strong easterly 'breeze, developed into a burning mass. -Alarms were sent to. Portsmouth and else- :W.here, and efforts were directed by many :Willing hands to rescue the few scor'e of People on the pier, some of them being .`unconscious, of the danger. Within less than .an hour the picturesque pavilion had been "completely demolished, and the promenade
SOUTHSEA PIER ABLAZE.

as nothing but a mass of twisted iron-work. •Disht for the timely rescue by some coast- guardsmen two persons, would have lost their lives. One, a pier porter, who had ‘vurked from an inadequate hydrant up to ,}le last moment, found his escape cut off. L.Vith him was a visitor, who had assisted efforts. They made frantic signals to e coastguards 'on *shore and • fortunately Z‘t,teceeded in attracting attention. So intense the heat that a wide detour had to ue made before the pier head could be leached. Thousands of visitors and residents cheered the coastguards as they vanded the plucky fire-fighters. The property as insured but not fully. The pier, which
was soo feet, was thirty-five years old, but pf recent years has been practically recoil. gructed.

div.head: DEATH OF A FAMOUS ACTOR
div.p: DEATH OF A FAMOUS ACTOR

The news of the death of Mr. Wilson Barrett, the famous actor, at the end of last week came as a shock and a surprise to his many admirers. Recently he had been suffering from intestinal trouble, which was diagnosed by the doctors as cancer, and an immediate operation was ordered. So Mr. Wilson Barrett went into a nursing home in Devonshire Street, London, and Sir Victor Horsley, the famous surgeon, operated at once, but his constitution would not stand the strain, and he sank under it. So young did he appear upon the stage that it is difficult to believe that the famous actor was fifty-eight, and withal he had had a most strenuous life. He never knew what it was to be idle for a moment, and his one recreation was a change of work. He would, as often as not, write, produce, and manage his own plays, as well as play the principal part, and he was as indefatigable in failure as in success. Mr. Wilson Barrett came of

Essex yeoman stock, which knew little of tilt. theatre, but early he -branched out for him- self, playing small parts for still smaller salaries till he established himself as king of melodrama and made his place in the fore- front of managers. He played in his time in every sort of part, and discovered many new men, such as Mr. G. R. Sims, who furnished him with "The Lights of London," and Mr. Henry Arthur Jones, who, as a member of his company, wrote "The Silver King." Mr. James Welch and Mr. 'Richard le Gallienne were others of his discoveries, but his most colossal success of all was "The Sign of the Cross," the great religious melodrama, wih is still fresh in everybody's mind. Mr. Wilson Barrett was, indeed, a many-sided man, whose place it will b 3 impossible to filL

div.head: UNION JACK CLUB.
div.p: UNION JACK CLUB.

That the Prince of Wales takes kzen interest in our soldiers and sailors has been amply shown on many occasions, and once More it look tangible form by his laying the foundation stone of the Union Jack Club. The Prince, who was accompanied. by the Princess of Wales, received a most enthusi- astic reception, vast crowds in Waterloo Road where the club is to be situated wait- ing many hours to give their Royal High- nesses a welcome. The club in question is to be a national tribute to the troops who fell in the South African war, and as its primary object will have the provision of temporary accommodation for soldiers and sailors pas-Ang through London. Nearly 200,000 soldiets and sailors and marines leave or arrive at Water- loo Station every year. It is being designed as a social and residential centre for these
ME UNION JACK CLUB AS IT WILL APPEAR W,IEN
COMPLETED.

wandering men in uniform. It is the inten- tion to provide more than 300 bedrooms— some of these have been endowed by towns, ships, and regiments. In addition there Will be lockers for kits, safes for depositing valuables and money, as also dining rooms, smoking rooms, reading and writing ropms, library, billiard rooms, and large central hall; where the members of the Services may meet freely. Over £60,000 will be required to carry out this programme, and of this sum more than 03,000 have already been pro- vided. Prominent among those present at tile foundation stone laying were Earl Roberts' and Lady Aileen Roberts, Sir Evelyn Wood and Captain Wood, Admiral Freemantle, Major-General and Mrs. Douglas, Earl Fitz- william, Captain and Mrs. Arthur Lee, and Sir G. Arthur. Replying to an address of welcome, the Prince said The creation in London of this club, as a national tribute to the memory of the sailors, soldiers, and marines who fought and died in the service of the country, has a special significance, for it testifies to the sympathy between the public generally and the services; and I ven- -ture to think that everything which is done to foster this feeling is not only of benefit to the services themselves, but to the State. This institution will I hope, stand as a lasting testimonial to the sentiments of grateful admiration which were aroused throughout the country by the gallant deeds of soldiers and sailors during the South African campaign." After the stone had been laid a long succession of ladies, gentle- men, and children ascended the platform and presented purses to the Princess in fur. therance of the club.

div.head: KING AND A CRIMEAN HERO,
div.p: THE KING AND A CRIMEAN HERO,

A popular action on the King's. part was his decision to select Sergeant J. Nunnerley, late of the 17th Lancers and one of the famous Light Brigade in the Crimea, for a special medal for meritorious services and an annuity as "a reward for his long and highly meritorious service, includ- ing the Crimean war," to quote the Gazette. This veteran is one of the few survivors of the "Death or Glory B y s," who wen t into action at Balaclavat4s strong and only mustered 3 5 after the charge ; and during the action he was most COD spicous for his gallantry He passed un-
SERGEANT NUNNERLEY.

scathed through theßussian fire; but when nearly up to the Rus- sian guns his horse was- shot under him. He proceeded on foot, cutting his way through the Russian Cavalry, till he was knocked down by a runaway horse. Regain- ing his feet he assisted in the rescue of three of the 13th Light Dragoons, one after the other; and then, capturing a stray horse, he remounted and galloped on up the valley. Sergeant Nunnerley, who had two brothers in the Crimea, is a fine upstanding old veteran, over six feet in height, and every inch a gallant old soldier. Such is the man who the king has delighted to, honour.

div.head: Local Magistrates and a Conscientious Objector.
div.p: Local Magistrates and a Conscientious Ob- jector.

At the Borough Police Court on Monday, Alfred Lawrenson, Old-road, Latchford, applied for a certi- ficate exempting his child from vaccination—lmme- diately the application was announced, the Mayor Messrs. Hayward and W. Roberts retired from the bench.--The applicant stated that another of his chil- dren had suffered illness through vaccination— Alderman Sutton put several questions tot the applicant and concluded by remarking "-I have nothing to say in the matter. It is altogether at mis- take in my opinion. You gentlemen can do as you like."—The alderman was about to leave the bench when Mr. Birchall said it seemed to him that' the magistrates were there to administer the law, and: not to criticise it. The legislature said that if there was a conscientious objection, the exemption must be granted. Mr. Balfour himself said the justices ought not to argue the question.—Alderman Sutton : lam not going to administer the law. The alderman then withdrew, and Mr. Pilling followed suit. The certifi- cate was granted by Mr. 13irchall and CouncillOr Thornton.

div.head: MEDICAL STIFF.
div.p: THE MEDICAL STIFF.

Dr. W. E. Barton, of Frodsham, reporte,l that his work was being done for the next three weeks by Dr. Pearson, of Glasgow. A letter was read from Dr. MacDougall conforming to the wish of th 9 Guardians that he should supply the name of his locum tenens when taking his holidays.
IMPORTANT RECOMMENDATIONS. OUT-RELIEF AND DISFRANCHISEMENT. THE MAINTENAvCE OF BOYS ON TRAINING SHIPS,

Mr. E. W. 4:4 den, ierk to the Prestwich Union, forwarded copies ot resolutions pissed by his Baird to the effect that training-ships should be utilized for training pauper boys, and that grants should be made from the national exchequer towards their maintenance; also that a person who has received for himself or family out-relief for a p3riod not exceeding thraa months should not be disqualified from voting at-Parlia- mentary, municipal or other elections. The Runcorn Board were asked to adopt the resolutions. The Acting Clerk said a similar recotumendation in regard to disqualification from voting was before the Board a short time ago, but they took no action in the matter.

Mr. Smith inove3 that the Boaid support the resolu- tion in regard to training ships. Mtl. Hallows seconded. It was for the country's good that lads were sent to the ships and the national exchequer ought to contribute to the cost. Admiral Jones Parry: I think the national exchequer does very largely help the ships. The Acting Clerk pointed out that the Board paid is. per week for the maintenance of boys on the "Inde- fatigable," in a,dditioa to giving a sum of about £5 or £7 for the sea oaths. The Government did not make any grants to Boards of Guardians, but they might assist the ships in other ways. Admiral Parry said the reason the ships helped the country very little was that many children were taken away from them when they reached their sixteenth year. Mr. Collier moved an amendment that both matters be referred to the Parliamentary Committee.
Mr. Piling seconded and the amendment was carried. ADMIRAL PARRY AND THE DISTRICT MEDICAL
OFFICERS.

Admiral Piirry moved that in future the appointments of District Medical Officers should be made annually. He expressed his disapproval of the present system of deductirp, 2 per cent, from the doctors' salaries each year in order to give them superannuation when they reached a certain age. In his opinion.it was an absurdity. The salaries paid were very large, the average, with vaccination fees, being £2OO. The whole of the salaries he thought, were excessive. When medical officers were appointed in future, the Board should make an agree- ment that there should be no deductions from the salaries and no superannuation. The Acting Clerk said that if the resolution were passed it could not be given effect to. The Local Government Board would not sanction an appointment for twelve months. They stated distinctly in their orders that the appointment must be permanent. In the matter of superannuation the Guardians could not help themselves, as that was another condition under which the officers were engaged. There was no seconder to the motion, which fell to the . ground _ _ _

Acimiral Parry had given notiee of another ma tion that the salary of Dr. Bower, the medical officer for the Budworth district, be reduced from £lOO to RSO. He disclaimed any personal motive for selecting Dr. Bower. His only reasons were that Dr. Bower was the last medical officer. appointed • he had the highest salary ; and had charge of the district to which he (Admiral Parry) belonged. He was willing to withdraw the motion, if it would hurt anyone's feelings. He suggested that a committee should inquire Into the whole question of the doctors' salaries. Mr.Roylance thought Admiral Parry had acted wisely in withdrawing the motion. Dr. Bower had to attend to twenty-one townships, and he (Mr. Roylance) was going to more that the salary be advanced by £5. Admiral Parry (ironically) : I'll second that.
Mr. Roylance thereupon pressed for his motion to be put, but the chairman told him that such a proposition could not be brought forward without notice.
THE COST OF NEW SCHOOLS.

Mr. 3.17. Collier moved that the Co-unty Council be requested to reconsider the!proportion payable!by them towards the building of provided schools add that when fixing this sum they take into consideration the current rate and rateable value of the Parish in which such schools are to be erected. Mr. Collier pointed out that when the Act was pftssed the County Council announced their intention of contributinr, half of the cost of new school, the parish in *lnc% the buildings were erected to pay the other half. About a month ago, the authority passed a resolutiori that they would only: pay one third. It was rather hard that the Council should make this rule, regardless of the needs of individual parishes. In many districts considerdblet suits had been expended on improvements and the rates 'wet° very high. He contended that in such parishes the County Connell should pay one half. In parishes where the rateable value was high and the rates were low. the County Council should pay the minimum sum and the township the maximum.
Mr. Wright seconded and the motion was carried. THE NURSING ACCOMMODATION AT THE WORKHOUSE.

Mr. Cunnah, master, wrote te/;(; di;;;:k, pointing out that the half-yearly report of the Medical Officer drew attention to the fact that the nurses' accommodation and lying-in wards required attention. Tn a further letter Mr. Cunnah stated that on the 2nd February resolations were passed that additional accommodation was required in bath wards and that a scheme of exten- sion shonl be prepared.—The resolutions were sub- mitted to the Board but were deferred until the elec- tions were over.
The Acting Clrk said. the subjerls were again considered by the Ffonso Committee on the 12th inst., and it was suggested that they should be brought before the Board. . .
Mr. Roylance thought the quarters fdid not require improvement vet, Nit better provision should be made for the nurses. There ought to be a separate build- ing for their accommodation.
It was decided to consider the matter at a sTtocial meeting of the House Committee, which' consists of the whole of the menf-ers of the Board.

The last anniversary to beheld at Warrington in con- nection with the Clergy Daughters' School and the Clergy Widows and Orphans' Fund—two institutions connected with the dioceses of Manchester, Liverpool and Chester—was observed on Wednesday. Mr. Reginald Bushell, of Neston, presided at a meet- ing of subscribers, held in the morning. Amongst those present were : —The Bishop of Chester, the Dean of Manchester, Archdeacon Wilson, the Rev. Canon Willis, the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, Mr. W. P. k'ullagher, Mr. R. H. Joynson, Mr. J. D. Buckton and others. A telegram was read from the Bishop of Manchester regretting his inability to be present. THE COMMITTEE'S REPORT. I SCARLET FEVER BRINGS ABOUT A CRISIS. The Rev. CANON Maass read the report of the Com- mittee of Management of the Clergy Daughters' School which stated that the past year has been a momentous one in the school's course; perhaps the most momentous in the 60 years since it was founded in 1841. On the 116th September the pupils reassembled after the summer I vacation in large numbers and, apparently, in perfect health, but they had hardly settled down to their duties when a serious outbreak of scarlet fever attacked 15 scholars and one mistress. On the 7th October it was decided to close the school,and later on to carry on the work by correspondence till the end of the term. The committee took once more into serious consideration the question of the removal of the school which had been ,for some time contemplated, and appointed a sub-com- mittee for the selection of sites. On January 6th, after a thorough investigation and purification of the premises, , the school was re-opened, but ten weeks after, on March 'lsth another slight outbreak took place which brought matters to a crisis, the headmistress' in her report, to the committee on the 23rd declaring her- self unable to undertake the responsibility of conductine the school at Warringtan after the summer and a deputation of the parents who attended the meet- ing, urgently requested that the school might be immediately removed. The committee promised the most careful attention, and on the 22nd April held a special meeting at which the offer of a house and grounds in Derbyshire, providing accommodation for over 100 girls, was submitted for consideration. General approval was manifested, and special meetings of great importance were called—the first of the trustees, the second of the General Committee, and the third of the subscribers, at which it was definitely decided to accept ; (1) the offer of the Darley Dale hydro, near Matlock, ' along with 50 acres of land, for £12,500, as the house itself was in excellent repair though one wing was ; unfinished, and it was known that it would require con- siderable outlay to complete and adapt it for school purposes ; (2), to remove the school thither during the '• summer holidays; (3) to admit a certain number of the i daughters of the laity provided that adequate pecuniary !advantages were secured to the daughters of the clergy. 1 The Council ealmestly hoped that the endowments and subscriptions would enable them to take the aame ; number of daughters of clergy on reduced terms as ! hitherto, and would suggest that, as in the case of the i Powys and Greenall scholarships, certain of the major and minor bursaries be named after the donors of such I sums as were considered sufficient to qualify. On the ! 4th July tenders to the amount of £2,024 were accepted I and an appeal issued for £2,500 to cover the cost of the removal, alterations, incidental expenses in addition to the £12,500 already required for the purchase of the ! estate. A sum of £15,000 is thus shown to be needed, towards which gifts and promises have been received to the extenfof £2,400 leaving nearly £13,000 still to be raised.
