stances." This means, of course, that all circum- stances are exceptional for Russia. Admiral SKRYDLOFF cannot spare men to form prize crews and he cannot spare the time to examine neutral cargoes ; so he gives the crew of a British steamer en minutes to save their lives and then sends ship and cargo to the bottom. This exceptional be- haviour may seem all right to Count LAMSDORFF, who is apprehensive of another row with his Grand Dukes; but to Mr. BALFOUR, speaking after a consultation with the Defence Committee and the Attorney-General, it is conduct which involves "a breach of international law."

This statement maybe embarassing to Count LAMSDORFF, who, whether he accepts it or not, has no control whatever over Admiral SKRYDLOFF. The country has to face all the facts, and it is no use telling us, as our cautious friend does, that "we shall be wise not to Complicate the questions arising out of the Malacca by any irritation at these new incidents." One breach of internatior_al law follows another, but we are not to heed them. The Russian admiral is at sea for the manifest purpose of creating these new incidents, but we are not ro think about him. Moreover, we are warned that " it is not our policy, as the supreme naval Power, to take any line which would unduly limic the right of search, for the running of con- traband cargoes is so much the practice of all neutrals in all wars that it can only be checked by arming the belligerents with sufficient powers of seareh and seizure."

Well, they are already armed with all the necessary powers. They can seize suspected vessels and hale them before a Prize Court. If the belligerent cruisers were properly qualified for this work, nobody wants to quarrel with them. But is it actually contended that we ought to sanction the sinking of neutra ships without any examination or adjudication whatever, because we may want to do the same thing ourselves when we chance to be at war. If so, this astonishing argument is taratamount with saying, " Pnrish international law,for we may have to trample on it when the time comes !!' All we ask is that the right of searching should be exer- cised with decency and not with desperation. The idea of taking Admiral SKR,YDLOFF in his "ex- ceptional circumstances" as a model of propriety for British naval commanders in some maritime war yet to come will not appeal, we fancy to the good sense of the public.

A correspondent of ours, one " Ppliticus," has set the Inquisition in operation, by which he dares to and does put a number of pertinent questions for our sublime editorial consideration. The point at issue is toe representation of Warrington—and what 4 bone of contention it is ! Friend " Politi- cus " espouses the Labour cause in one breath and disavows membership of the Labour party in the next. He is therefore a somewhat uncertain quantity—probably of little assistance to Labour and no menace to Liberalism. But he wants to know why we desire a compromise ?" In order that Mr. Crosfield may be more certain of getting in. That is why, clear " Politicus. We are not afraid of being candid, and we have made no secret of our aim. " Politicus " appears to have considered this our ulterior motive while offering the hand of friendship to Labour. It was cer- tainly the motive, but not ulterior, and no special acumen was necessary to discover it. A party compact between Liberal at.d Labour we have not suggested. Anything of the kind is impracticable under existing conditions, but a prevailing spirit of sweet reasonableness would be advantageoas to• both sides in our opinion. The Labour party cannot carry its own candidate to the head of the poll, and by making a futile effort at this juncture the interests of the workers would be backwarded to a deplorable ex- tent. Now the Labour party does not hold a monopoly of consideration for the workingman by any means. There are Liberals who would do more for the democracy than any L R.C. candi- date with his arbitrary principles, and we believe Mr. Crosfield to be a Liberal of this type. The fact that he is to some extent a capitalist is an advantage, for without capital,even Labour can do nothing. Let theLabour party conspire to throw Mr. Crosfield, and Tory mis-representation will receive another lease of harmful existence in War- rington. Is there a single Labour man who desires Mr. Pierpoint to once again enter West- minster as M.P. for Warrington? We trow not, if he considers his own and his fellow workers' welfare. The return of the present member is the first thing to be prevented in the interest of Labour, and this object can only be obtained by the election of .11r. Crosfield. rhen, if the latter forsakes the workingman let us have a working- man, Labour, or Socialist candidate by all means. Here, friend " Politicos " you have the editorial view in a nutshell. Does it suffice ?

'When we announced last week that the inquiry was closed we were under the natural impression that it had been closed by the unanimous vote of the six commissioners by which it was conducted. This,we now regret to find, was not the case. The inquiry was brought to a summary conclusion on Thursday last week, by the simple process of putting the matter to the vote, and as there were only two of the Non-. Trading representatives present, the motion was carried despite their ineffectual protests. A letter, which we publish in another column expresses some of the indignation felt by Mr. Norbury Williams, the involuntary absentee on this important occasion. Obviously, had he been present, the inquiry could not have been closed when it was, and it savours somewhat of sharp practice for the Corporation Commissioners to exercise thus arbitrarily their accidental possession of a majority. We very seriously question their right by a majority, to apply the closure. The inquiry was a joint investigation by differently appointed commissioners, and it should only have been closed when both sides were agreed that the appointed task was done. That the nominees of the Corporation should take it upon themselves to cry halt to the investigation is a feature of the proceedings not likely to leave the best impres- sion upon the public.

Messrs. Birchall, Greeniug and Jolley are evidently anxious to be rid it the inquiry at the earliest possible moment, for ILI idition to apply- ing the closure with truly Baltourian riv.,,our,they have this week issued their report on the result of their eleven months' sittings. His Worship the Mayor, has, probably with the best intentions, given this report the publicity of the press, and it will be found verbatim in another column. We are sorry to have to find fault again here, but it appears to us that the wisest and fairest course would have been to hold back the report until the findings of the other three commission- ers were ready,and then to have issued the two reports conjointly for the consideration of the ratepayers. Though the Corporation Commis- sioners say "there is no evidence of an improper influence having been used to secure contracts or sub-contracts," and "nothing to support the allegations of corruption," we must ask our readers to suspend their judgment. until they have heard both sides of the case. This same report gives the names of a large number of aldermen and councill ors who are or who have been shareholders or officials of limited companies trading with the Corporation, and also a list of the companies themselves with the extent of their trading during the specified period. Some of the figuees may be instructive, but the majority are worthless, seeing ,that no use- ful deduction can be drawn from them. Appen-

dices C and D set forth what the ccm- missioners term " a few transactions of a questionable nature." They are also described as " relatively unimportant," but they name the late Alderman Shaw Green for having a direct interest, and Aldermen Francomb, Heaton, Smethurst, and Sutton an indirect interest, 'in transactions with the Corporation which appear to have been irregular." Nothing is said about the propriety or cixtent of the trad- ing by individual members of the Council with the Corporation through limited companies, though it was at the abuse of this very thing that the agitat- ion directly aimed. Presumably we shall have to wait until the Non-Trading Commissioners have reported before this point is adequately dealt with. It can only be by a comparison of the two reports that the public will be enabled to form a sound judgment on the matters forming the basis of inquiry. • =VS" •

With regard to the minutes of the proceedings at the fifty-six sittings of the inquiry,we under- stand that the Town ooun3il will have to decifle whether these are to be printed and circulated. They make a very bulky volume, but we think a sufficient number should be printed to supply the demand of those ratepayers who desire a copy. If necessary a small charge per volume might tie made. In any case there should be some means of giving the public ready access to the minutes of the proceedings of an inquiry for which they have got to pay—and pay heavily too.

Speaking in the important capacity of Chairtnan of Parr's Bank, Ltd., Mr. Cecil F. Parr delivered a speech of more than usual interest at the meet- ing of shareholders held at Warrington on Thurs- day. He did pot confine himself to matters relat- ing exclusively to the bank, but took a wide view of financial matters generally, and called attention to some tendencies of our national life which require careful thought. The decline in bank deposits gave him an opportuuity of showing that the country is much poorer than has been the case for some time past. Toe savings bank and friendly society returns both show a distinct fall- ing off. Whilst holding the opinion that less work and less wages are largely accountable for this, Mr. Parr puts his finger on two growin4 evils when he points out as contributory causes" the great and growing prevalence of betting amongst the lalaouring classes," and "stock exchange gambling amongst classes above them." it is not often that chairmsts of banking companies refer to the evil tendencies of modern life, but few will be prepared to deny that the betting and gambling .evils are unhealthy signs of the time. Iu is difficult to say how much they are responsible for the decline in bank deposits, but Mr. Parr is in an exceptional position to know, and there are grounds for believing that they are important factors in contributing to the present unsatis- factory position. Mr. Parr had also a word of warning to utter to municipalities who are bidding for deposits by the oiler of a high rate of interest. Such competition with bankers he considers "unwise and unfair," and if it continued, he ex- pressed the opinion that bankers might be obliged to take some concerted action for their own protection.

Warrington will know the Clergy Daughters' School no more. The last anniversary was held in the town on Wednesday and the students will commence the next term at Darley Dale, where a hydropathic establishment has been transformed into school premises for them. Warrington, which his been the home of the institatiou for over 60 years was parted with on Wednesday witlmat even an expression of regret. in fact, the recent outbreaks of scarlet fever which have brought about the decision to remove the school to Darley Dale were almost welcomed, because, in the words of the Bishop of Chester, "they had enabled the committee to triumph over the obstruction and artifices of those woo would not have consented to a removal to Darley Dale by any less forcible argument." For many years there has • been a disposition amongst some members of the committee to take the first favbur- able opportunity of moving the school. Unfor- tunately for Warrington that opportunity has come about in a totally unexpected manner. The only origin for the scarlet fever outbreaks which can be suggested by the Medical Officer of Health, who has carefully inquired into the matter is that one of the girls acted as a " carrier " case, bringing the infection from home, or some source of infection outside town, with her. There is nc. reason to believe that the outbreak was due to the "atmosphere " of Warrington, which is a subject on which some outsiders have formed a wrong impression. Tao removal of the school will b 3 regretted by all well- wishers of Warrington, but there will be no one so ungracious as not to wish for Sc. Elphin's a happy Pleura in its new home. • 'vyyj

Apart from financial considerations, it is unpleasant to rfieect that increased pauperism in Warrington should render the existing Workhouse a icommodation inadequate. It may appear to some that the Guardians have of late years spent too freely on buildings, and the announcement that a further extension. has been decided upon will, to say the least of it, be unwelcome. Stilt the tact has to be faced that the number of inmates has for along time been steadily increasing, anA last winter the House was seriously overcrowded. Judging from the details presented to the Board, the congestion cannot unfortunately be wholly attributable to temporary trade depression. The point was emphasized that the increase was mainly in the sick,infirm and aged classes. The spacious Infirmary has been filled to overflowing, for owing to lack of room elsewhere inmates who did not require skilled attendance have had to be accommodated there. The new building will be intermediate in character between the Infirmary and Workhouse proper, and will be arranged for the reception of at least one hundred aged and infirm inmates. Looking at the whole of the cir- cumstances, the Board appear to have been justi- fied in their course of action, and ratepayers may derive some comfort from the injunction that the structure is to be of "as inexpensive a nature as possible."

M. de Plehve is the lastest victim of Russian Nihilism—or should one say of the Russian system of government? The dead Minister has met his end at the hands of those whom in life he did his best to suppress. M. de Plehve became Minister of the Interior through the assassination of M. Sipiagnine, his predecessor in the post, and. ever since his appointment he has been conspicuous by the severity of his rule and the ruthlessness with which he pursued the conspirators with whom Russian political life teems. His death, by the , explosion of a bornt), is the revenge of those against whom he contended; but it is not merely the demonstration of a personal feud. The dead Minister is sacrificed to a system, for which in part, perhaps he was responsible; and his death, coming closely on that of General Bobrikoff, indi- cates how deeply Russia is stirred by th..l revolu- tionary forcer, within her at this moment. M. de Plehve's influence was strong in the Government, and was thrown on the side of the most reactionary forces. The bomb at the Warsaw railway station means more than the death of one powerful Minister.

JULY 1904.

The Malacca is at "EXCEPTIONAL Algiers, and there is no CIRCUMSTANCES." reason why her rnlease should be delayed. Her sister ship, the Formosa, taken into Suez by a Russian prize crew, was released with a prompti- tude which suggests that Russia is no longer dis- posed to uphold the seizures in the Red Sea. But the fact remains that they still continue, and, for aught we know to the contrary, this is the outcome of the struggle between the Russian Admiralty and the Russian Foreign Office. The Grand Dukes may have refused to cancel their instructions to the commanders of their privateers, though Count LAMSDORFF has ordered the prizes to be given up as soon as they put into port. This may seem to be a caricature; but the chaos which passes by the name of a Government at St, Petersburg is capable of anything. Long experience has shown that it is foolish to trust any assurances from that quarter, and history is simply repeating itself. Conces- sions which may be made one day to reason and good faith may be revoked the next day. What is the Russian official attitude towards the incident of the Knight Commander?

We are told by one cautious commentator on these puzzles that the sinking of the Knight Com- mander " cannot be referred to any deliberate in- structions on the part of the Russian Govern- ment." How does he know that? Who can tell what instructions were given by the Grand Dukes to Admiral SIiftYDLOFF before he started on his new adventure? It is reported that in the opinion of the Russian Foreign Office the sinking of Reutral ships is justifiable " under exceptional circum-

Trip to Chester. On Monday, the members of St. Peter's Church _mothers' meeting had their annual trip to Chester. They left the schoolroom in waggonettes at about 8.30, reaching Chester about one o'clock, after a delightful drive. The party then dispersed, some visiting the cathedral, and some Sailing up the Dee. A substantial tea was provided at four o'clock. The weather was all that could be desired until five o'clock, when rain fell heavily. The homeward Journey was commenced at six p.m., and, although the rain was incessant until the party reached Prodsham, it did not seem at all to mar the mothers' enjoyment. The party were accompanied by the Vicar, Mrs. Percival, Mrs. Bamforth, and many other Iriends.

Fire at the Borax Works. At four o'clock on Sunday afternoon, information - was received by telephone at the Warrington Fire • Station that a fire had broken out on the premises of -the Borax Company, Ltd , Chester-road. The brigade turned out in charge of Superintendent Turner with a steam engine, and on arrival it was found that the premises at the north end of the works over the boiler house were on fire. The structure was built of wood and corrugated iron. Three powerful jets were soon 20t to work, there being a plentiful supply of water. The firemen worked well and prevented the fire spread- mg, and after an hour's work the flames were extin- x guished. The boiler house, laboratory, and sheds, over the salt pan house were destroyed. Fortunately the damage, which is heavy, is covered by insurance. The brigade were complimented by Mr. Fleming, the .manager, upon their smart work.

div.head: • The Proposed West Lancashire Cricket League.
div.p: • The Proposed West Lancashire Cricket League.

There was a meeting at the Patten Arms Hotel on Tuesday evening of representatives of the various clubs who intend forming a West Lancashire Cricket League next season. Widnes notified that they with- drew from the league, the laxity of support given to the summer sport in Widnes necessitating them taking such a step. No replies had been received from Wigan and Tyldesley, and it was decided to adjourn the meeting until August 16th, when fixtures will be arranged for 1905. A sub-committee was appointed to frame rules, and Mr. T. P. Bradshaw (Warrington) was appointed hon. secretary, and Mr. C. W. Emmett (Earlestown) hon. treasurer. Up to the :present,six clubs have signified their intention of joining the league. It is intended, if possible, to have ten clubs in the first division and ten in the second division.

The Work of the Religious Tract Society. The Rev. W. Young, 8.A., district secretary of the Religious Tract Society, preached at Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Su:lday morning and at Wycliffe Congregational Church at night. His object in visit- ing Warrington was to arouse ;nterest in and secure --upport for the Religious Tract Society. In an Interesting review of the society's work since its foundation in 1799, he said that although it was .originally founded for the printing and dispersion of ' religions tracts, the work of the society was now ,much broader, and one million publications were • Issued each week. This department of the society's Work was entirely self-supporting. The work for Which he appealed was evangelistic. The -society aided missionary societies and institutions of various kinds throughout the world with gifts of tracts, books and periodicals issued by the society and in this way ably seconded the efforts of missionaries and 'evangelists. For this work £25;000 was contributed by subscribers last year and he was anxious that there 'should be more subscribers in Warrington to assist the society in this branch of philanthropic work.

'Spiritualism.

The first quarterly meeting of-the S.W. Lancashire -Union was held in the Spiritualist Hall, Sankey-street, Warrington, on Saturday afternoon. The objects of the union are to band together the societies already existing in the district, to help those that are weak, and by means of literature and propaganda meetings start societies in towns where the movement has at present no organization. Mr. J. J. Parr, of Bootle, president of the National Union of Spiritualists, pre- sided. The rules of the Union, which had been formulated at a preliminary meeting held at South- port, were adopted. Mr. Warlow, of Birkenhead, was elected president; Mr. W. Stout (Warrington), vice- president; Mr. R. A. Owen (Bootle), secretary; and Mr. Fletcher (Wigan) treasurer. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Warrington society for :their entertainment of the District Union. After the business meeting, a public tea was held, followed by a Public meeting, which was fairly-well attended. Mr. Warlow presided, and addresses were given by the Chairman, Mr. J. J. Parr, and Mrs. Batie, of Halifax. Mr. A. Wilkinson, of Halifax, gave several clairvoyant delineations of spirit friends, in a number of cases-full names being given. Mr. Rarr moved and Mr. Stout seconded, a vote of thanks to Mrs. Batie and Mr. Wilkinson. Miss Furness sang very effectively, "The Better Land," and Miss Fulwood, a lady visitor, gave a 'capital rendition of "The Flight of Ages," Mr. Joseph Poster in each case accompanying on the organ.

Farewell to an Old School. Archdeacon Wilson, of Rochdale, preached on Mon- day in the chapel of St. Elphin's Clergy Daughters' School to past and present members at the last reunion of the school in its old home. • The material home of fills school, he said, has been in Warrington for 60 years. For two generations this school has been sending out women into the world who have loved this place. Sacred memories, of many kinds, have gathered round its walls and playing fields. I shoulcl not think highly of any one, past or present, Who parted from this place without a sigh, or even a tear; without a feeling of irrevocable loss and change. I should not wonder if there were one or two who thought that. the school could never again be the same; 'who felt inclined to bid it farewell; to lay it, so to sneak, in its grave, and turn their backs on it. But it would be a mistake; it would mistake the shadow for the sub- stance, the semblance for the reality. I doubt not that the old (..zirls of St. Elphin's will recognise in the new St. Elphin's, their own alma maiev, unchanged in character, though in a new dress. How great is the debt owed to the school by past members of St. Zlphin's I know very well; and I hope and believe that St. Elphin's owes them a debt also ; and will ever do so. If St. Elphin's is to continue to be a joy- ful mother of children, it must be because her former bnpils make her name to be honoured, by always speak- ing and thinking of her with affection and l'esPeet, and by being always worthy of her. Yon, he said, are the inheritors of a school which has Fathered round it a deen affection. Many hundreds of tomes in England think with loving gratitude of this school. Never at any moment in its history did it .tend so high in public renutation ; never were its sonour lists more brilliant, its tone better, the attacb- nlent of its old members more manifest. And this is Ynnr inheritance. It is an inheritance more precious t,linn that of buildings and Playing fields, but it is of .?Plicate growth, perishable. evanescent. It is an inheritance that lives in the hearts and prayers of all "fus who belo,,g to the school: most of all in the •ilearts and prayers of yon who live your daily lives it. if in your hearts the ideals die, then the inherit- °nee is lost, the trust has been betrayed.

The Armed Burglar at Warrington. At the Liverpool Assizes on Tuesday, Joseph Hudson (36), moulder, pleaded guilty to having at Warrington on May 6th burglariously entered the house of William Ford, cashier to the Co-operative Society, and stolen 12s. 7d. He also admitted having been in possession of a revolver.—Prisoner, it will be remembered, entered Mr. Ford's house,secured his keys, and was attempting to enter the office of the Co-operative Society when he was disturbed. An exciting chase followed, during which prisoner dropped a loaded revolver. He was run to earth behind Emmanuel Churcli.—Prisoner was committed to gaol for twelve months.ll/4

div.head: Warrington and District Association Football • League.
div.p: Warrington and District Association Football • League.

The adjourned annual meeting in connection with this league was held at the Marquis of Granby Inn, on Thursday evening, Mr. T. P. Bradshaw presiding. Tivo clubs applied for admission—Earlestown and Warrington St. Paul's. After hearing their appli- cations St. Paul's were admitted to the second division of the league. It was considered that the Earlestown Y.M.C.A. club was strong enough to be included in the first division. The representative of the Y.M.C.A. club promised to bring the matter before his committee. The two divisions will consist of the following clubs: ' —First division, Latchfotd, Latchford Brittania, War- rington United, Stockton Heath, Thelwall, Warrington St. Mary's, Warrington Albions, Lymm, and possibly Earlestown Y.M.C.A. Second division : Daresbury, Latchford Reserve, Christ Church, Penketh, St. Barnabas, Stockton Heath Reserve' Warrington Central, Warrington Albions Reserve, Warrington St. Paul's, Peasley Cross, Warrington St. Mary's Reserve. The committee was elected as follows : Messrs. Marley,\ Foulkes, Banks and Kite. The officers appointed are : President, Mr. T. P. Bradshaw ; secretary, Mr. C. T. Cox ;treasurer, Mr. W. H. Smalley It was decided to make an alteration to rule 5, which' now stipulates that all matches must be of 90 minutes duration, unless otherwise mutually agreed upon, and not in any case must it be of less than 60 minutes duration. Any match uncompleted may be ordered to stand as it is as a completed match, or re-played for the full period of time as the executive my direct. Poor Children's Summer Camp. Yesterday morning the second contingent of eighty- four boys who have spent a week under canvas at Prestatyn returned to Warrington, and • their places were taken by another detachment in the afternoon. Although the boys have not been very favoured in regard to the weather conditions,they appear to have spent a pleasant and beneficial holiday. Games have been indulged in with great zest, the Warrington cricket club having kindly sent some tackle. On Monday wretched weather was experienced. The wind was so strong that one of the marquees collapsed, but ths bell tents in which the officers and boys sleep with- stood the storm well, and all inside remained dry. The meals had to be served to the boys in their tents, thus necessitating ' a great deal of incon- venience. During the week there have been short rambles in the country and along the beach, and sea bathing has been keenly enjoyed. A visitor who saw the boys at Meliden where many of them attended church on Sunday, . inquired how the camp was managed, and afterwards forwarded a subscription, desiring it to be recorded in the Visitors' Book under the heading "For as much as ye did it unto one of these Hy little ones, ye did it unto Me." The officers in camp are Messrs. Fred J. Emson (officer-in-charge), F. H. Aukland, A. Malcolm, G. Dawson and Inspector Hackett, whilst Mrs. Emson and Mrs. Aukland have come into 'camp each day and rendered valuable assist- ance. Next Friday it is hoped to send a batch of girls for a week's holiday at the camp.

div.head: EDUCATION ACT.
div.p: THE EDUCATION ACT.
The Passive Resisters at Stockton Heath.
INTERESTING PROCEEDINGS.

It was once said and with graphic effect that the law might be slow, but that when it did move,its arm was long and far reaching. Whether it is always just is a matter of diverse opinion and especially over the present Education Act. In any event, the mighty law, as represented by Mr. Edwin Bradshaw in his capacity as assistant overseer; accompanied by a policeman, on Tuesday night visited the residences of the Revs. J. S. Hughes, H. Dunnico, and Mr. T. Law, with the object of levying the distraint for a small sum in each case which these gentlemen had conscientiously objected to pay, and had the mcral courage of standing out for their opinions. Why the policeman should go IS not apparently clear to some minds. It appears that it is the custom for a policeman to accompany a bailiff or other person levying a distraint, to see "that there is no breach of the peace." Faecy there being any prospect •of respectable citizens like the Revs. J. S. Hughes, H. Dunnico and Mr. J. Law committing a breach of the peace ! However these passive resisters are evidently in the eyes of the law looked upon as a dangerous class of people and it is as well to be on the safe side. In this case however we are pleased to report that the fears of the law were groundless, as Mr. Edwin Bradshaw and the policeman escaped with their lives, but not before they had taken the watches belonging to these gentle- men who gave them up without a struggle. We learn further that the names of these gentlemen are being struck off the voters, lists, but it is just possible that when the law has satisfied its claims and demands, they may be re-instated. Up to the time of writing no date has been fixed for the sale, but there is little doubt thatit will be some date next week.

div.head: Rev. F. E. Powell and Dr. Clifford.
div.p: The Rev. F. E. Powell and Dr. Clifford.

The Rev. F. E. Powell writes to the "Daily Chronicle" of yesterday as follows : Dr. Clifford need not wonder at the opposition of the more thoughtful and logical Liberals to his passive resistance movement.

If his movement were directed against rate-support of all religious teaching whatever, he would receive much more sympathy. But he is content to acquiesce in, and to continue a system which compels law-abid- ing Anglicans and Romans to pay for the undenomina- tionalism which satisfies Dr. Cllfford,and his friends, who have no conscientious scruples in using their rates in support of that which is as abhorent to many- Anglicans and Romans (to say nothing of Jews, Agnos- tics, &c.) as Anglican or Roman teaching is to Dr. Clifford. It is this narrow sectarianism and spurious Liberalism which accounts for the lack of sympathy and support on the part of the more intelligent and consistent Liberals of which Dr. Clifford complains. Equal facilities for all religions is the' only just and logical alternative to pure and rigid secularism in our State schools. FRANCIS E. POWELL. Sewerby Vicarage, Bridlington.

div.head: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH OF
div.p: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH OF
WARRINGTON.
ENDING JULY 23rd, 1904.

Daring the week, the following *births and deaths were registered :—Warrington Registration District births, 34: deaths, 21. The excess of births over deaths was 13. The birth-rate was equal to 25'9. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 15-9 per 1,000, against 13.8 the average of the wevious 4 weeks and against 18'5 the corresponding period of last year. The death-rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was equal to TS per 1,000, against 30 the average rate of the p.revieus 4 weeks and against 6'l the correspond-I lag period of 1903. The ages of mortality were :- 0-1 1-5 5-15 15-25 25-65 65—up. Total 6 5 1 fi 3 21 The deaths included-2 from scarlet fever. 1 from whooping cough, 1 from influenza, 1 from Diarrhea, 1 from phthisis, 3 from lung diseases, 12 from all other causes. div.head: IMPORTANT SPEECH BY THE CHAIRMAN.
div.p: IMPORTANT SPEECH BY THE CHAIRMAN.

The CHAIRNIAN in moving the adoption of the report. and balance sheet, said events during the past half-year had been stirring enough politically, but from a com- mercial point of view it had been somewhat dull and uneventful. In common with other kindred institutions they showed this half-year a slight shrinkage in their profits, which was due mainly to two causes. Not only had they had less money to lend, but they had lent it at less remunerative rates, than those which prevailed last year. The margin of profits therefore had been narrower and of course, he was afraid their expenses had shown no tendency to decrease but rather to increase. He was afraid that tendency was inevitable. It was not that they had done less work. They had actually done more work, for their total turnover was greater by a good many millions, but the fact was, they had done more work for less money. He would just give an illustra- tion of the comparatively unremunerative employment of their money. They would see by the balance sheet that the money at call and short notice amounted to £6,288,000. As a matter of fact for the most part of the half-year, they really stood nearer four or five millions. That money was taken from them by brokers who lent it out again for a term on the market. Of course the price they gave the bank was entirely dependent upon the price they themselves were able to employ it. During last year the price in. London had ruled fully ten shillings—a full y per cent , less than last year. On that point alone there was difference to the worse of between £lO,OOO and £12,000. The total of their money lodged as it appeared on the balance sheet hardly seemed to bear out his statement, when they had had less money to use. They would see as a fact that £27,000,000 which appeared on the balance sheet, was swollen by the payment in of over one million pounds just in the ordinary course of business, either the day before or the actual 30th June, and had been withdrawn again two or three days afterwards. It was really a piece of involuntary window-dressing which they begged to disclaim all credit or discredit as the case might be. Last year they had to write down their investments to the market price of that day, and since then there had been a very considerable rise. They never took any such rise into their -profits, however much they might have written down previously their securities, nor in this estimate of the half-yearly profits was the remuneration included which accrued to them in connection with THE JAPANESE LOAN. The issue of that loan was a record success, being sub- scribed 30 times over. Ile hoped the eagerness with which it had been taken up, expressed in some measure the keen sympathy of the English people with their gallant allies who were fighting for their existance on the other side of the globe. (Hear, hear.) On behalf of the general; manager and staff, he might tell them. , also that a further record was established in the expedi- tious handling of the vast number of application forms, I allotment letters and the return of the allotment money where necessasy—in short, the successful dealing with the multiplicity of detail which was inseparable from an operation of that kind. He was glad to tell them I that their profits had been little affected by bad debts.i They amounted to the very small fraction of one per' cent on the many millions of money they lent or:,. He thought he could give no greater practical As-roof of what a very excellent general manager the2-;fad got,who, as he had told them already, could gr',..sp and arrange and carry through all the numberless details of a great operation like the Japanese loan, and yet, he could with equal success I watch all the numberless individual accounts with which the, Bank had to deal from day to day, the wrong handling of which might very easily convert a trifling profit into a very serious loss. (Hear, hear.) The sum carried forward was £73,000 against £65,000 last half year. A year ago the amount was £107,000, but owing to the fall of consols they had to take £50,000 and to write them down to 85. In January last, he took occa- sion to point out the great advantage of having so large a" carry forward," which enabled them to meet a strain of £50,000, without any undue call on their resources. It would be the policy of the Board again to build up gradually that" carry forward "to at least its former figure. For these purposes, they would see that they were leaving another £5,000 unappropriated, instead of allocating it to any special account, thus making a "carry forward" of 2'73,000. In spite of the dull times they were passing through, he was glad to tell them there was a steady and satisfactory increase not only in the number of their shareholders but in the number of accounts, showing be thought clearly that they were fully retaining the confidence both of depositors and of investors. (Hear, hear.) He had to express regret at the retirement of their Leicester manager. He alluded to

div.head: DECLIN.TE IN BANK DEPOSITS.
div.p: THE DECLIN.TE IN BANK DEPOSITS.

The reasons were very much on the surface. As some of themknew, possibly to their cost, the country was poorer, and bankers balances were depleted to meet current requirements. It was the same story with the deposits of the labouring classes. The savings bank re- turns showed a falling off of over a million pounds ys compared with the savings of last year. Perhaps a still graver sign was that barely half the usual number of members had joined any of the numerous friendly societies up and down the country, whose most import- ant function was the encouragement of thrift. Less work and less wages doubtless accounted for much of this, but he feared that the great and growing preval- ence of betting amongst the labouring classes was res- ponsible for a good deal of it, just as Stock Exchange gambling was answerable for much of the present finan- cial prostration amongst classes above them. Still further evidence of bad times was furnished by the latest returns of the revenue from income and property taxes. Receipts from these sources had fallen from £7,000,000 the figure which was the corresponding figure of last year —to £4,700,000. That discrepancy could only be partially accounted for from the difference in the income tax between is. 3d. and 11d. All those facts must tell on bankers' balances. There was another reason, he was sorry to say, why bankers' deposits were not so likely to increase so steadily in future.

THE COMPETITION OF MUNICIPALITIES. They were becoming exposed to a new and serious form of competition—serious possibly in its consequences to the country at large as well as to bankers. Municipali- ties—he did not speak of every municipality but it was a very general practice—had already borrowed as they knew, many of them somewhat heavily on the security of their rates, and now, they themselves were inviting deposits at rates which it would be not only dangerous but ruinous for bankers to attempt to compete with. It was bad enough that the Government under cover of its prestige should accept millions of deposits from the public without keeping any cash reserve against it, but that immicipalities should bid for deposits by the offer of a high rate of interest, and lock up the money so gained. in schemes possibly unproductive, possibly even disas- trous—(hear, hear)—with only their already heavily burdened rates for security, and no reserve whatever of cash,this was in his humble opinion a proceeding fraught with very dangerous consequences. (Hear, hear.) Bankers in the past had always been ready within reason to accommodate public bodies with money for ; temporary purposes, or pending the issue of a loan. ; But if such unwise and unfair competition was brought to bear upon them in the future, bankers would have to consider the desirability of protecting themselves by some concerted action. He noticed that the Chancellor of the Exchequer, speaking at the bankers' dinner at the Mansion House last June told them possibly with the hopefulness of youth that he saw signs of abetter indus- trial situation approaching. He was sure, he trusted for his own sake and for themselves as well, that he was right, but for his (the Chairman's) part, perhaps it was the prudence of old ace—(laughter)—he could not quite see it in snail a rosy light. He moved the adoption of the report. Mr. E. W. Nix secondecrand the resolution was passed unanimously. . • VOTES OF THANKS TO THE DIRECTOI3S.

Dr. GASKELL (St. Helens) proposed a vote of thanks to the directors for thl3ir services during the past half year. Mr. JOHN STONE seconded and expressed his satis- faction at the satisfactory balance. The vote was carried with acclamation. div.head: IRONWORKERS' WAGES.
div.p: IRONWORKERS' WAGES.
THE QUESTION OF NORTHERN "EXTRAS.".

One of thc most representative conferences ever held in connection with the iron trade took place at the Primitive Methodist Schools, Leabrook, Wednesbury, on Saturday evening, under the presidency of Mr. W. Ancott, president of the Ironworkers' Association. The object was to consider the claim recently put for- ward by the employers' section of the Midland Iron and Steel Wages Board for the abolition of the 6d. per ton allowed to Midland puddlers to compensate for the extras paid to Northern puddlers. The whole of the thirty-six operative members of the Wages Board were present, the total attendance aggregating about ninety delegates. The Warrington representatives were Messrs. J.*Elwell jun., J. Rudge, and C. Algie. The Chairman struck a warlike note in opening the proceedings. The demand was unrighteous, and they had come to the parting of the ways. After keeping the men waiting a quarter of an hour at the last meet- ing of the Wages Board while the employers consulted in private, the chairman, Sir Benjamin Hingley, brought forward a suggestion for a 5 per cent. reduction, on the ground that the men in the North were not receiving the "extras."

For twenty-nines years, the allowance, which was initiated by the employers themselves, had never been questioned, yet the employers now seemed to have set their minds on its abolition. His own view was that they must resist the reduction, even if it meant the ending of the board. Reports from all the districts followed, every speaker without exception, declaring the readiness Of his con- stituents to defend the sixpence against attack. Mr. J. Cox, the secretary, commented on the fast that in this instance the policy of resistance had been suggested by the men themselves rather than the officials. He gave a most emphatic denial to the state- ment that Northern employers were not paying the " extras."

The trouble was due to the severity of Midland com- petition, iron manufacturers selling from 10s. to 15s. below competing houses. The struggle for orders was greater in this district than in any part of the world. Losses sustained in that way were not going to be filched froni the poor under-paid puddler's wages. God forbid that the Board should be wound up, but if it was, they would give it decent burial and find some other means of adjusting wages. He warned the em- ployers that if they upset the present relationship of 6d., they would in future want 9d. and perhaps a is., aad they could prove their right to it. On the motion of Mr. Mullett (Smethwick) seconded by Mr. W. H. Wright (Wigan) a resolution was carried with acclamation, advising the workmen not to ac3ept, any wages arrangement made by the Midland Wages Board which does not recognise the long-standing agree- ment as to "extras."

A further resolution was adopted, on the proposition of Mr. W. Johnson (Smethwick), seconded by Mr. J. Brock (Great Bridge), as follows :—That in the event of the employers' section of the Midland Wages Board giving notice to terminate the present wages arrange- ment, it is hereby resolved to call a conference of the whole of the Midland iron trade to decide what further steps shall be taken by the association.

div.head: Meeting at Birmingham.
div.p: Meeting at Birmingham.
THE MEN MAINTAIN TEIEIR POSITION.

An important meeting of the Standing Committee of the Midland Iron and Steel Wages Board was held at the Grand Hotel,Birrningham,on Tuesday afternoon4Sir Benjamin Hingley, presided, and in view of the import- ance of the discussion on the question of Northern "extras" there was a large and representative attendance.

The accountants presented the result of their investi- gations of the sales of iron by the eleven selected firms during the months of May and June, the result being an average selling price of £6 7s. 2.29 d. This was as against an average price of £6 89. 5.51 d. for the two previous months, and represented a reduction of is. 3d. per ton. This would have justified under the sliding scale, a reduction of 3d. per ton in puddling, and 2i per cont. for millmen, but having regard to the fact that no i reduction had taken place n the North of England. the board decided in accordance with their resolution of July .31st 1902 to continue the present rate of puddling at Bs. 6d. per ton from August Bth to October Ist, the millmen's wages to be in proportion, thus main- taining the recognised relation of 6d. per ton above the Northern figure. The production of the various classes of iron during the period was 26,863 tons, a slight decrease on the yield of the two previous months. The employers, in bringing forward their proposal i for the abolition of the 6d. per ton given n lieu of Northern extras, urged that these Northern extras had ceased to exist, and that the Northern ironworkers no longer obtained any advantage over the Southern op<?ra- tives. The competition, too, between the two districts was so keen that the Staffordshire firms could not longer afford to pay more for their labour than their competi- tors. The operatives however, disputed the statement as to the withdrawal of the Northern extras, and urged that the proposed reduction was not legitimate and could not be supported by facts. At a recent confer- ence of the Ironworkers' Association it was decided to resist the proposal even if it necessitated the breaking , up of the Board.

-Luckily however they were not called upon to go to extremes, as the following letter from Mr. J. R. Winpenny, the Employers' Secretary of the Northern Board, put rather a different aspect on the question : "In reply to yours of yesterday, daily prize money of one shilling per furnace for full heats is paid by the firms connected with this Board. There is practically no level-hand working at present, and therefore no level-hand money is paid. As regards i Monday working money, this s paid by those firms which work en Mondays, but less than half the members of the Board do so."

After a general c9nversation7ihe Chairman remarked that the employers were sat stied with the evidence that the Northern extras were still paid, and they were accordingly quite ready to withdraw the proposal. Eventually Sir Benjamin Hingley moved, and Mr. S. Harris (vice-chairman) seconded the following resolu- tion, which was unanimously agreed to :—" A letter from Mr. Winpenny to Mr. Jones, the secretary, having been read, to the effect that the Northern extras still exist, the Board recognise and are satisfied with the statement to that effect. The. proposal is therefore withdrawn." In the discussion Mr. Harris, the opera- tives' representative, testified to the excellent spirit shown by the employers. •

div.head: HEADMASTER'S REPORT.
div.p: THE HEADMASTER'S REPORT.

The HEADMASTER, who was received with applause said :—My first duty this afternoon is• a pleasant one and that is to give you all a hearty Welcome. It is customary for me on this occasion to lay before you a report on the progress of the school during the past year. During this year we have had two inspections by outside authorities. The first was held in February by Inspectors apnointed by the Board of Education and the second last week by an examiner nominated by the Oxford Local Examination Delegates. The school is examined annually under the Oxford Board and most of the boys in the sixth and fifth forms sit for the certificates granted by the university. Last year we did exceed- ingly well in this examination. We sent in 14 candidates and. there were no failures. As regards the separate subjects we had 14 passes in mathematics,l4 in French, 13 in Latin and 12 in religious knowledge, English and Greek. Among the senior candidates L. G. Corney was placed in the first class of the honours division and was distinguished in Latin and Greek. Our other distinc- tions were H. Dutton and A. R. Owen in Latin and J. R. Alderson in mathematics. The certificate results for this year are of course not yet to hand, but the Examiner has sent in his report and it will perhaps; interest you to tear his general remarks :—"The favour- able impression which I formed of Warrington Grammar School last year has been enhanced by my second visit. There are several directions in which I seem to trace distinct improvement, and many of the individual boys have made very marked progress. Though, of course, the results attained vary with the varying ability of the boys, the standard throughout is high, and all the results point to the excellence of the training received. I should like indeed to see greater grammatical accuracy in the language papers, but even in this respect there is improvement as compared with last year. The number of subjects in the school curri- culum is very large, too large, I should be inclined to say,were it not that when such good results are attained in all, I feel loth to recommend the abandonment of any single one. The behaviour of the boys under examination proved the excellence of the school's tone and discipline. lam glad to note that no change has taken place, since my lastvisit, in the excellent staff of masters. The addition of another master would, how- over, be very useful. The school is fortunate in its staff, fortunate also in its excellent premises." This has been an anxious and trying year both for masters and boys, but the extra strain has been bravely borne‘ and we have been rewarded with a most satisfac- tory report from the Board of Education in London. The governing body of the school has carefully con- sidered the whole situation and has applied to the Board of Education for the recognition of the school as a secondary school. This important step forward will not injure the status of the school, but will merely necessitate some re-arrangement of the curriculum together with the provision of a new lecture room and a physics laboratory in order to meet the requirements of the Board. We shall then be in a position to earn the Government grant, which will mean increased effi- ciency on our part as we shall be able to have the services of an additional master and thus develop the modern side of the school. Greek and German will in the future become alternative subjects and more time will be given to French and Science. The report of H.M. Inspectors contained many valuable criticisms, and useful suggestions, and most of the latter we shall adopt after the summer holidays. I think it will be generally lowed, by those who have seen the report, that th e criticism on

THE TEACHING OP MODERN LANGUAGES is open to great question. It should be understood that a certain school of professors in Germany some few years since started a system called the direct or collo- quial method of teaching modern languages, and by the way I may state that this system has, I understand, been discredited in part, in the land of its birth and it is not allowed, in its entirety, in Prussian schools. However, whether for good or ill, there is an attempt now to force it upon English schools. The method we have hitherto used, and which I suppose most other schools in this country are still using, is the indirect or grammatical system. It really resolves itself into a question of whether we are to study mere utility and thus sacrifice mental discipline and literary culture for the sake of greater fluency in speaking. A man may be ' bilingual without possessing culture. However, we ' intend to make a trial of the system in our Lower Forms. There is a serious impediment to our adoption of this new idea in its entirety, and that is examina- tions. Wo have to prepare boys for various examina- tions in modern languages, and last year, as you have already heard, we passed all our boys in French up to the standard of the advanced French in the Oxford Local Senior Examination. As long as the present style of examination exists, we cannot alter our method of teaching in the Upper Forms. The change must come from the other end, i.e., from the examination end, if such a change in method of teaching is necessary or desirable.

Our other successes during the year include :—J. R. Alderson, who has passed with distinction (18th place) in the Preliminary Examination of the Institute of Chartered Accountants ; A. B. Miles, late head boy and scholar of Queen's College, Cambridge, has graduated B.A. in the Second Class of the Classical Tripos ; A. F. Corney, University of Oxford, Honours in Classical Moderations; C. H. Joseph, Final Examination for the degree of M. 8., Univer,sity of Liverpool; W. B. Forshaw, -Inter- mediate Examination with honours of the Incorporated Law Society: D. J. Dunn, Final Examination of the Institute of Chartered Accountants; G. B. Holford, R. , Pierpoint, and J. W. Scott, Final Examination of thei Incorporated Law Society; J. A. Jones, the University of London Intermediate Examination for the degree of B.A. ; M. J. Glover, Intermediate Examination in Arts, Liverpool University; T. M. Oliff, Camborne Mining School, First Class Certificate in Mine-Surveying. It is with great regret that I have to record the retirement of Mr. Charles White from our Governing Body. Mr. White has been a real friend to the school for many years, and his sound and practical advice has been a great help to me personally. He has further shewn his deep interest in the work here by offering a valuable prize for the best piece of English verse, to be competed for annually by the boys. and in addition he has subscribed handsomely to the University Exhibition Fund. I am sure we all hope that Mr. White may enjoy many years of quiet repose in the retirement which he has so justly earned. (Applause.) I am sorry that we are disappointed to-day. Lord Cross I had consented to distribute the prizes, but he is de- tained in London by important business in the House of Lords. However, the Chairman of our Governing Body, Mr. J. Charlton Parr, has at the last moment very kindly acceded to my request that he should fill
Lord Cress's place, 9.nd I am most grateful to Mr. Parr for his help and support in such an emergency. (Applause.) The second ode of Horace was then recited in Eng- lish verse by L. G. Corney.

div.head: MR. PARR'S SPEECH.
div.p: MR. PARR'S SPEECH.

Mr. PARR then addressed the gathering. He said that was not the first time by a great many that he had had the pleasure of meeting the Grammar School boys in their temple of learning, but it was the first time he had had the pleasure of addressing them from that plat- form—a privilege which he owed to the absence of Lord Cross—and had the honour of presenting the prizes to those boys whose good work, scholastic successes, and general good conduct had entitled them to the rewards which it had been his pleasant duty to hand to them. He had been associated with the school from very early days, though he- could not claim the distinction of being an old grammar school boy, and a few words of advice and encouragement from one who had the good of the school very much at heart might not be out of place. First he would congratulate very heartily those fortunate ones who had passed before him as prize winners. He would also congratulate their parents, for he knew full well from personal experience the pride and pleasure they felt in their boys' successes. He would add a few words of sympathy and encouragement to those who had tried and failed. They must remember that all could not win and consequently some must fail, and they must not 'think the time and trouble they had given to their studies would lose their reward. They would have, so to speak, a store of knowledge reaped and garnered for another day and although success had not crowned their efforts, they had the approval of those whose appreciation was best worth having, and they hod also the comfortable feeling of self approval which invariably and very pro- perly followed work diligently and conscientiously done. Many of them would no doubt have read the Prince of Wales's advice to the boys of the training ship "Worcester." He said "We live in an age of education and it is necessary for success in any -walk of life that we should work hard." Again he said "Be thorough. Whatever you do,de it as well as you ean. Put your;whole heart and soul into it." He (Mr. Parr) felt that he could not improve upon that terse and manly advice, but he would recommend it strongly to every boy in that school. (Applause.) It was too much the tendency of many people to be satis- fied with a smattering of knowledge, if he might so express it, following from subject to subject with, butterfly volatility, touching all but fathoming none To those he would quate the lines of Pope "A little knowledgeis a dangerous thing Drink deep or taste not the iPierian spring." A little learning was dangerous because it might make a man self-satisfied and pedantic, might deceive him into thinking he knew a great deal of many things when he had only touched the fringe of his subjects and knew very little about them. That was not the tendency encouraged by their headmaster,nor was it the tendency of the education received under his able superintend- ence in that school. On the contrary he felt he could not better sum up both than by using the expression of the Prince of Wales "Thorough "—thorough in their aims and ends. (Applause.) "In conclusion " said Mr. Parr "remember that you bo 7s have the great unknown future in your hands. We are passing away. A few short years, and we shall be gone, and you—boys now, bat men then—will have the honour and welfare of this magnificent empire confided to you. Remember the good old saying Aim high and you will strike high.' Place a high standard before you and try to live up to it. The proud position of our great country was won by the good and noble qualities of those who have gone before us—our naval and Military supremacy by the courage, the discipline, the endurance, and determination of our soldiers and sailors, our commercial supremacy by the energy, the enterprise, and the honourable dealing of our mer- chants and traders at home and abroad, and our scientific and mechanical attainments by the study, tie self-sacrifice and indomitable perseverance of our men of light and learning who devoted their lives and their talents to their country's service. Let these great memories be always before you, and let them spur you on to imitate, to equal, aye even to excel, if that may be, the best and the greatest of them. Though it is only the few to whom it is given to shine in the world and before the world in proud pre-eminence, to each and all is given ample opportunity to he, useful, honourable, estimable members of the society in which their lot has been cast." (Applause,)

div.head: PLAYS.
div.p: THE PLAYS.

The students submitted an interesting programme in a way which did them great credit. Several choruses were rendered with a fine swing, but the special features were the plays in French, Greek, and English. The French play was" Dans le pifSge" (Trapped), a comedy. by Mr.F.C.Herzog,the dramatis personae being as fol- lows :goseph;Pommeau(dragoon),J.R. Alderson:Madame Labouret, H. Dutton; Caroline (her housemaid), H. 0. Adams; Chiffonnet (burglar), R. S. M. F. McMurray; Police-Constable, A. F. Grice. A scene from " The Frogs "of Aristophanes was presented by the following: —Dionysus, L. G. Corney; Xanthias, J. Ba,mfortb. ; Aeacus, A. R. Owen; Maidservant of Persephone, J. M. Burgess; Donkey, R. Whitehouse; prologue (Quince), C. S. Woods; Pyramus (Bottom, a weaver), R. Kennon; Thisbe (Flute, a bellows-mender). A. C. Horobin ; Moonshine (Starveling, a tailor), R. Wilcox; Lion (Snug, a joiner), H. Wallington; Wall (Snout, a tinker) H. Nield ; Lysander, F. Carlisle; Demetrius, R. M. Carnson. All the performers in each play acquitted themselves well, and were heartily applauded. The National Anthem having been sung. an enjoyable gather- ing was concluded with lusty cheers for the ladies, the governors, the headmaster and staff, the old boys, and ourselves."

div.head: REPORT ON THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
div.p: REPORT ON THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
Observations of the Inspectors.

For the first time in its history, the Warrington Grammar School was in the early part of this year, ex- amined by inspectors appointed by the Board of Edu- cation, under section 3 of the Board of Education Act, 1899, referring to secondary schools. The report is a very comprehensive one. We extract the following details

div.head: ADMINISTRATION AND FINANCE.
div.p: ADMINISTRATION AND FINANCE.

The Governing Body is reported to be constituted in accordance with the scheme, but inasmuch as that in- strument has not been amended since it was approved in 1880, it appears that its provisions respecting the constitution of the Governing Body might, with advan- tage, be revised to meet the present altered conditions. With regard to the financial position it is reported : "Although the school has a good endowment, the ex- penditure has for several years past exceeded the income. I The year 1899 began with a balance in hand of £2631 13s. 7d.. which was increased during the year to £3BO 7s. 11d. Since that time,however,there has been a deficit each year, averaging more than £lOO, and on the 31st December, 1903, there was an adverse balance of 2125135.3 d. Notwithstanding this excess of expenditure over income,it would appear that the school is at present understaffed, and the Head Master much overworked. If the school obtains recognition from the Board as a secondary school, division B, the grants to be earned in future from the Board may be expected to provide the cost of an additional master, but the normal deficit, as it may be regarded, will be met. The outgoings and expenses of management are unusually high, and some small saving may be effected under this head, but

it is difficult to see in what other direction retrench- ment can be made. The cost of a good first grade education is necessarily high, and if the school is to be maintained at its present standard without increasing the amount of the tuition fees, substantial assistance must be forthcoming from the Local Educational Authority.

div.head: SITE AND BUILDINGS.
div.p: SITE AND BUILDINGS.

The school is situated in a bad part of the town, with surroundings of mean streets and factory chimneys. It is only on one side, however, that the factories are close enough to be actively objectionable, and on two sides the school is surrounded by open ground of considerable extent, a great part of which is the property of the trust. It is generallyadmitted that the school ought to be moved to a more suitable site, but the price of land in the better parts of the town is very high, and it is therefore important that the present site and buildings should be sold to the best advantage. This object can- not be attained if there is anything like a forced sale, and the wisest policy of the governors will be to make shift with the present buildings for another year or two until the opportunity for an advantageous sale occurs The school building cannot be described as attractive and in many respects falls short of the now accepted standard of requirements for secondary schools. At the same time, the class room accommodation, allowing for two classes being taken at the same time in the large schoolroom, is, on the whole, adequate for the present numbers, and the rooms are comparatively free groin the more serious defects. In only one of them is the lighting really bad,r.amely,in the one next to the large schoolroom,where the light is entirely at the back of the pupils. For science work there is a small well-equipped chemical laboratory, fitted with good demonstratiotl table and benches for 16 students. This at present serves the combined needs of lecture room and laboratory, but it is not adequate in size for both pur- poses. The forms are too near, and too much below the level of the demonstration table to admit of the students obtaining a good; view of any experiments that may be shown, If the Governors decide to modify the curriculum so as to enable them to adopt the Board's regulations for secondary schools, division B, it will be necessary to provide a lecture room and physics laboratory of simple type. These could be provided, at relatively small cost, by converting one of the disused dormitories into a lecture room and a large room in the tower above into a physical laboratory. The cost of the necessary structural alterations need not be great. Apart from the foregoing, the most pressing need is better cloak room and lavatory accommodation. As regards the latter, the provision for the whole school is limited to one tap and two basins, which are emptied into a sink.. The Head Master has a suggestion for supplying this need in a cheap and practicable way. STAFF.

The Head Master appears to be eminently qualified for his post. He is not only an enthusiastic and capable teacher and a good organizer, but gives a whole-hearted devotion to his work. The excellent relations that exist between him and his staff on the one hand and the staff and boys on the other impressed the Inspector most favourably. As to qualifications, the staff on the whole is a good one.

div.head: GENERAL REMARKS.
div.p: GENERAL REMARKS.

The tone and discipline alike appear to be admirable. The school has undoubtedly provided a good education in the past, and will in the future continue to play an important part in the educational scheme of the Borough. When the Secondary school (division A) was opened by the new education authority, it was feared by the governors and Head Master that this school, with its low fees, might have a disastrous effect upon the future prospects of the Grammar school. Although the division A. school is full to overflowing, apparently it has not affected the numbers in attendance at the Grammar school, in spite of the fact that there are at least 50 boys at the new school. In a Borough like Warrington, where there is a large artisan population, and where manufacturing interests are paramount, a. secondary school on the lines of division A. was very much wanted, and the rapidity with which this school has filled,points unmistakably to this conclusion. There is undoubtedly room for both schools; indeed it is not unlikely that the success of the division A school may ultimately prove a means of strengthening instead of weakening the position of the G rammar school.

div.head: ELECTION IN HOWLEY WARD.
div.p: THE ELECTION IN HOWLEY WARD.
Large Majority for Mr. Sankey.

Mr. Jacob Sankey succeeded on Monday in his second attempt to become a member of the Town Council for Howley Ward. It will be remembered that he con- tested the ward when a vacancy occurred owing to the election of 'Mr: Alderman Bennett to an aldermanio seat, but was defeated by AIL Adam Horrocks,the Non- trading candidate. On this occasion Mr. Sankey had as his opponent Mr. Thomas Chantler, beerhouse-keeper, of Mersey-street, who came out as an independent Non- Trader. A good deal of mural literature was circulated. Mr. Chantler published a letter from Mr. Councillor Dodds, commending his candidature, and he also issued the following reasons why the electors should vote" for him :—" (1) because he is not the nominee of a political party; (2) because politics have been the curse of our municipal life, and because the political compact in the Warrington Council has been the cause of the shameful waste of money that has so shocked the town; (3) because his opponent, Mr. Sankey, is the nominee of a political party, and will be bound hand and foot to the notorious compact ; (4) because • Mr. Chantler has been a consistent Non-Trader for years. His opponent professed to be one when he was defeated; now he has not a word of commendation for the principle; (5) be- cause Mr. Chantler is a well-known friend of working men ; he knows their needs, having been a working man himself; (6) because he is an honest, straightforward man, and one of yourselves !" In addition, the voters were asked to "Remember the £30,000 police courts; , the Arpley ' dangerous ' corner; the slack contract scandals! and that all our troubles have resulted from the corrupt compact between the two political parties in the Council.

Mr. Sankey, who was the nominee of the Conservative party, repinted the following letter from Alderman Evans :—"The Council of my native town have thought fit to bestow on me the honour of alderman, and I am glad of this opportunity to thank the electors for the confidence they have shown in me during the ten years I had the pleasure and honour of representing them as a councillor of the ward and to assure them that I will continue to do my best for their interests. The electors are now about to choose a successor to myself to repre- sent them in the Town Council, and I respectfully place the name of Mr. Jacob Sar key before them for their favourable consideration. Mr. Sankey has lived over 30 years in the ward and is in direct touch with all its interests, and I am sure the electors could not have a better or more useful member to represent them. I have therefore every confidence in asking the electors to vote for Mr. Sankey." Polling proceeded quietly during the day, but after the workmen had finished work at night, there was a rush for the polling booths, and the officials were kept busily engaged until 8 o'clock. The polling station was at, the National Schools. Messrs. J. Houghton and T. H. Spinks and Messrs. S. Wright and A. Starkey— were the presiding officers and poll clerks respectively. The poll closed at eight o'clock when the blot boxes were conveyed in cabs to the Town Hall, where the counting was proceeded with in one of the committee , rooms. Alderman Francomb was the returning officer and he announced the result in the room as follows : Mr. Sankey Mr. Chantler 266

Majority 297 There were three spoiled papers. Councillor SANKEY7bin proposing a vote of thanks to Alderman Francomb and the Town Clerk and his excel- lent staff, said the whole of the proceedings had passed off in a friendly manner and it was on of the pleasant- est elections which had taken place in the ward. Mr. HANTLER seconded, and observed that it had been a pleasure to work with the officials. ;Not a wrong word had been said. (Hear, hear.) The motion was carried. Alderman FRANCOMB,in reply,said he had been much struck with the good feeling which had existed between the candidates who had been talking together all day. And, after all, that ought always to be the case. Thera should be no quarrelling. The fight had been a fair one, and both could not win. He hoped Mr. Clhantler would , be successful next time.
The result was then declared from the top of the steps in front of the Town Hall. A large crowd assembled to hear the result. SPEECHES AFTER THE POLL.

Councillor SaNKEY.addressing the crowd below, said : Electors of Howley Ward, I am much obliged to you and particul irly to the ladies and gentlemen who by their votes:and support have to-day made me the repre- sentative of the Howley Ward in the Town Council.. (Cheers.) I assure all who have helped me in the can- vass and at the poll of my gratitude and thanks. I will do my best to merit the confidence which has been placed in me, and will do all I can with my colleagues in the Council to help to advance the town's best in- terests. I feel amply repaid for having given you another chance to rectify the mistake you made at the previous election by the splendid majority you have recorded in my favour to-day. (Applause.) Mr. CHANTLER : I thank the electors of Howley Ward who have voted for me. Perhaps I may have better luck next time. I have fought the election on principle and I have the same principle in view I had before the contest started this morning. I don't be- lieve in politics in municipal life. I have exposed the money spent on the police buildings, and if I have only done that I have done enough. I am satisfied. (Ap- plause.)

A strikihg example of the irony of fortune is to be found in the fact that Patrick Hannan, the discoverer of the Kalgoorlie goldfield, which ranks among the richest in the world, was recently compelled to apply for assistance to the authorities at Perth. Hannan,who is now past the prime of life, made his great discovery n the early nineties. The West Australian Govern- ment has now granted him a pension of £2OO.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
BRUTAL ASSAULT ON t WOMAN._

At the Warrington-ii-o-liC.;-"Cirt on Saturday, before Mr. Birchall and other magistrates, William Finn, of Ship Yard, was charged with assaulting Mary Gri!fiths, with whom he co-habited.—Superintendent Monaghan said the parties had lived tog'ether about five years. Shortly after eleven o'clock on Friday ntght they went upstairs and commenced to quarrel. Prisoner abused complainant and she threw a jug at him, but complainant said it did not hit the man. Complainant left tie bedroom and went to sleep with the landlady, Mary Mitchell. At four o'clock in the morning prisoner went into the room and told Griffiths to go into her own bedroom. She did so, and prisoner seizing a boot, commenced to strike her about the head with it. He then put his boots on, and kicked her savagely about the body, head and legs. Complainant went downstairs, and prisoner followed and commenced to kick her again. She screamed and the landlord came downstairs and found her bleeding profusely. He put the prisoner out, and complainant went into Bridge-street and com- plained to Constable Hewitt. She was taken to the Infirmary, and it was found thit the little finger of the left hand had been broken. Afterwards the Constabie arrested him.—Prisoner now stated that he was very drunk, and all that he remembered was being struck on the head with a jug—The bench c.)nvicted prisoner of an aggravated a3satilt, and sentenced him to three mouths' hard labour. EMBEZZLEMENT BY A TRAVELLER—LENEENT SENTENCE.

At the Warrington Police Court yesterday, Charles Henry Hammond, traveller, 53, Pa,dgate-lane, pleaded guilty to embezzling £lO 13s. 3d. fro:n his employer, William Charles Halliday. draper, Lancaster.—Mr. A. Browne prosecuted and said prisoner was one of about thirty travellers employed by Mr. Halliday. He was engaged on April Bth to travel Warrington and sell drapery, &c. His salary was 30s. per week with 21 per cent commission on all cash returns over £l5 per week and when the average returns reached £2O the salary was to be increased to 355. per week and 5 per cent commission. It was the prisoner's duty to send every Wednesday night a report, and cash under .C2O was to be forwarded to Lancaster. On July 20th he sent in a report that the collections for the week amounted to £l2 ss. 6d. After deducting salary and expenses, the sum payable to the prosecu- tor was RIO 13s. 3d. The cash did not arrive and on July 22nd prisoner telegraphed that it had been sent that morning. As the money was not re- ceived prosecntor's manager interviewed the prisoner who made him believe that he had actuallysent the cash on. On returning to Lancaster be found that the money had not come and he again saw the prisoner who persisted that he had sent it. At another interview he began to make excuses, and the prosecutor took out a warrant. Mr. Halliday pressed the case, because prisoner had a good situation and had no need to go wrong. Whathad become of the money they did not know. as prisoner must have disposed of it all in a week.—Prisoner said that he got into bad company and lost the money. He had fully intended to refund it.—ln consideration of the fact that there were no more defalcations, the magis- trates decided to send prisoner to gaol for fourteen days.

div.head: Warrington Borough Police Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Police Court.
Minor Cases.
SATURDAY.—Before. Mr. Birehall (in the chair), Alder- man Bennett, and Messrs. Hayward, R. T. Fairelough and Jolley.

DISCHARGED.—Henry 'Anderson, of no fixed abode, who was remanded on Thursday on a charge of being in possession of a rug, again appeared before the magis- trates.—Superintendent Monaghan said the police had been unable to find an owner for the rug, and he asked that prisoner might be discharged.—Tnis was agreed to.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Sutton, Councillor Thornton, Messrs. Birchall, Hay- ward, Pilling, and W. Roberts. SCENE AT THE CENTRAL STATION.—Henry Allison, of no settled abode, was charged with making use of •obscene language at the Ceatral Station on Saturday night, and with assaulting Robert Humphries, a con- stable in the employ of the C.L.C.—Humphries said the prisoner arrived by the 8.50 train from Manchester and -commenced to use very filthy language. He refused to leave the premises w'nen requested, and witness had to eject him. Half way dowa the steps, prisoner struck witness in the face with his list.—A line of 10s. and costs was imposed. DESTROYING HIS FATFIER'S PROPERTY.—WiIIiam Bramhall, a young man living at 4, Dalton-bank, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly on Dalton-bank on Saturday night, and with doing wilful damage to two doors, a window, and washing mug, the property of James Brarnhall, his father. He was further charged with assaulting John Bramhall, his brother.—The evidence showed that prisoner came home drunk, and found the doors locked, as the family had gone out to see the departure of the Volunteers. He was so annoyed that he began to kick at the doors, throw various articles at them, and do a great deal of damage to other property. His brother John came upon the scene as he was banging at the back door with some spouting, and on being remonstrated with prisoner struck his brother.—Prisoner's father said that when his son got drink there was "no doing any good with him.'' —Prisoner was bound over to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay the costs together with £1 towards the damage.

31iNoft CASES.-I:Jonathan Barton and John Gleave, Lord Nelson-street ; Joseph Birchall, Cloth Hall Yard, and John Whittaker, Jolley's Court, charged with fight, in,c, were bound over and ordered to pay the costs; John 'Shaw, 57, Wellington-street, was fined ss. for driving a hackney carriage without a licence.—lnspec- tor Taylor said the defendant formerly held a licence, but had not applied for one this year.—John Hargreaves Sharp-street,was summoned for disorderly behaviour in Sharp-street on the 17th inst., and Louisa Hargreaves was charged with using obscene langnage.—Both de- fendlnts were bound over and ordered to pay the costs.
