div.head: MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: MOTOR NOTES.

It is a pity that the limit price for light ears compet- ing in the forthcoming official trials is not extended to £250. With a few notable exceptions, a really good and reliable car cannot be purchased, with tyres in- cluded, under at least two hundred guineas, whilst most of the small cars, intended for more than two persons, run from £220 upwards.

The two-seated car is not an unqualified success, since only one passenger is possible, unless a youth is also carried who can be accommodated upon the footboard; but this plan is not to be recommended, since it makes the weight wrong and throws an unfair strain upon the springs and axle which was never contemplated by the makers.

Overloading any car, indeed, is never fair to the manufacturers, for when they design one to hold, say, four persons comfortably, they do not provide tyres, springs and axles strong enough to take seven up. Yet one frequently sees four passengers squeezed into the tonneau built for two, and an additional passenger travelling on the footboard, in addition, of course, to the two legitimately occupying the front seats. The practice is •to be condemned, and only in the case of real emergency—such, for instance, as taking up an extra passenger from another car in the event of a breakdown or an accident on the road—should the vehicle be permitted to be overloaded.

A remlrkable motor, capable of developing high h.p. and easily attachable to any existing cycle is, we are informed, shortly to be placed upon the market at the modest retail price of £7 10s. The Millennium is certainly getting very near. Unfortunately, it is not quite within sight yet, as the new invention provides no means for strengthening the already comparatively weak frame, mechanically speaking, of the ordinary " diamond- framed " machine.

The motor expert who contributes some interesting notes to the " Echo " draws attention to the great difficulty which exists for starting the motor of mans a large car. "The twisting of the handle," he says, "and the strength that is som3times required in over- coming the compression are exceedingly fatiguing to all but those blessed with a sound constitution." This is very true, although the sweeping indictment does not apply equally to all cars, of course. Take the 4 cylindered Decauville for example. This is an excep- tionally good starter, and, having once been set going and then stopped for ten minutes or so, she will invari- ably start up quite ready from the switch. Even with the first start of all, after the car has been standing in the stable perhaps all night, one sharp half-up Rard turn of the crank is quite sufficient to set her going.

A good inflator is such an absolute necessity to the motorist that it is extraordinary to notice how little care is taken to secure one that is really efficacious. Economy in this respsct is always a mistake, for a powerful pump is more than worth the money paid for it. In the same way, every item included in the tyre repairin,, outfit should be of the best quality obtainable. Poor solution is worse than useless, since the time and patience spent in repairing patches with it are merely thrown away, whilst it is infinitely more satisfactory to lay in a stock of good repairing rubber than to attempt to use up fragments of spoilt tubes,—a plan that is fre- quently adopted, and, it may be added, usually with discouraging results.

Plenty of French chalk should be carried and should be used most generously in dusting over the completed repair. It should also be sifted inside the outer cove so that there is no possibility of any sticking occurring later on,when the inner tube has been replaced. A largo tin of this is cheap enough, but for some inscrutable reason, the motorist appears to regard it as being almost as valuable as gold-dust, and (in the comparatively rare event of having any with him), almost invariably uses it in the stingiest and most misarly manner conceivable.

In one of. the large provincial towns a cyclist has recently been fined for "hanging on" to an electric tram-car, this practice, apparently, being contrary to the bye-laws of the tramway company. The incident serves two purposes. It calls attention to the general realisa- tion of the grave danger which is undoubtedly invited by those wheel-men who persist in forcing every fast travelling vehicle to pace them; and, incidentally, it shows that, in that particular town, the electric cars mnstadmittecily travel at a tremendous speed if they are regarded by cyclists as eligible pace-makers.

Stopping suddenly comes under the charge of driving furiously, as a professional chauffeur has recently found to his cost. He brought his vehicle to a standstill so unexpectedly and without giving warning to those drivers following up behind that they crashed into the rear of his car. Asked by a constable for his licence, name and address, he darted off again, but with the limb of the law hanging on to the car, and when in- formed that he would be pulled off his seat if he did not stop, he discreetly slowed up as requested. In addition to a fine of £lO, his driving licence has been suspended for a period of six months,for it was proved that the man was undoubtedly intoxicated.

Now, any man on duty in a state of intoxication is a danger to the public, and in such a case a fine is surely an inadequate punishment In addition t 3 the suspension of his license a magistrate should have it within his power to sentence the offender to inprisonment without the option of a fine even for the first offence. Careless driving is bad enough; but careless driving induced by drunkenness is nothing less than criminal.

A writer in the "Irish Field" comments upon the lack of accessibility noticeable in the majority of motor cars, and cannot understand how it is that motor manu- facturers "wilt not take more trouble to have the parts of a motor which require most frequent adjustment put in an accessible place, as at present even such small things as taking out sprking plugs requires on some cars considerable time."

This indictment is, unfortunately for the motor trade, a very true one. Indeed, one of the best cars on the market to-day is absolutely spoiled by. the designers through negleat of this one important detail. Yet there is really no legitimate reason why all the parts should not be quite get-at-able,,and, if this were more generally appreciated and cars were better designed, the necessity for a pit—that stumbling block, with the average hOuseholder—would be obviated.

The absence of mud, dust and grit from the working parts makes a wonderful difference to the running of the motor, and it is really surprising that more cars, and especially those turned out by really well-known and reputable firms, are not better protected in this nvitter. When the 'mechanism is left absolutely exposed, the owner can always improve upon the manufaCturer's conception of a finished car by making a temporary shield with well slung linoleum underneath the car. It is not particularly sightly; but this is very immaterial when its presence means a very certain saving to the motor.

div.head: EIFFEL TOWER LEMONADE.
div.p: EIFFEL TOWER LEMONADE.

This well-known article is partly made in Italy in the midst of the Lemon Orchard's, hence its fresh, delicious flavour of Ripe Lsmons and its wonderful cheapness. Dr. A. B. Griffiths, the famous food analyst, says: "It is impossible to produce Lemonade of a higher standard of excellence." A 41d. bottle makes two gallons.
Warrington Woman Tries to Drown Herself.

At Sale Petty Sessions on Monday, a young woman named Jane Jordan, of Ireland-street, Winwick-road, Warrington, was charged with attempting to commit suicide.—The evidence showed that at 11.15 on Satur- day morning, Mr. Henry Jenkins, coachman, 4, St. lAudrew's-avenue, Deansgate-lane, Timperley, was [ walking along the bank of the Bridgewater Canal, between Tirnperley and Brooklands, when he passed Ithe prisoner who was crying. When about a yard beyond,he heard a splash, and turning quickly saw that the girl had jumped into the water. He leaped to the side of the canal and stretched out his arm, bringing her to the side and lifting her out. Despite this experience the young woman wanted to jump into the water again, but was restrained. She was later taken into custody by Sergeant Bourne, of Sale.—ln , answer to Mr. H. L. Harris, 'deppty magistrates' clerk, Mr. Jenkins said that just before she leaped into the canal the prisoner threw a, small piece ot paper which she had been carrying in her hand on to the canal bank. The paper was produced and it bore the followia.g :—" Jane Jordan, 3; Ireland-street, off Winwick-road, Warrington."— *Prisoner hall been employed as a servant by Mr. George Gibbons, Beaufort-avenue, Sale, and on Satur- day morning the family left the house, prisoner being in charge. On returning they found the following note .—" 8, Tennis-street, Old Trafford. Mr. and Mrs. Gibbons. I have left your house as I could not live at home any longer. lam going to try to find a river and am going to drown myself. as they don't want me at home, and I am tired of life. Yours truly, Jane Jordan."—Sergeant Bourne said when he charged the prisoner with the offence, she replied "I don't know what caused me to do it unless it was being left in the house alone."—Prisoner was committed for trial to the next Knutsford Sessions.

Mr. Hamilton Rice, one of the best-known and most popular members of the Constitutional Club, London, committed suicide there on Thursday afternoon by shooting himself with ra revolver. He was of a cheery disposition, and no reason can be assigned for his com- mitting suicide.

div.head: CONGESTED STATE OF THE WORKHOUSE.
div.p: THE CONGESTED STATE OF THE WORKHOUSE.
NEW BUILDING TO BE ERECTED.
The State of Trade in Warrington,
INTERESTING DEBATE.

The principal business at the meeting of the War- rington Board of Guardians on Wednesday was the con- sideration of the means to be adopted to relieve the congested state of the Workhouse. Mr. A. Brooks pre- sided, and there were also present :—The Rev. Dr. Mercer, Mrs. Clay, Mrs. Wilkinson, Miss Broadbent, Messrs. T. Ashcroft, J. Ball, J. Billing°, R. Bolton., John Clarke,R. Forshaw, W. Flanagan, W. Hickman, W. Houghton, A. J. Jolley, G. Mather, T. Ritchie, J. C. Sutton (clerk), J. F. Awbery (master), and A. Wright (superintendent of Padgate Schools). It was reported that at a meeting of the House Com- mittee it was resolved to turn out of the House every able-bodied man. The report of the special committee appointed to deal with the congested state of the House was considered. An amendment that the subject be deferred for six months having been defeated, it was resolved that the following recommendation of the special committee be submitted to the Board : " That a building suitable for the aged and infirm inmates, intermediate in character between the Infirmary and the Workhouse proper, and of as inexpensive a nature as possible, be provided, to accommodate at least 100 persons, and so arranged as to allow for further extension when needed."

In moving the adoption of the minutes, Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said the increase in the numbers of indoor poor had been receiving the attention of the House Com- mittee for a long time past. A year ago matters got into such a state that a special committee was appointed to inquire into the subject, and Mr. Pilling and he spent a considerable amount of time in ascertaining the num- bers in the House during the slackest and most crowded periods for several years past. They did not merely accumulate figures out of books or accept statements prepared by officials, but they went very carefully into the specific information that was available and worked out some averages which he would like to place before the Board. For the five years 1899 to 1903 they took six week periods in the quarters ending Michaelmas and Lady Day which might be called the emptiest and fullest periods respectively, from the Workhouse point of view. The average numbers each week in the emptiest part of the year were :-317, 332, 352, 388, 443. During the more crowded period (January to March)the figures were :-368, 366, 418, 451, 463. There was a marked increase in both the summer and winter periods, and it was in three classes—the sick, infirm, and aged. He wanted the Board to realize that it was not a question of able-bodied persons at all that they had to face. They had not really any able-bodied people in the house. The committee went into the figures in August at the request of the House Committee, with a view to prepar- ing for last winter. They made an estimate that it would be probable that in February of this year the average numbers in the house might be expected to be about 500. Some members thought at the time that the committee had made a rather extravagant estimate but it was compiled on the most careful and moderate lines, and proved to be an under-estimate, the actual average during February being 536. The Board must bear in mind that they had to provide not for the average but for the maximum, and there would be dates when the number reached 560 or 570. He would like to emphasise the point that last winter was not a severe one. The weather was open and mild, and if it had been severe, as well as the trade being bad, it seemed fairly clear that they might easily have had 600 inmates. The Tarvin Union had been approached, and made an offer to take twenty males in good health if the Board would pay them 7s. per week. That offer was of absolutely no use towards the solution of the difficulty. On July 15th a special meeting of the House Committee was held, and after receiving a tabu- lated statement from the :Mastershowing the number of beds in each department of the house and hospital and the number occupied the previous night, they passed the resolution which was now submitted. A crucial point to be considered was "Is this increase of indoor poor temporary or permanent ?" To help them to arrive at a just verdict on that question he would point out that taking the last three census returns of the Union (1881, 1891 and 1901) the population had increased nearly 50 per cent. The Workhouse accommodation had not increased. In 1881 the population was .70,218; in 1891, 83,471 ; and in 1901, 100,012. That meant that the population was increasing at the rate of 2,000 a year. Therefore in ten years they might expect to have to administer poor relief for a popula- tion of 120,000 and in twenty years for 150,000. That seemed to point very strongly to the fact that the increase they had to face was not a temporary but a per- manent one. Another aspect of the question which tended to support that view was the trend of modern legislation. The effect of the Employers' Liability and. Workmen's Compensation Acts—whatever their indi- vidual opinions as to the wisdom or otherwise of the measures might be—was to prevent men getting on in years from obtaining employment where there was any risk whatever. The tendency was to drive men getting towards sixty years of age out of work and increase the difficulty which the Board had to face. Dealing with the question from the administrative point of view it might be asked " Can the numbers be materially reduced by more rigid treatment of the inmates in the house?" To that question he for one gave an emphatic" No." He ventured to think that anyone who had taken an active part in the work of the House Committea for the past four or five years would realize that that "No "was ' justified. The increased numbers in the house were not in any way due to laxity of administration. It might be suggested that the numbers could be reduced by a freer administration of out-relief. If that were so, her believed the reduction would be only of a temporary nature. He also said in the most emphatic manner that_ both on social and economic grounds a temporary re duction obtained by that means would be wrong. He did not want to embark on the very wide field of dis- cussion about the propriety or otherwise of free out relief, but he must say a few words about it, because it was most important in its bearings on the question. The experience of generations proved that a strict policy of out-relief administration, if it was consistently adhered to for a period of years, ensured a diminution of pauperism, a reduction in the poor rate, and a raising of the level of comfort and the standard of living, while laxity of administration, and a readiness to grant small Isums to applicants for relief rather than subject them Ito the house test, inevitably led to progressively increasing pauperism, social degradation, and high rate:. 1, That principle held good both for urban and rural areas as was evidenced by the experience of the Bradfield and Whitechapel Guardians. These authorities has pursed the policy of restricting out-relief on definite lines, and the result had been a steady reduction in the amount of out-relief, until it was now exceedingly low. If the Guardians in those Unions could almost abolish out-door pauperism there was no reason why it should not be done in Warrington. It was essential that there should be a suitable Workhouse with adequate ; accommodation, and he was firmly convinced that if the methods he had mentioned were adhered to for a few years in that. Union their true poor rate would soon fall very materially. It seemed to him indisputable that additional accommodation would have to be provided. The mere growth of population would necessitate that, and any further delay wculd only make matters worse. If the recommendation of the House Committee was approved, it would be two years before the buildings were ready. If the proposal did not commend itself to the Board he felt justified in asking if anyone had an alternative to suggest. A number of other methods had been considered by the House Committee. The first was whether it would be desirable to complete the Infirmary on the original !Ans. The building at I present accommodated 196, but the plans were so arranged that additional wings could be erected to increase the number accommodated to 352. After full consideration of the cost and probable effect of the extension, the committee were agreed that it would be inexpedient to suggest it. Another proposal was that the Workhouse should be enlarged by pavilions, but that also was considered inexpedient. A third sugges- tion, which rather commended itself to the minds of some members at the outset, was that they should erect workshops so arranged as to secure easy supervision, and thus liberate a certain amount of space which was now in use for various kinds of work. That scheme was also felt to be inadequate to meet the difficulties, and with a full knowledge of the facts the, sub-com- mittee presented their recommendation and the House Committee confirmed it. Mr. HICKMAN asked how the diminution in out- relief in the Bradfield and Whitechapel Unions affected the number of indoor paupers. Mr. JOLLEY said he had not the exact figures, but the tendency of strict out-relief, was to reduce the number of indoor poor. Mr. ASHCROFT asked what the experience of Lanca- shire Unions had been. The CHAIRMAN said he did not think any Lancashire Unions had adopted the scheme so strictly as the Brad- field and Whitechapel Board". He believed the cost of maintaining inmates had diminished in both those cases, and the outdoor relief had come down almost to nothing. Mr. FORSHAW seconded the confirmation of the minutes. He pointed out that maintaining paupers in the House was generally more costly than granting out- relief. He complained that some members of the corn- mitteeseemed to take little or no interest in the grant- ing of out-relief, but sat reading books and newspapers. " No." )
,Mr. ilicKmAN : Name them and we shall know who (the sinners are. _ _

Mr. FORSIL&W : Watch them yourself and I think you can name them. Continuing, he said that if no other way of escaping the difficulty could be found, he thought the committee's proposal was the best method of dealing with the matter. Mr. ASHCROFT asked what the probable cost of the new building would be. The CLERK said that if the resolution were passed, an architect would be appointed, and he would report 0n

the details. At present it was impossible to suggest what the expense would be. Mr. CLARKE moved an amendment that the recom- mendation be not approved. He had always understood that the poor rate was to feed the poor, and not merely to build workhouses or hospitals. He thought it very unfair to reduce people by sending them into the Work- house when they could keep them for much less outside. The Rev. Dr. MERCER seconded. He did not differ with the proposition itself, but as regarded the opportuneness of the present time to carry it into effect. Sooner or later they would be bound to build or provide in some way for the increase of paupers. He sympathised with Mr. Clarke's contention as to out- relief, not so much on the question of cost but on the effect it had on the characters of the recipients. He thought that with the efficient services of the relieving officers they would be able to administer out-door relief so that only the deserving cases would receive it, and the cost, he contended, would be considerably less than the provision of larger buildings. Neither the Employers' Liability or Workmen's Compensation Acts were likely to bring a supply of paupers with whom the Board could not cope within the next ten years. Mr. Jolley gave an estimate of the population for ten and twenty years hence. They did not, however, want a building of the capacity to deal with that increase, to be standing for the next twenty y ars. The state of trade was execrable, but that only made people abso- lutely unable to deal with the increased rate that might be imposed upon them. Many people would tell them that they were simply "keeping on' and nothing more. They were trying to keep out of the bankruptcy court, although from what he heard it would be a blessing for some to go into the bankruptcy court,because they would come out richer than they went in. (Laughter.) He thought the matter might be postponed for six months, as at the end of that period they would be in a better position to declare whether the need was imperative, or whether they would be likely to tide over another ten years until the actual increase of population demanded that they should build. During the next six months he considered they were likely to have a decent increase in trade and work. Possibly the Ship Canal improvements would begin in autumn, and they would mean an extra supply of cash coming into the town.

The CLERK said it would not be necessary to state a time for the reconsideration of the question, as it could be re-opened at any time. Mr. HICKMAN supported the amendment. He did not think they had exhausted all thsir ingenuity in the matter even yet, although there had been so many meet- ings. He held in his hand a statement that there were five empty rooms in the house. Could'ut they fill those up? He objected to erecting any more buildings in "that part of the world" if they could possibly avoid it. He had always been an advocate of a new Workhouse and Infirmary being built out in thecountry. His opinion was that before many more years had passed they would have to remove from that part of the world—(Hear, hear, awl laughter)—and build a Work- house elsewhere. They had passed through a very severe crisis so far as trade was concerned,but he held beleived there were now prospects of an improvement. If they did anything at all, they ought to enlarge the hospital, as the congestion was the worst there.

Mr. BILLINGE said it appeared that however they turned the figures some provision would have to be made for the indoor poor. They must face the difficulty whether they liked it or not. The normal increase of population demanded more accommodation, and if all the mills re-commenced work on full time to-morrow it would not alter the facts of the case that the Board was trying to meet. They were dealing with the regular per- manent in door poor. The Infirmary was being practi- cally converted into a Workhouse, and it was filled with a class of people who did not require medical aid. So long as they were kept in the Infirmary they would have to be attended professionally and not by other paupers. They were at present spending £5,000 per annum in out-relief, and they would always have as many applicants as they cared to give to. Mr. JOLLEY said he believed that if Mr. Clarke knew all the facts and was in as close touch with them as the members of the House Committee, he would not have proposed the amendment. The object and adminis- tration of the Poor Law ought to be to diminish pauperism and not to increase it or create it. He was afraid the policy Mr. Clarke advocated would increase and widen the area of pauper- ism and so inevitably to degrade larger number of the community. Dr. Mercer said they did not want to erect a building for twenty years hence. If the Board undertook to build at all they must not fritter away their money by putting up a building they would have to enlarge in five years. They must look ahead. He would strongly emphasise the point that the clngestion they had to deal with was not that which was going to exist ten or twenty years hence, but that which existed to-day and which exisited in a very severe form last winter. In the hospital, beds had to be placed in the corridors for weeks during the winter period because there was no room for them in the wards. They had actually toiplace beds in the waiting'rooms adjoining the board room. The • people in the Wotkhouse had to be treated like human beings, and if Mr. Hickman had attended the meetings of the Special Committee and the House Committee of which he was a member he would have known that there was not one empty room that was fit or suitable for the accommodation of the poor. The inmates should be provided for in a decent, Christian, and humanitarian spirit. In regard to the removal of the Workhouse into the country, even if they decided in a few years' time to transfer the in- stitution, it would not alter the fact that they had to pay for the buildings they had there. They had in- curred liabilities and to some extent were anchored there. Whether it would have been wise to have trans- ferred the institution a few years ago was a matter for discussion. As it was, they had to repay the loans out of which they provided the present buildings. The committee honestly believed that the course they recommended was the most economical way of meeting the difficulties.

On a vote being taken only six voted for the amend- ment which was therefore defeated. The resolution was put to the meeting and carried. Mr. HICKMAN moved that Messrs. W. and S. Owen be requested to prepare plan,. Mr. ASITCROFT seconded .... • _- . _ •

Mr. MATHER said he had nothing to s,ty against Messrs. Owen, but he thought other young und rising architects in the town should be given a chance. Miss BROADBENT suggested that several architects should be asked to send in competitive plans. It was decided that Messrs. Owen should be asked to prepare the plans. The following committee was appointed to further consider the question :—The chair- man, Rev. Dr. Mercer Mrs. Clay, Messrs. Jolley, Mather, Forshaw. Ashcroft, Hickman and Billinge.

div.head: CASE OF.SMALL-PDX.
div.p: A CASE OF.SMALL-PDX.
A case of small-pox having been discovered in the House, it was resolved that all visiting at the institu- tion should be suspended for a fortnight. THE TARING OF AN INVENTORY.

The CHAIRMAN moved that subject to the approval of the Local Government Board the sum of £25 be paid to the Master for preparing a new inventory of the property of the Guardians. Any payments to other officials who assisted were to be made from this allow- ance.

Mr. IlicKmAN contended that the sum was excessive and moved that .El 5 be paid. Mr. Asßcßorr seconded, and characterized the pro- posal as outrageous. He himself was not in favour of granting any extra allowance. Only four voted for the amendment, which was lost, and the motion was carried.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.
GAMING.-At the Warrington Occasional Court, on Monday, before Mr. T. A. Frost, Joseph Smith, of no fixed residence, was fined 20s. for gaming in Old London-road, Stockton Heath.

STOCKToN HEATH GARDEN SOCIETY.—On Tuesday evening about 40 members paid a visit to the gardens and grounds of Mr. Vere B. Davies, Birchdale, Appleton. The garden and grounds were looking very neat and trim, but some of the flowers, of which there were a great variety, particularly the parties and violas appeared to be suffering from the continued heat and dryness of the weather. The members very much appreciated the kindness of Mr. Davies in allowing them to pay their visit.

div.head: 1 Railway Servants Church Parades.
div.p: 1 Railway Servants Church Parades.

1 The members of the Warrington Branch of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants,held special church parades ot,t:Sunday in aid of the orphans' fund. 1 A procession Was formed at one o'clock in front of the Town Hall, and, headed by the branch banner and I the Borough Prize Band, it paraded several streets ;of the town. Arriving at Friars-green Chapel, a special service was 4eld, the preacher being the Rev. H. Dunnico. There was only a moderate attendance. 1 In the evening, the procession was again formed and 1 proceeded to the Working Men's Mission, in Thewlis. street, where another service was conducted by Mr W. Light. A good congregation assembled. An organ 1 solo was rendered in a creditable manner by Master A. IFairelough,who is only 12 years of age. The collections, which were made at each service and en route, I amounted to £lO.

At Truro, on Thursday, Annie Jane Terrill, a srinster 'of independent means, was remanded in custody on a charge of arson. The prisoner was last week ejected Hom a house at Penningforth, where she had lived with over 500 cats running loose. The owner had issued a claim for £lOO damages to the house, and late on Mon. thy night the prisoner was seen to enter the house, and to depart after midnight in a cab for Camborne. A little later the boufa. was found to be on fire in four different places, and serious damage was done to the building.

div.head: (CoPYri.9lt) ANGEL JENKS.
div.p: (CoPYri.9lt) ANGEL JENKS.
By J. A. HAMMERTON,
Author of "Trial and Triumph," "The Actor's Art," "City Sketches," "Told by the Police," "My Pipe and I," &c.

Many years ago, when I was the editor of the Laysford Leader, an old-fashioned provincial news- paper, whose sage opinions were seldom quoted be.,ond the rather limited area of its circulation, I used to find it a source of innocent amusement to try to recall the faces and characteristics of the lor,g line of boys who had filled the role of P.D (or printer's devil) during my occupancy of the editorial chair. It was a pastime which involved some strain on the memory, for these youngsters, who were hired to do odd jobs about the com- positors' room and badger the editor for "copy," seemed to appear in the office by some mysterious agency and as strangely to vanish again into the out- side world.

I would be sitting at my desk, busy penning a leading article on some topic of the moment, when stranr voice at my elbow would say: "Copy, please." I would look round, to behold an unknown youth of fourteen years or thereby, standing cap in hand and minus a jacket; I would give him such pages as were ready and he would go. He would come again and again, for some weeks, months perhaps, with his eternal "Copy, please," and be served mechanically. Then a day would arrive when a strange voice sounded once more, and a strange figure stood there. The same words were spoken, the same thing done; and thus the P. D. 's came and went as they are doing to this day in thousands of newspaper offices throughout the country. But from out the long procession of ink-stained imps who passed my editorial desk I recall one whose form and characteristics distinguished him from the rest. He was a lad of not more than fourteen, rather lanky and big boned, with a face that was neither ugly • nor pleasant. His cheeks were somewhat sunken and his eyes, deep set, gleamed brightly, suggesting a lively, fun-loving nature, which the lines of the well-modelled mouth confirmed. His nose was decidedly turned up, and just by as much as it was upturned was it coated with printer's ink the first time my eyes beheld him. I never saw him, so far as I can recollect, without that smudge of black on his nose; it became his sign manual, and suggested "Smut" as an appropriate name for him. As "Smut" he was known all the time he laboured in the office of the Leader, and that was many months; for he seemed to delight in his occupation, and the cheery voice in which he always asked for "Copy, please," and the smile in which the blackened nose stood out like a pivot- point, robbed the request of its monotony. Indeed, when Smut invaded the sanctum the supplying of copy became less a mechanical per- formance than it had hitherto been. I was the first to make advances, for at the beginning Smut was shy of speech, but as soon as the ice was broken he spledily became communicative, and would open such important topics as the fresh defeat of the Laysford Wanderers,, or the bad con- dition of the ground for to-morrow's play. "And whereabouts do you live, Smut?" I asked on one occasion, when I wished to give him an errand if it lay in his direction. "Down in the Sandpits," said he blithely, naming one of the lowest quarters of the town. . _ _
"Btit that's a queer plaje for a respectable lad to live, isn't it? I thought they were a bad lot down there."

"An' you're just right, I can tell you. We calls it Little 'ell,' sir." "Quite the place for a printer's devil, eh ? " And Smut's teeth shone white through the lips that opened in a smile. Not that the teeth were actually white, but contrasted with the face they appeared so. "They are a bad lot down in the Sandpits, sir, he went on, evidently pleased to supply me with some particulars of life in that locality. "Why, that chap as did for his old 'ooman lust week uster live against our 'ouse. 'E did, air; an' e wunst gin me a penny for fetchin 'is beer." Smut said this as if he felt the distinction of claiming acquaintance with the murderer. "Then Swinton, what killed a pal in a sparring match, 'e lives down in the Sandpits; au' a downy cove 'e is, sir," he resumed rapidly, anxious to make the most of the time I evidently had to spare, ikngering meanwhile with dirty hands the bundle of copy I had given him in a way that would not add to its legibility.

"But," said I, breaking in on his flood of reminiscence, "what about your own folk? Surely they're not as bad as their neighbours?" "Oh, it depends, sir. The old lady, she's all right, but the old roan's a wrong 'un, 'e is, sir." "A bad thing to say about your own father, Smut."

"Bad or not, it's right, and I'd like to punch is 'ead when I'm growed up, I would. 'E's allus on the booze, 'e is, an' e licks the kids—that'd Nan and Billie, the young 'tins, you know. 'E uster lick me, too, but not now, sir. No fear. 'E knows I ain't a kid now. But he do treat the old lady shameful, an' some Sat'days she's on'y got my money, 'e 's Mewed all 'is. An' e makes good money, too, sir, as much as sixteen bob a week." The look in Smut's eyes as he said thisAphowed that he had dreams of the luxury which his drunken parent might have secured for his home by a wise expenditure of his wealth. How long Smut would have chattered on on such occasions as these Ido not know, but he had generally to be pulled up after a few minutes, and often in the full tide of his narrative, by a reminder that he had come for COPY and the comps Might be gasping for it upstairs, at which sugges- tion he was off 'like a shot, and, no doubt, had a ready excuse wherewith to mollify the overseer. I did not deem the moments spent in these little chats with Smut quite wasted, for his was an interesting personality, and it has always seemed to me that individuality is that which gives savour to life. Moreover, it was only when I wished to refresh my mind for the task of grappling with some of these "weighty questions of the day" that I indulged in such familiarities with Smut on his calls for copy. And thereby, I also found Myself in possession of some first-hand informa- tion concerning the life of the poor. "And how do you spend your evenings, Smut?" I asked on another occasion. "What do you do with yourself when you get away from the office? "Oh, in summer time I plays football with some other lads on the waste ground." "But football isn't a summer game, is it? " _ _ .

"No, the big 'tins don't play it then. But ours ain't a reg'lar ball, you know; we makes it our- selves, and then in the winter 'tain't light at night to play." "And the kids.' What about them?" "Why, I takes 'em to the park on Sat'day or Sunday afternoon, w'en the old lady's a-washin' up." "Ana in winter ? "

"Oh, I goes to the Band of 'Ope, and I takes the kids there 'times. The Band of 'Ope's a little bit of on right, _for they've a big are there, an' we 'ave songs, an' pichurs on the magic lantern, au' at Chrismus they gives us a jolly good tuck in an a present for nix. It's on right, sir, an' the teachers is jolly kind, though my old man 'e don't b'lieve in 'em; says they're 'umbugs as lead the young people astray an' makes 'em disrespeck their parents." - _

"Since you're a Band of Hope boy, then, you won't be likely to follow in the footsteps of your father." "No fear! Follow 'im ? Not much. I've signed the pledge neither to touch, taste, or 'andle, and ninny's the row I 'ave with the old chap 'cause I won't fetch 'is beer. But 'e doesn't lick me. 'E knows_better'n that."

_ "Very well., Smut, I hope you'll always think of him as an example of what you should avoid, and try to lead a temperate useful life in whatever calling you may adopt." "Oh, I'm goin' to stick 'ere, sir, and be a printer. ". "You wouldn't like to qualify for a reporter would you? " "One o' them other writ-in' chaps? No thenk you, I prefers the machine room." "And you'll have used a lot of our ink on your nose before you've spent many years there, I fancy." - . - - -
"It's my 'ands, sir, as I can't keep' clean, and you See, you can't 'elp totichin' your nose with your 'ands. Least, I cm, t. Thanks sir; yes, I'll 'urry."

About this time I happened to form a friendship Irith a lady and gentleman who had for some yearr laboured in an unostentatious way amonest the puur ot Laysturd. J. %%14b greatly urawn to nenry Radford, who, despite the cares and worries of an important business, could contrive to give so much

of his time to practical work for improving the lives of the "submerged tenth." We soon became fast friends, and our mutual interest in young people led to frequent diacussions concerning our juvenile friends. One night Radford grew eloquent in his praise of a certain lad who was a regular attender at the mission. He had broken him to harness, and naturally viewed the result with the same satisfac- tion that the horse-breaker looks upon the buck- jumper he has turned into a well-behaved animal. "When I came to Laysford, three years ago," said Radford, "this youngster was regarded as a hopeless member of our Sunday-school at St. George's. He had defied every rule, he had flouted every teacher, he had been turned out several times, and yet he seemed to like the gatherings. At the committee meeting, when I was appointed superinteadent, his sins were recounted to me in a way that. made one fear his future would not be particularly bright. His name was Jenks—a name that did not predispose one in favour of its owner. . Well, what's to be done with Angel Jenks ? ' • said I, using the term, as you can suppose in the way that Artemus wrote sarcastic.' " "The word was an inspiration,". I observed. "The name stuck, I'll warrant." "Stuck! I should think so. From that. day to this the lad has been known by nothing else, and he seems rather proud of his soubriquet. Well, it was decided I should tackle him, and tackle him I did. I studied his nature, watched his little evidences of character, and was not long before I concluded that there was some real grit there, and the makings of a goo i man. The heavy hand and the ready frown were no terrors to him, they were only food for his laughter. A firm hand he needed ; but he was won most readily by sympathy. I fount' out that he liked to be dealt, with as a little older than his years. And he was distinctly honest. For instance, if he knew of any lad stealing anything from another—they're a ruin lot in a mission school, you know, and especially down the Sandpits way—he'd never hesitate to accuse the wrong-doer, no matter his age or size, before the class, and probably run the risk of - Immelling for his pains. "About a year after I took him in hand the few boys who were older than he had left the school, ; and his interest in it suddenly deepened. At a meeting of the Band of Hope one night my wife land I, as well as the two ladies who assisted us. were a few minutes late in getting to the hall, and as we arrived we were greatly amused to over- hear Angel Jenks shouting to another lad: ; Winkles, you shut that door, and me and you'll teach these 'ere kids ! ' Such a little thing as that gave me a clue to the lad's character, and he was ; soon karmed with all the authority of a monitor. As a monitor he was, and is, in fact, to this day, most useful, for, being up to all the little tricks of the youngsters he is always competent to stop any of their naughty games. The proved policy, you know, of making is gamekeeper of an old poacher. One of his early sins was to appear at the Band of Hope with his head swathed in linen bandages, only the eyes and nose being visible, and his voice so husky that you couldn't hear what he said was wrong with him. This was his idea of a practical joke, and when during his monitorship others tried to carry down the tradition he speedily intervened." "And you remember about that great Christmas treat ? " remarked Mrs. Radford to her husband, with a merry twinkle in her eye, for she had t keen appreciation of fun. "Tell about Jenks and his behaviour then." Thus urged, Mr. Radford went on : "This will shew you what that youngster was in the rough—the sort of thing we had to tame. It was the first Christmas treat in connection with the Band of Hope during my time, and Angel Jenks had just arrived at the transitory stage in his development. At the table over which I was personally presiding I had him on my right; not so much to give him a seat of honour as to have him under my immediate control. Well, you talk of gluttony! You should have seen that young j rascal polish off the eatables, and boast of drinkiag ten cups of tea." "Gracious!" said I jestingly. "Ten cups of Band of Hope tea? What a stomach!" "Now,. don't you condemn our tea untasted," retorted Radford good hutnouredly, "there's many a worse brew. But you're taking me away from the point, man. I had noticed Jenks was con- fining his attentions to the pastries and neglecting the good bread and butter, so I said: Won't you have some bread, Jenks?' No,' he replied curtly. No, what?' said I, expecting him te add ' thanks ' ; but he - said: No fear, when there's pastries still agoin'.' What a lesson in home influence we had there, eh ? " "And the end of the feast, dear," put in Mrs. Radford again. "Yes, the end of it all, to be sure," spY; Radford, slapping his knee at the recollectiot "No Roman skeleton would have robbed. ths'. youngster of his appetite. Well, after the banquet —as we used to call these humble muffin struggles —was over there was the usual entertainment, and Jenks enjoyed this hugely. At one comic recita- tion he laughed so heartily that he fell off the end of the bench on which he was sitting. And there he lay, helpless with laughter and a too hearty feed. The lad next him said: Shall I lift yc„, up, Jenks ? ' and the angelic one replied: Yes, Hanks, lift me up, but don't bend me.' " "The young savage!'" was my comment. "Precisely. Yet that's the boy that is as circumspect and well-behaved to-day as if he had been reared in a home where the amenities and not the crudest miseries of domestic life were present. It just shews you what sympathetic treat- ment of the little British barbarian will accomplish." Radford watched the rings of smoke from his cigar curl upwards with a satisfactory look on his face, and no doubt le had reason to be pleased with his efforts, for the man who can tame a law- less yon,th from the Sandpits has done something to be proud of. His last words about Angel Jenks that night were: "There's real grit in that lad, and it will shew itself some day, just mt murdee will out." It wog not for some time after this conversatiG.t that made the discovery at which my readers have, no doubt, guessed already, Angel Jenks and Smut were one and the same. Yet all the time I had known him he had managed to keep both characters as distinct as Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde. He was Angel Jenks at the Sunday-school and Band of Hope; Smut, dirty nosed and garrulous, at the office of the Lead,er, and he had, no doubt, a third personality which was presented only to his friends of the Sandpits. • • But the reason why this history of Angel Jenks has been penned must now be stated.

It was a glorious day in early summer, and on such a day I know no part of England that can look so beautiful as the country around Laysford. The town itself, a congeries of industrial villages that have grown up side by side, with arms linked in arms, and awakened one morning to find them- selves a city, is by no means an uncomely place, for industry has not destroyed all its nattiral beauty, while the quaintness of its houses is always a source of pleasure to the visitor. Round about, the country is opulent in attrac- tions. Great, well-wooded plains stretch away from the town on every side, and then the land rises into tree-clad hills, beyond which again we see in the purple distance the far-away mountain- tops. It is truly a place "where every prospect pleases, and only man is vile." For Jenks's father was by no means a rare specimen of the local labouring class. The trail of drink was over the town in those bad old days, and certainly in the Sandpits there was not a single house in which one or more of the inmates did not go to bed drunk on Saturday night. The day of which I write was a Saturday, and had been chosen for the annual excursion of the Band of Hope, at which function Jenks was usually in fine form. Like all the other members he looked forward to it with eager anticipation, and its memory served to please his mind until the time for the next outing was narrowing down. Of this particular excursion he was more enthu- siastic than ever, for its destination was the sea- shore, and it was the first time that the conductors of the Band of Hope had gone so far afield, Laysford being a long distance inland. Few lads of Jenks's class in the town had ever seen the sea before; indeed, hundreds of grown-up people in Laysford have never witnessed that wonder to this day. _

It will be easy, then, to realise the excitement of our little friend as the day approached on which the train was to carry him and his class- mates to the shore of that great, mysterious, rest- less thing which bore on its bosom ships so large that the vessels which plied upon the Lays are mere cockle-shells compared to them—that watery highway which stretched away from Engle to the vnone unknown lands of the Southern APRs. Jenks's only•knowledge of which was due to occa- siunal pictures and stories in the magazines dis- tributed at the Sunday-school. His drunken parent had been behaving worse than ever of late, and as a result poor Jenks was

_ disgusted to find his little brother and eliter cola not share in the joy of this trip to the seaside; Their boots and their only respectable clothes ha, been pawned, and they were left with such rags that he felt it his duty rather to give to his mother the money he had saved up intending to pay their trip tickets. It was only one and sixpence. He even had qualms of conscience in deciding te?, go himself since the youngsters were to be deniea the pleasure, and his mother was so in need of every penny that could be obtained. But they were, after all, only "kids" yet, ht/ reasoned, and perhaps they'd think more of seeini the sea if they waited till they were his age. Air anyway, he was a monitor, and, of course, if didn't turn out the excursion mightn't go on properly. Thus, he easily persuaded himself that it was not only desirable to go, but necessary. What a glorious day it would have been for him if the kids had Only been there! This was the thought that always came uppermost in his mind se the train went dashing past pretty little country stations, whose names Jenks had never time W spell out. And when it rushed through the swat ing summer woods, and the earthy smell, that ut always good in the nostrils of the young, m _weg borne into the carriage by the breezes from land, his mind went,back to the two little wretches he had left disconsolate in that miserable dwelling in the Sandpits. No wonder Jenks was in a poor humour for all the delights he saw. Nothing so dulls the keen edge of enjoyment as the inability tb share one pleasure with those one loves ; and Jenks, despite his assumed contempt for them, really loved, because he pitied, his little brother and sister. The teachers noticed his unusual dulness, taw were at a loss to account for it; the other scholars were too engrossed with the myriad wonders Of the journey to discover that Jenks was not entering into the fun with his accustomed heartiness. When the crowning marvel of the day unfolded its gleaming length before them as they rushed to meet its white foam on the sands, with their long drawn out "Ah!" of satisfaction and surprise, Jenks was only heard to say: "If the kids coula just see this!" He could at least carry home to them- a little souvenir of this great day in his life, and so he gathered a few shells: the despised commonplace of the seashore to most of us, but real treasure- trove to Jenks. These were in his hand inside his jacket pocket when he made his way along the Sandpits late that night, and he gripped them so tightly that he seemed to find in them a talisman which evanished his now squalid surroundings,- and brought to hire again those cooling sea breezes and the noise of the surf as it 'broke on' the sandy shore. Although he was unusually late in arriving st his miserable little home in the back court, hig father was still absent; and, indeed, that besotted creature had not been seen by his wife since be left in the morning, the public-house having claimed his undivided attention since his pay wag placed in his grimy fist. The wretched woman sat awaiting his return on a brokers chair beside a grate, in which flickered scanty fire that only served to make the misery ef the apartment more pronounced. She raised her head wearily as the latch lifted, and in stepped our Jenks with a smile on his face and a sprig of lilac in his cap. "Wed, lad and thee's gotten back?" was her languid greeting. " 'Ad a nice out?" "Yes, mother," Jenks answered, with some shor of eagerness, for he never dreamt of disclosing his inner thoughts to his mother. "I've brought these 'ere shells far Billie and Nan. They're asleep, s pose? " But a noise in the room adjoining told him th 4 the youngsters were awake and expectant; and im another moment they ran to him from their dark some corner to hear his story of the wonders he had seen on his far journey. The shells were a new sensation to the little ones, who had only seen those of the common shell-fish sold in Laysford market-place. Their eves sparkled as they fingered the pretty things, and held then' to their ears at Jenks's bidding to hear the echo of the far resounding sea. "They're real nice," said Nan, lots more? "
"an' was there

"Any's amounts, Nan," answered Jenks' "Heaps!" "An' was there lots o' water in the sea: queried Billie, with wonder in his eyes. "Oh, an awful Lig lot," said Jenks, feeling inadequacy of his vocabulary to describe wilt , himself had seen with mute amaze.

Thus they were prattling N;il ''''''' door opened, and in rolled the father. • His eyes were bloodshot; his clothes showed that he had been in the gutter, perhaps knocked down in a brawl. He was in one of his ugly moods; drink affected him variously, and his sad wife could never tell how she would find him at the end of a debauch. "Why's them kids outen bed a' this time o night?" the wretch asked, as he swayed towards the fireplace. "On'y a-lis'nen to me tellin' about the seal said Jenks.

"You shut up; speak when yer spoken to." wail the response. 'Nan, y' brat, c'me 'ere, an'..r.". thrash ye for 't." But thus spoken to, Nan ran for protection behind her mother, who was still sitting with her face buried in her hands.

This incensed the father, who, picking up the poker, the only fireside utensil which the house possessed, made a move to strike her, when Angel Jenks stepped in front of him and said, his ayes gleaming defiance: i• "No you don't, when I'm here. It's your blame she didn't see the sea 'erself. She's done nuthin' wrong." Infuriated, the drunken father glared at his aon, who had for the first time openly defied biro; and saying, with an oath: "So you'd preveri me, ye young devil, would ye ? " he struck the lad a heavy blow on the head, adding: "Take that for yer cheek."
Poor Jenks fell like a log on the floor. He had just returned from his first long jourtiff 7 his brutal parent had despatched him on anothei —the longest he would ever take.

Often, in after years, when the Radfords end others, who knew the lad either as "Smut" or "Angel Jenks," have been talking of his sad little life's story, a wee curly-haired girl, who came to bless these good people after Jenks took his long voyage to the hidden land, would say: papa, was he really an angel ? " "Yes, dear—now."

Mainley, painter &c., met with rather unpleasant accident on Saturday morning Iss, He was engaged with another man in painting at toe Tanning Co's. works, on a flat roof, when the ladder 0,0 which he was standing, slipped, throwing hip forwatt A large skylight was •directly underneath, ad throug° this he crashed, and down to the floor beneath, a droP of about twelve feet. First aid was at once rendered bi one of the workmen, and. the Warrington Ambulance was telephoned for, and quickly arrived on the scene. The injured youth was conveyed to the Infirmary, he had fortunately escaped with a shaking and sligut cuts, and was discharged on Wednesday last. div.head: Tlig HALF-WAY HOUSE.
div.p: Tlig HALF-WAY HOUSE.
FREE TRADE GONE.
RETALIATION GOING.

NOBODY took Mr. Balfour's Fiscal policy of attetaliation seriously. It was such an obvious refuge from political cross-currents, that its Leniporary character was its only recommenda- Lion. Between the out-and-out Chamber- lainites on the one hand, and the equally determined Unionist Free Traders on the Other, there was no hope or help for Mr. alfour except in some half-way house which, while not entirely opposed to one section of his party, was a distinct encouragement to the Other. Mean inziess.

RETAL-lATION may, of course, mean anything or nothing. It may COV'er the rankest Pro- tection, or be consistent with the purest theory of Fiscal freedom. It may be a simple matter °if foreign policy, of international relationships. /tecently we have seen the Government making treaties with the two chief European nations; such treaties could be extended to trade as easily as they dispose of territory. In fact, the treaties as they stand are by no means unconcerned with trade interests. Bargaining between nations over trade is rossible without a violation of Free-Trade principles. On the other hand, Retaliation may cover all that Protectionists want. It may require the imrccition of hew:), duties upon imported Foods. It may require, as indeed Mr. Balfour u3hl us it would require, a complete reversal of the preent Fiscal policy of this country. ut still to speak of Retaliation without giving any further definition of its application Is to use a meaningless phrase for the purpose °..f deluding the public. This was probably 'lr. Balfour's intention.

°Pposed to Preference. THOSE people who have hoped against hope that the Prime Minister would come down on the Free-Trade side of the fence have not been 'IOW to point out that Retaliation was neces- liarily opposed to any scheme of giving a Preference to the Colonies. To give an ltdequate preference to the Colonies would :Tivolve a permanent tax not only upon the 'ood of the people, hut upon raw materials as Veil. No fair and just system of giving a Preference to Colonial produce could stop short °I taxing the raw materials which the Colonies „ Produce, and taxing it to the same extent as the food. But the imposition of any perma- trmt tax upon these articles would make a eYstem of Retaliation impossible. A system of Retaliation by the imposition of duties upon foreign imported goods rru3t ?lot only give the power to impose such duties. It must also give the power to take them off ,Igain whenever necessary. The whole idea of Aletaliation is one of bargaining, by which one t'ountry can induee another to reduce hostile tariffs. "If you tax our goods we shall tax Yours; and if you take the taxes off our goods will take them off yours "—there you have ,brle matter put into simple, every-day language. vvhether or not such a policy would or could Illeet with any success is another mattet. The thief point to be remembered is that, once we Vad promised the Colonies to put a permanent ha upon certain foreign imports, our power to t"argain with foreign countries and our power "0 take off taxes upon their goods would be Zone. °Pposed to Protect!on.

t. For. very similar reasons a policy of Retalia- -2011 is opposed to Protection. You can only have a system of Protection when the duties nich are put upon foreign imports are made vermanent; and, as we have already seen, it Would be impossible to carry out a policy of taliation unless the Government had perfect Ireedom of negotiation; that is, freedom to Llce off duties when and how they liked, with- ,ollt cousidering the interests of any particular tl'acles. Mr. Chamberlain, in the early clays (4.4 his campaign, said this freedom of negotia- tion was necessary. Said he at Birmingham, ‘)/1 May 15th, 1903:

We will recover our freedom, resume the power Of negotiation, and, if necessary, retaliation, Whenever our own interests Rnd our relations between our Colonies are threatened by other People. 11./7hen Mr. Chamberlain made this 'Aotement 4ic had not adopted Protection; indeed, in the Llaine speech be declared himself to be a Free "--rader' and opposed to Protection. The idea Protextion is to build up home industries °Y keeping out, or at least checking, foreign t.Prapetition. Directly you adopt protective noti es you encourage industries which other- Ivise would not exist, or would not exist to 811(th a particular extent. While some trades would be ruined, other manufacturers would commence to build and invest capital; the conditions of their trade would have ty be altered, and various changes in business would have to take place, 411 of which would involve %IT serious outlay. It will be immediately seen that once protective duties were imposed liPon foreign goods it would be very difficult `4l take them off again. To take them off Vould inflict serious hardship 'upon those panufacturers and others who had altered neir business and invested their capital in der to meet the new ccnditions. But, as we '4ve seen, Retaliation could not be carried out Without this freedom to take off protective pies. Thus you cannot have Protection and aliation at the same time.

--- Retaliation Unsuccessful. 1. RETALIATION is by no means a new policy. .3/4ike Protection, it has been tried by other .(111ntries, and without success.' It has inflicted Itliury to the trade of all the nations who have Oulged in this method of warfare, while ILlose who have looked on have 'reaped the Ileflt. The French and Italian tariff war ?stilted in a loss of over £9,000,000 a-year to ne two countries. If anybody will give the ratter careful thought they will realise that etaliation can have no other effect. That Mr. Balfour never seriously intended adopt this policy seems quite evident from 111,e fact that by the mouth of two •of his chief n'tinisters he has sent his blessing to Mr. ichemberlain upon his latest effort to drum the onist party into Protection. Protection 1114 st, in any case, be the end of Retaliation; Zlld Mr. Balfour, who has used that meanino-- reBB phrase for party purposes, is now on the i!ftd towards the final goal which I\dr. Chamber- has set up.

div.head: FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES.
THE LICENSING BILL.

In spite of strenuous opposition on the part of the Free Churches, Temperance organisa- tions, and a large number of public-minded citizens, the Licensing Bill has almost run its course through tlie House of Commons. This result has caused much sorrow and bitterness among the Free Churches. The Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., President of the National Free Church Council, issued a letter to the ministers and members of the Free Churches call- ing on them to unite in a day for prayer, that even at the eleventh hour this calamity might be averted. Many of the Free Churches took this course. General regret is felt that the "Representative S' Church Council should have endorsed the policy of the Govern- ment in this matter.

div.head: HOLIDAYS.
div.p: THE HOLIDAYS.

The air is full of holiday movements, and the Free Churches are more and more taking an interest in people's holidays. For those people who are able to visit Switzerland the Free Church Council announces special services. These will be conducted at the Grand Hotel, Eiger, Grindelwald, on Sunday, August 7, by the Rev. A. T. Kirby, A. T. S. (of Southport), and the following Sundays in August by the Rev. Adam Scott. The Rev. E. A. Johnston Ross, MA. (of Cambridge), is to conduct the services during September.

div.head: SEASIDE CONFERENCES.
div.p: SEASIDE CONFERENCES.

An important series of meetings is announced by the National Free Church Council, at Scar- borough on August 29 and 30, and at Blackpool on August 31 and September 1. The Rev. F. B. Meyer will preside at these meetings, and the Rev. Thomas Law, Rev. Thomas Waugh, and others will take part. At these two popular resorts there are sure to be a large number of Christian workers from all parts of the country, and the idea is to arrange two days of interesting and instructive meetings for people thus gathered together. On the first night at each place there will be a great de- monstration, and the nexp morning there will be a " Sunrise " Prayer Meeting at seven o'clock. This will be followed by a gathering of ministers and Christian workers at eleven o'clock, and a Bible Reading in the afternoon. There will be an informal conference over tea on Girls' Guild work, to be followed in the even- ing by another public meeting, to take the form of a great Christian Endeavour Rally. Mr. J. Compton Rickett, M.P., the member for tho borough, is to preside at one of the meet- ings at Scarborough. There can be no doubt that this series of meetings will prove very popular, and should be the inauguration of a new movement.

div.head: MINISTERS' OXFORD CONFERENCE.
div.p: MINISTERS' OXFORD CONFERENCE.

The Ministers' Holiday Conference will be held this year at Oxford, the dates being September 12th to 17th, inclusive. At the invitation of the Rev. R. J. Campbell, who has conducted these meetings the last two years, the' Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., as President of the National Free Church Council, has been :a- quested to assume the principal respottior ;:ity for the conduct of the meetings. It is prf,uti-• cally decided that the National Council will shortly take over the management of these conferences.

div.head: ACTION AT THE BY-ELECTIONS.
div.p: ACTION AT THE BY-ELECTIONS.

The National Free Church Council has been taking a more or less prominent part in the recent by-elections. It is recognised by the Government supporters that the Education Acts have induced Nonconformists to vote against them. The Conservative party have con- centrated their efforts, in many instances, in an attempt to divide the Nonconformist vote. At Devonport at the last moment statements ware issued that Dr. Clifford did not support Mr. Bern's candidature. and at Sowerby use was made of the telegram from Johannesbutk; en Chinese Labour. At the last by-election—at Owestry—letters of some Nonconformist Unionists, written before the passing of the Act, m- were reprinted, in order to allege that an i portant section of Nonconformity was in favour of the Government's Education policy. Needless to say these statements were not very success- ful, hut Free Churchmen need to be on their guard against attempts to divide their forces on this great issue.

div.head: EXAMPLE .CIF FREE CHURCH UNION.
div.p: EXAMPLE .CIF FREE CHURCH UNION.

An interesting example of the value of i'roe Church union conies. from Blackpool. Some little thee ago the Rev. Walter Leicester, Methodist Free Church minister, wits pros- trated by serious illness, which necessitated. his abandonment of work. The Council, at its. meeting, felt that something more than a 111011.% resolution was required, and immediately the, several ministers of the town volunteered to. occupy Mr. Leicester's pulpit for five different Sundays and provide their own supplies. The, congregation affected gladly Accepted the offer, and the arrangement has given great satisfac- tion. The Churches have been blessediu sharing this gracious deed. ,
OPENING OF LEYSIAN MISSION ETTELPINGS.

The Leysian Mission Buildings, which were opened not long ago by the Prince of Walesr are described in this month's Free Church. Chronicie. The writer claims them to be the finest settlement premises in the world. The. buildings have been erected at a cost of £112.000. There are some 125 rooms in the. building. The premises are divided 'into three settlements—the Sisters', the Leysian School, and the Moulton House. These three settle- ments will provide a staff of 60 workers, who either in part or the whole time will be actively interested in the mission.
GIPSY SMITH IN SOUTH APMCA..

The extraordinary success which attended. the efforts of Gi?sy Smith, the National Free Church Council's missioner, in South Africa has continued. At Kimberley, where the visit was attended with much excitement, the missioner was given the use of the carriage and pair used by Mr. Chamberlain and Lord Milner. At Johannesburg, a special building had been erected at a cost of ' £,0400, me, here over 3COO persons thronged to hear the Gipsy night by night; a very fleciP 4411Pres- sion has been made on the town. Gipsy Smith will probably I egin his ivork in England again at the beginning of November. Arrangements are being made for a big welcome home to be given when he arrives in London.
DR. CLIFFORD'S LIFE-STORY.

Everything that Dr. Clifford writes is sire to be interesting, speciallY if it be about himst4lL Dr. Clifford has commenced in the Free C'hurch- man a series entitlod, " Pages from my Life. Story." He gives in the August number of tleit magazine "A Glimpse of English Village Life La the Forties," and an interesting glimpse it

The famour Amati violoncello played by the late Friedrich Gruetzmacher, of Dresden, for forty years has been sold to Mr. Albert Gowa, the leading violon- cellist at Hamburg, for the sum of £1,300. When Mme. Louise, an Isle of Wight palmist, told a police constable who visited her in disguise that he would shortly take legal proceedings in which he would be suceessful, she told the truth. At ityde she was fined on the constables evidence,

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
Warrington Corporation and Stockton Heath Market. IMP3RT ANT BUSINESS.

This Council held its fortnightly meeting on Tuesday at Dutton Workhouse, Mr. G. Pilling (vice-chairman), presiding. There were also present :—Admiral Jones- Parry, Messrs. T. Wright, J. Stokes, J. Spruce, J. Hallows, J. Whitley, C. Roylance, A. G. Guest, J. L• Jones, J. Mounfield, T. Antwis, J. Bolshaw, H. Eyes, G' Egerton Warburton, J. Whitlow, J. H. Davies, J. Smith, W. Harrison, S. Horton, J. Fryer, R. Billington, W. E. Hough (acting clerk), A. E. Hulse (assistant clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer of health), J. Swinton and W. Diggle (surveyors), and J. Farrington (inspector of nuisances.)
WESTON IMPROVEMENTS.

Mr. Diggle estimated that the cost of improvements which the Weston Parochial Committee recommended should be carried out in the village would be £6B us. It was decided that the work be proceeded with. THE STRONG COMPLAINT FROM MOORE.

Dr. Adams reported that there was still some ground of complaint of the smell arising from the sewer at the bottom of Mr. Bleckly's garden at Moore. A certain amount of smell arose from an open conduit over the railway. As a remedy he suggested repeated flushing or the piping of the sewage across the railway. The rest of the sewerage arrangements were under the crops, and could not be inspected.

div.head: NORLEY WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: NORLEY WATER SUPPLY.

The Local Government Board wrote with regard to the Council's application for sanction to borrow £3OO for works of water supply for Norley,that they were not prepared to approve the partial scheme submitted as they were satisfied that a proper supply of water for the whole township was necessary. The Council thould ascertain what was the best and most economical scheme of supplying the whole township. If it was decided to obtain a supply otherwiselthan from the Vyrnwy mains, the Board should be furnished with (1) information as to the daily yield of all sources from which a supply might be taken as ascertained by gaugings over a lengthened period,(2) a report by a competent chemist upon analysis of samples of water obtained from all such sources, and (3) a report made after a careful ' survey of the surroundings of the sources. The Acting Clerk said the Council had already given instructions to Mr. Timmins to prepare a report to the above effect. BEDFORD STREET, STOCKTON HEATH. _ _ _

In reply to the Council's'application for an order in- vesting them with the powers of an urban authority under the Private Street Works Act 1892 in respect of Bedford-street, Stockton Heath, the Local Government Board requested that a resolution might be passed by the Council undertaking to take over thestreetas ahigh- way repairable by the inhabitants at large when the re- quired works had been carried out and a copy of the resolution forwarded to the Board.
On the motion of Mr. Whitley, seconded by Mr. Hallows a resolution that the Council take over the street was adopted.
THE WARRINGTON FIRE BRIGADE'S SERVICES IN RURAL DISTRICTS. _ _ _

Mr. J. Lyon Whittle,TownCle;COi Warrington,wrote asking to be furnished with the rateable value of such of the townships as the Council thought should have the services of the Warrington Fire Brigade. The establishment expenses averaged £525 per annum for the last five years and he thought that each authority hav- ing the services of the brigade should Contribute to such expense in proportion to the rateable value. The township should as far as possible be kept within a five mile radius of the Borough, but if a part only came within the 5 mile limit the Corporation were prepared to allow the Brigade to attend fires in the whole of such township. Mr. J. L. Jones said he matter bad been discussed by the Moore Parish Council rind he was instructed to ask for an approximate estimate of the charge. The Acting Clerk said he had interviewed the Deputy- Town Clerk who said he was getting some figures out and would forward them. Until it was known how many parishes on the Warrington side would join in the expense, they could not estimatewhat charge would fall upon the Cheshire townships. It was a matter which the Parish Councils themselves had full power to deal with. The matter was deferred until further particulars are forthcoming.

div.head: THELWALL IMPROVEMENT.
div.p: A THELWALL IMPROVEMENT.

The following resolution was forwarded from the Thelwall Parish Council: "That the District Council be requested to put pressure upon the Ship Canal Com- pany- to put in repair the roadway under the Canal Bridge in Waste-lane, Therwall." The Surveyor said the repairs had almost been carried Out. WARRINGTON CORPOR ATION AND STOCKTO-N HEATH. MARKET.

Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, Town Clerk of Warrington, wrote pointing out that the Warrington Corporation were owners of the markets and fairs held within the borough. Such markets and fairs had been held in Warrington from a very ancient period, being confi-ned by Royal Charters in the reigns of Henry HI. and Edward I. and by the War- rington Improvement and Market Act, 1854. Within recent years a rival market had been set up at Stock- ton Heath within the district of the Rural Council. This market had ostensibly been established just outside the Borough for the purpose of evading the tolls levi- able upon all market commodities sold within the Borough. It was clearly a disturbance of the markets belonging to the Conporation. Before taking the instructions of the Corporation as to commencing the necessary steps for the closing of the market, the writer asked for the opinion of the Rural Council on the matter, and if they 'were prepared to take any such steps. Mr. Whitley : Can it be called a market when no' tolls are levied?
The Chaitman : The Corporation think they are entitled to tolls. I don't think we are in a vasition to discuss this matter.

_ The Acting Clerk said he communicated with the Town Clerk by telephone, and Mr. Whittle sieemed to have been a the -opinion that the roads on which the market mas held belonged to the District Council.' They did not, and therefore the matter could not be dealt with by that District Council. Be had not seen, the charter under which the Warrington market was I established, it might be that the Corporation had right to prevent •peopie establishing,niarketslwithin w five miles radius, but he did not know. Clearly the Cot-weil could notZdo much in the matter because the market WAS TrOt held an their highways. Mr. Hallows wished to correct a mistake in the: Town Clerles letter. The origin of the market was not' to defraud 'Warrington. Potatoes used to he sent to, Manchester by boats -filom London Beidge,,and dealers- got into the habit °teeming to Stockton Heath to buy what theyrequired before the cargoes wove dispatched.; Mr. Whitley said there was not the least-doubt that, if the Corporation did not take steps to :prevent the market being held, something would have to be done by the local authorities or the District 'Council. Only, on the previous Friday there were no fetaar than 180. vehicles at the market, and some contained as many asi sixty-ilve hampers of potatoes. Reckonin,g the average load at twenty hampers, the total was 3480Miampers for a single day. The market was held on three days per week. _
-The Chain= : The market is on Coun-ff Council' roads. Mr. Bolshaw I -think another week -will about finish it. It was decided that no action be taken iwthe matter..
TSIPROMMYLENX •SfJHEIVE FALLS TRIIOUr.' H.

Mr. H. M. iDavies,wrote intimating that he was unable. to contribute £2O towards the cost of the improve- ments at Church-street, Frodsham. He cornkidered that, his previous ,offer which included the giving,ef the land and team labour, a generous one. The Acting -Clerk said Mr. Davies offered £lO but the Council •did not think that was sufficient. He supposed the improvement wotfid now fall through.

div.head: ME TIME OF MEETING.
div.p: ME TIME OF MEETING.

Admiral Jones-Parry in accordance with notice,moved "That the resolution passed at the meetir4 of the Council on May Srdfizing the time of the meeting of the Council at three o'clock during the summer months and two o'clock during the winter he rescinded:and that future meetings be held immediately after the conclu- sion of the Board of Guredians, but in any case not later than three o'clock in theaunmer months and two o'clock in the winter." The motion Waf3 agreed tto. Mr. Stokes : You have ,v;-en this time, Admiral Parry. Admiral Parry: You ought to give me & silver medal. (Laughter.)
