div.p: PRE‘,TODI-0-T. Fe-rXTIL WATER SUPPLY.

_ The sanction of the Locat Government Board was received for the borrowlrtg.of £382 for works of water supply for the township .of The Council fixed the ebarge for water at Prestan-o- th'-Hill at 3d. per week on houses not exceeding Z 3 per annum rent, and 10 per cPnt.. on all other property. "AS ABO M INA MY. " NUISANCE AT ‘VALTON. MR. F. MONKS'S •COM PLAINT.

Mr. Swinton reported that he had taken levels along the road from Stockton Heath Swing Bridge to the Stag Inn, Walton, and found that there was sufficient fall for a sewerage scheme to connect with the present Stockton Beath sewer in Ellesn ere-re.ad,but the fall would have to be about one in four hunched and the sewer at the Stag Inn 4ft. Ohm. to 5 feet deep. A new sewer from Twenty Steps Bridge to the Stag Inn could be got 6 feet deep at the Stag Inn with a fall of one in '275. There was plenty of fall to this road from the rest of Walton on that side of the Ship Canal. M. Mounfield said that' during the dry weather an abotr'nable nuisance had been caused by the .tench arisii.g from the present sewer which ran through Mr. F. Monks's garden. If the present conditions continued the result would probably be serious. Mr. Monks was very moth about the matter, and something ought to be done as soon as possible. His opinion was that Walton should have a sewer independent of Stockton Heath. To join with the lattt r parish would not be a satisfactory solution, for the sewer would always be getting stopped up, and it would be a constant source of expense and friction between the two parishes its to who should clean the sewer out when the stoppages occurred.

div.head: MODERN LAWN TENNIS.
div.p: MODERN LAWN TENNIS.

Mr. William Heinemann has published a book on "* Modern Lawn Tennis " by P. A. Vaile which will, we -think, rank ihighly with all devotees of the game. The .author is not a " champion," and unlike champions who I have written about the game he refrains from going I:above our heads. Mr. Vaile is, however, an expert player and a student of slawn tennis. What he does not know about the game is hardly worth knowing, and moreover he makes a paint of imparting his knowledge , man intelligible, helpful, and readable fashion. In his 1 preface he says "it ~.)es not occur to a champion 1 that the very A.B.C. in all its detail must :be marked out and shown; and then to go i, to the other extreme there are many important points in connection with the flight of the ball, the manner of making, or missing well-known strokes, which are not fully and explicitly dealt with. . . ." Mr. Valle starts right at the beginning, and advises as to laying out the court. 'Then follow some sound words of advice as to the "implements," after which the reader is taught how to grip his tacket and play the game. From the service to the "smash" and "cut" every stroke is dealt with lucidly and attractively. Mr. Vaile ; tells you where you should be, and even where the ball I should be under the circumstances. All the reader'has to Ido is hit it 'with the. centre" of the racket. In addition ito the chapters on strokes of the game, there are others which deal with both singles and doubles, ' mixed doubles, tactics in each, tournament play, , personalities, roll of bonour, rules, &c. Then there are , the illustrations and diagrams. We have reserved the best for the last. Mr. Vaile's book is rendered unique by the series of beautiful action photographs taken 4.,Tecially by Mr. G. W. Beldam, the Middlesex cricketer. Mr. Beldam has a genius for lightning snap-shots of .players in various games, and he has "caught" most of the "cracks" in the act for the benefit of Mr. Vaile and his readers. The photos are excellently reproduced and, together with the author's diagrams, make tha look all that could be desired by the tennis player, how- wer humble or honoured. Six shillings is the price of • "Modern Lawn Tennis"a.E.dlno enthusiast willbegrudge it.

Stockton Heath and Warrington Light Railways. The Widening of Old London Road. Sir,—The object of my communications was not to attempt the futile and unprofitable task of convincing Mr. England, but to correct his mis-statements and to give the facts of the case. This having been done, no useful purpose will be served by a discussion of Mr. England's private opinions or his preference for the opinions of others over plain facts. The preference for darkness rather than light is by no means new. Nor do I desire to place any obstruction in his way of escape out of the difficulty in which he voluntarily and recklessly placed himself. gladly therefore accede to his request to be excused from looking up law reports and books, particularly because, judging from his previous essay at interpreting and quoting legal documents, I very much doubt whether he would understand or be able properly to quote the same. The rumours which Mr. rmgland hears do not seem to be heard by anyone else, and I imagine that be is either the victim of some friendly chaff because of his eager credulity, or he has not yet given up' playing at ghosts.' The land in front of the Red Lion is private property and so much of it as has been thrown into the street was acquired by the Corporation under Notice to Treat; and with regard to the potato market, the Corporation have no m )re power to stop this than to stop Mr. England's morning milk.—Yours &c. H. J. WESTBROOK.
Stockton Heath, 28th July, DOI

The Representation of Warrington Sir,—ln your editorial columns you have referred;. I believe, once or twice to the idea of a compromise between the Liberal and Labour parties. Perhaps, then, I may be pardoned if I take up the Labour cause and place before your readers their position from the stand- point of party interest. Why do you wish a compromise? Are you afraid -that the power of the Labour Party will upset Mr. Crosfield's chances? Apparently you are, and you desire, I suppose, to consolidate what you call the pro- gressive vote in favour of one candidate, Ms Croslield. Ought the Labour Party to help in this con- solidation? Is it in the best interests of the party that they should do so? It is, I think, very much open to doubt whether they ought even to entertain the idea of a compromise, which evidently they do not. Apart from the fact that there is an objectionto political com- pacts and a feeling of antagonism to both the orthodox parties on the part of the geueral or middle working class, there are one or two other reasons why the Labour Party should pursue an independent coarse. Take this view of the matter. Suppose the Labour Party do support Mr. Crosfield and he does not get in. Have the Labour Party gained anything thereby? No, Rather will they have lost what in this short life of ours cannot well be afforded to pass by—time and opportunity. Bat suppose he does get in, what then will be the gain of the Labour Party? The gain, if I mistake not, will be the gain of tho Liberal party, and not of the Labour Party. Again, who cannot see that the tight of the Labour Party will then be a much stiffer job than it is to-day. Enmity mast sooner or later arise between the two. What does the Labour Party exist for if not to put Labour men into Parliament? Is it likely that the Labour Party are going to calmly and serenely put the rope round their own necks to be hanged by your party for supplying the men to do the hanging operation? Is your party any more likely to fall in love with the Labour Party? No sir, I do net believe it is. How then you can expect the Labour Party to accede to your requests certainly mystifies me. Would it be con- sidered very much more outrageous if the Labour Party suggested that you shonl.l combine with them to return their candidate, even if he shouhl happen to be a stranger? And would the Labour candidate under giuch conditions stand any less chance than your candi- date under similar circumstances? I think not. Another view of the case may be put after this fashion. Supposing we do have a three cornered fight and the present Tory member is aglin returned, who suffers most—your party or the Labour? I think your party will have suffered the heaviest blow, for at the most the Labour Party can only enter this next election to test their strength and to prepare for the future. Taking all things in all I think the Labour Party would do well to have as little to do as possible with any liberal Labour Alliance. There may be narrow- minded Labour men, the party itself may be considered selfish and narrow,but it is no more selfish and narrow 'than the other two parties. And finally let me say thin, that thp Labour movement is growing, and however things go at the next election you may be sore of this,-that the Labour Party will make a fair show. A Lailieur candidate would not be without support from Liberal and Conservative voters, and my candid opinion is this, that with a wise, reason- able, energetic and continuous campaign conducted by seine of the hest Labour men we have, a fairly good Labour candidate would produce something portaging of the nature of a surprise to both our Liberal and Tory friends. I write this from a Labour Party stand- point though not a member of the Labour Party itself. Any further comments you like to make on this subject will be welcome. Remember, however, I only eiya what I myself ,conceive to be the Labour'Party side of the question. In conclusion let me ask you this question. Is it a -wise policy for the Labour Party to put their Mist in Liberal capitalists, however moral and well meaning they may be?
" POLITICUS."
Rev. I!. Dunnico and his Critics.

Sir,—l regret having to ask for further space in which to continue a worthless and profitless discussion. Were it not for the fact that it gives me an opportunity of exposing the hollow pretentious of "P.B. " " A.A.' and the clique they represent I should decline to have' any further dealings with what may be truthfully termed *coterie of wrargling and meddlesome gossips. I should be perfectly justifed Mr. Editor in publishing the full names of your correspondents, for although they have written in your .columns anonymously they have not hesitated to boast about tkeir dishonest methods in certain circles. Rowever if they have not the moral courage to disclose their own identity it is because they know that they would be laughed to scorn by all men who have the slightest regard for truth and honour. May'l for one morient deal With "lA. A." Evidently he is a disciple of Marie Correlli and' that explains everything. -I prefer myself to follow more reliable and trustworthy people than Mario Correlli, but "Birds of a feather flock together." Now "A. A." complains of nay mode of controversy and asserts that very rarely have I written in a'Christ-like spirit. To that accusa- tion I give a direct negative. I can quote from the utterances of Christ far stronger and more sarcastic terms—than any I have ever used—when called upon to deal with permits acting from mean and sordid motives. No man wko has met me on equal terms can say that I have ever wren attempted to take an unfair advantage, but wheue clique of nobodies too cowardly to face the music arrange to attack me under various noms de plume and by dishonest tactics then I feel perfect- ly justified in "answering them according to their folly." Let me give an example of the upright dealings of people'" who have a deep sense of the sacredness of their cause." " A.A.' in last week's issue takes a garbled quotation from a letter written more than a year ago in. reply to an attack made upon a sermon I then delivered, by one subscribing himself "Protestant." Now this enlightened "Protestant " stooped to do a meaner and more contemptible trick than any honest Jesuit wettldstoop to. After writing to the "Observer " anonymously he wrote privately to me, signing him- self a" Well-wisher," calling my attention to the unjust and cowardly attack made-upon me,and ttrging me for the sake of those who might be led astray to reply to same. This is the type of correspondents who have a deep sense of the sacredness of their cause an the type that one is expected to deal with in a lamb-like spirit. Such -people are hyprocrites " of tae first water.' Another member of the sameclique who has appeared under at least half-a-dozen different notes de plume within the last few months recently attacked " Social Brotherhoods" and various other things and joined " lona "in a tirade against political clubs. Possibly there is room for reform in all organizatious, but if your readers had known that this self same purity campaigner might frequently be found in a low music hall then his letter would have been valued for what it was worth, and even " lona " would have been compelled to admit that there were bigger hyprocrites outside the church than in it. The crax of the whole matter iies here. "P. B. " claims " A. A." as her friend,and"Protestant"is a friend of "A. A.'s." These threeappear under at least is dozen ,` floras do plume," and it is this little clique of nobodies which is ever on the alert to take an unfair advantage. The whole affair would be amusing if it were not so despicable. My letter, Mr. Editor, has already grown to alconsiderable length, and so I will reserve my reply to "P. B." antil next week, and that will bring the correspondence to a close so far as I am concerned.- -Yours sincerely,
IL DUNNICO.
The " Distress " Concert.

At the half-yearly meeting of the Warrington I.L.P. a report was presented by the auditors in account with the recent concert held in aid of the distress. It was found after expenses that there was a surplus 'of £4O ss. which has been distributed as follows :—To Rev. W.Bracecamp's Fund, £1 55.; Iron Workers Distress Fund, £ll 55.; Salvation Army Distress Fund, £ll 55.; Ragged School Distress Fund, 'lll 55.; Salvation Army Walking Day Fund for Poor Children, £2 12s. 6d.; Ragged School Walking Day yuad for Poor Child,ren, 124. 6d.; total, £4O ss.

div.head: FASIIIONABLE WEDDING AT
div.p: FASIIIONABLE WEDDING AT
FRODSHAM,
Garratt —Norman.

An important and interesting wedding took place on ' Thursday afternoon at the Frodsham Parish Church, the contracting parties being Lieut. George Herbert Garrett, late of the South Lancashire Regiment,and subsequently of the Ist Nigeria Regiment son of the late Mr. George-Garratt,solicitor of Runcorn and Frodsham and Miss Olive Mary Norman daughter of the late Mr. C. M. Norman and Mrs. Carpenter. The church was crowded with a large and fashionable congrega- tion, which included over 200 guests. The Rev. H. B Blogg, M.A., (Vicar) officiated, assisted by the Rev. E. Chorley, Vicar of lace. The service was fully choral; Mr. C. H. Hibbert L.L.C.M. officiating at the organ, and rendering a fine selection of music during the arrival of the guests. The bride who was given away by her uncle, Mr. Douglas Norman, of London looked very pretty in a charming gown of white crepe de chine with deep flounce of Tambour lace and ruches of chiffon, and berthe and drapery of beautiful lace to match, with high belt and sash of crêpe de chine. Her veil was of Brussells net with wreath of real orange blossoms. She wore a spleildid diamond pendant, the gift of the bride- groom, and' carried a lovely bouquet of choice flowers, also the gift of the bridegroom. She was attended by Isix bridesmaids, the Misses Florence Emilyand Beatrice !Mary Garrett (sisters of the bridegroom), Miss Emily Maud Weaver (cousin of the bridegroom), and the Misses Phyllis, Aenid, and Doris Carpenter (sisters of the bride), who wore charming costumes of ivory silk voile over glace' silk, with transparent yokes of gathered chiffon, and fichus of voile trimmed with lace, and deep belts of pale blue and pink ribbons. Across the shoulders were worn stoles of combined pale blue and pink chiffon. Their hats were of white crinoline trimmed with pink sweet peas,pale blue ribbon and tulle. They ea^h carried bouquets of sweet peas tied with pale blue ribbon, and wore blue pendants of French enamel set with pearls, the gifts of the bridegroom. Mr. Harold P. Weaver acted as bast man. The hymns "0 Father, all creating," and "Rest in the Lord" were heartily sung by the choir and congregation, and the psalm "God be merciful unto us:r taken toMacfarren's setting in B flat. The full choi were in attendance and the service fully choral As the happy pair left the church kendelssohn's "Wedding March " pealed forth from the organ, while the usual showers of confetti and rice Were greatly in evidence. The bells rang out chimes at intervals during the day. The reception was held at Castle Park,Frodsham mamas being erected on the lawn. Messrs. Bollands of Chester, caterers supplied the wedding cake and conducted the whole of the arrangements, Messrs. Dickson and M..ssrs. Garnett being responsible for the floral and other decorations at the park. Mr. Joseph Gorst, draper, Frodsham,supplied Drill Hall decorations for Lieutenant Garratt's supper to 300 inhabitants. The honeymoon is to be spent. in Sutherland, Scotland,prior to Lieutenant and Mrs. Garratt taking up their residence in Egypt where the former has received an important appointment. The bride's travelling dress was of pale grey voile trimmed with white lace insertion, tangerine velvet and ruches of grey chiffon. She wore a grey hat with trimmings of tangerine, and a white ostrich feather stole. The guests included Mr. and Mrs. Carton de Weart, Mr. and Mrs. W. _ HOUSEi of Commons, Westminster, Tuesday, 26th July, 1904. Thomas Birchall, Esq., J.P., Warrington. WARRINGTON TRADING INQUIRY.

Dear sir,—l have just received here a copy of the "Warrington Guardian" of Saturday last, containing a statement to the effect that the Inquiry was closed on Thursday last. I was unfortunately unable to be present on the latter date, having to attend the Man- chester Assizes on a subpcena, and the decision (which I now hear of for the first time) has come upon me as a complete surprise. I must, without a moment's delay, enter my strongest protest against it. , I hope to be able to get hack to Lancashire to-morrow when I will consult with my colleagues as to the obtain- ing of certain further information from the Corporation books, and otherwise. Without this information you COUNCIL COMMISSIONERS PRESENT must know that the Inquiry will be incomplete, even if it is not rendered a complete farce. THEIR REPORT. I I will write you further when I get back, meanwhile enter this protest at the first moment after I hear of ; the remarkable step you took on Thursday night. if Nothing to Support the Allegations of With kind regards, yours faithfully, S. NOMMTRY WILLIAMS. Corruption " P.S.—Under the circumstances, I feel justified in sending a copy of this letter to the Warrington papers. S.N.W.

The Commissioners appointed by the Corporation tl inquire "into all trad.ng by past and present mem- bers of the Council or officials of the Corporation with the Corporation, either direct or indirect, through limited companies or officials of such companies, or as contractors or sub-contractors, or any dealings o r transactions of any kind whatever between members of the Town Council or officials of the Corporation and the Corporation," have presented their report to his Worship the Mayor (Alderman Bolton). We have been favoured by the Mayor with a copy of the report, his Worship being of opinion that as the matter had been so long before the public he felt it his duty to take the public into his confidence at the earliest possible moment by allowing the report to be published. The report reads as follows TRADING INQUIRY. _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ July 29th, 1901.

To the Worshipful the Mayor, Sir,—ln submitting the results of the inquiry into the trading of the Corporation from April Ist, 1896 to March 3 at, 1903, upon which, at the request of the Town Council, we have been engaged for nearly a year,,,Ye report that after examining many thousands of documents,eve ry official or servant of the Corpor- ation able to give evidence on matters within the terms of the reference, and such other persons as were willing to appear before the commission, and after carefully weighing and testing the whole of the evidence, we find that in respect of trading transac- tions between the Corporation and limited companies in which members or officials of the Corporation were interested, there is no evidence of an improper influence having been used to secure contracts or sub- contracts for such companies and no evidence of any improper influence having been used during the execution of such contracts or sub-contracts. We find further that the public interests were always carefully safeguarded in respect both to the purchase of materials and the carrying out of various works ; competitive tenders being duly obtained awl the low- est usually accepted. Where the lowest tendera were not accepted we have ascertained by careful inquiry that there were adequate reasons for such action and that the tenders finally accepted were those which in view of all the circumstances of each Case were the most favourable, and that the acceptance was made in the interests of the ratepayers. There appear to have been a few transactions of a questionable nature ; they are set forth in appendixes C and D. With these, relatively unimportant excep- tions we have found nothing to support the allegations of corruption agains tthe members and officials of the corporation which were so glibly made by the leaders of the agitation, which preceded and produced the Inquiry. On the other hand.' during our protrac- ted investigations, we have found many proofs of earnest and single minded work for the 'public !good by members of the oorporatisn and of devotion to duty on the part of officials and servants. We desire to place on record our thanks to every official who has been called before us as a witness or who has helped in the preparation of documentary evidence or the collection of information for the Commision. Any qhformation asked for by any individual Commis- sioner was always supplied as promptly as possible, courteously and cheerfully. We hand you herewith all the documents relating to' the Inquiry, including minutes of evidence and of the proceedings at all but the first and second sittings of the Commission ; at these no shorthand note was taken. The para- graphs in the prints are numbered consecutively and the numbers cited in the appendixes to our report refer to these. div.head: Premature Closure.
div.p: a Premature Closure.
FOUR CENTURIES OF LAND HOARDING.

I have shown you how this fortunate family was richly endowed by Henry VIII., and Edward VT. with gifts of thousands of acres of monastic lands, and Church plunder, and how judicious " deals" in confiscated estates enormously increased the value of the property. And I have shown you how prudent marriages with wealthy heiresses brought large estates from other aristocratic families to enrich the Cavendishes. But it is one thing to acquire houses, and lands, and wealth, and it is another thing to keep them when you have got them. Our land laws are specially designed to build up and perpetuate large estates, and the Duke of Devonshire's land is all entailed, and tied up by settlements, so that it never comes into the market, and cannot be sold. One of our well known dukes some ' few years ago became bankrupt, and owed his creditors enormous sums of money, but they could not sell a single acre of his estates. Now let us see how much land has been accumulated in the Duke of Devonshire's family. The New Domes- day Book published about 30 yews ago, tells us that the Duke owns land in fourteen different counties : Derby, York, Lancashire, Sussex, Somerset, Lincoln, Cumber- land, Middlesex, Notts, Cheshire, Stafford, Cork, Water- ford, and Tipperary. These estates amount to 193,315 acres, and the rents at that time were £171,801 a year. Lord Waterpark, who is an illegitimate offshoot of the Cavendishes, owns 8,850 acres in Derbyshire and Tipperary; Lord Cheshatn, who is also a a,vendish, owns 11,486 acres in half-a-dozen counties : and the Hon. Richard Cavendish owns 7,027 acres in Bucks Stafford and Denbigh. If you add all these together you will find that this family owns 230,285 acres of land in England and Ireland. The Duke of Devonshire owns seven of the finest I ancestral homes and mansions in the kingdom. Devon- ' shire House' in Piccadilly, is his London residence; Chatsworth House, in Derbyshire, is his finest country seat; Hardwicke Hall, a few miles away, is an old Eng- lish mansion, built by Bess of Hardwick° ; Lismore Castle in Ireland, is in the centre of his Irish estates. He also owns biker Hall, and Crompton Place, and Bolton Abbey. He is the patron of forty-two livings in the Church of England,and his nominees enjoy an in- come of more than '210,000 a year. The Cavendishes have always been good landlords and good citizens, but I would not trust any man with the control of such vast estates, and permit him to tie them up, and refuse to sell them for generations. This system of land-hoarding is at the bottom of many of our social troubles,and nothing will cure it so effectively as the taxation of land values, whether the land is in use or not. This is the startinc, point in our land re- forms, and when we have gained this, all the rest will come in due time.

div.head: VOLUNTEERS IN CAMP.
div.p: VOLUNTEERS IN CAMP.
ENCAMPED ON SALISBURY PLAIN
The Week's Work,

Warrington had another touch of military excite- ment on Saturday evening when the main body of the local Volunteer battalion departed for their annual encampment on Perham Down, Salisbury Plain. The streets were thronged with townspeople, and the volunteers had a rousing "send off" reminiscent in a small degree of the memorable scenes witnessed during the South Airican campaign. The men looked very spic and span, and their smart soldierly appear- ance was commented upon on all hands. The tedious journey south was safely accom4ished, and although the weather during the week has been unsettled, the work of the battalion has not been seriously interfered with. It is hoped that the men will benefit by the change, and that the encampment of 1904 will be remembered as a successful and profitable period of training.

div.head: MOUNTED INFANTRY AND CYCLISTS.
div.p: MOUNTED INFANTRY AND CYCLISTS.

On Saturday morning a detachment of Mounted Infantry and Cyclists, with cooks and officers' grooms, to the number of 100. left Central Station for the camp. The men paraded at the Drill flail at 10.15 and were medically examined by Sergeant-Major Adams (medical officer) and Captain and Adjutant Bundock. Their departure was witnessed by a large assembly. The sections were under. the command of Captain C. Haslam, Captain L. Roberts, Lieutenant Layton and Surgeon- Captain Curtis. [FRoM OUR OWN CoRRESPONoENT INT CAMP.]

Our correspondent in camp writes : Warrington's "citizen soldiers" or, to give them their full title, the Ist V.B. (P.W.V.) South Lancashire Regiment, made a start for their annual training on Saturday. The Battalion "fell in" in front of the Town Hall shortly after 6.30, and, after a brief medical inspection, Marched off, headed by the regimental band playing a lively selection of music. A large crowd gave them an enthusiastic"send-off"from the Central Station, and knots of youngsters cheered the "warriors "along the railway as far as Padgate. The route taken was through Derby and Cheltenham, and great interest was shown in the lovely scenery till the men were too tired, and then sweet slumber predominated. Lulgershall was reached at about 4.30 and the volunteers made a start for camp, which they reached at 5.45. When the men had been allocated to their tents, the welcome bugle- call of " cookhouse " was sounded, and what the genial Quartermaster was pleased to call a "slight snack" was served, so as to give an appetite for breakfast. Church parade was held after breakfast on the parade ground when an address was given by the Rev. W. Bracecamp, who accompanies the battalion as chaplain. In the afternoon most of the men stayed in camp.but a few visited Ludgershall and Andover. The camp is situated at Perham Down close to the site of the 1901 camp. There are under canvas the Ist V.B. Royal Welsh Fusiliers, 2nd V.B. Cheshire I Regiment and the Ist V. B. Herefordshire Regiment, who, together with the Warrington men, fora, the 30th Field Army Brigade. The brigade officers are :—Brigadier, Col. M. Quayle , Jones, C. 8.; aide de camp, Capt. G. H. duCros,2nd V.B. Royal Warwick Regiment; brigade-major, Capt. L. J. Bois, D. 5.0., Devon Regiment; senior medical officer, I Brigade-Surgeon Lieut.-Col. P. B. Giles, Ist Hereford , Rifles • brigade signalling officer, Capt. C. E. Bromley, ' 2nd Cl:eshires • brigade cyclists' officer, Capt. W. E. Burton, 2nd deshires. The officers of the Prince of Wales's Volun- teers (South Lancashire Regiment) : are Lieut.-Colonel J. A. Edelsten ; Majors J. D. Fairclough and B. Fairclough ; Captains G. R. Crosfield, C. F. Cary, E. F. Willcocks, C. L. Williamson, C. Ha-slam and P. N. Avery (mounted infantry) ; Lieutenants E. E. Ridgway (mounted infantry), R. IVIcM. Roberts, F. R. Monks, A. B. Layton, J, T. Thomas, Ist Doyens (attached), instructor of musketry, and H. G. Roberts; , Captain A. F. Bundock, South Lancashire Regiment (adjutant) • Captain A. F. G. Potter (quarter-master); Surgeon-Captain J. N. Patterson (Newton) and Surgeon- Captain W. Curtis (medical officers) ; and the Rev. W. Bracecamp (acting-chaplain). The commisariat department is in charge of Captain and Quartermaster A. F. G. Potter, Quartermaster- Sergeant J. Willcocks, and an army of cooks in charge of Sergeant-Cook Taylor. Surgeon-Captain P. N. Patterson, Surgeon-Lieutenant W. Curtis, Sergeant J. Massey and 18 men have charge of the hospital, while there are 14 signallers under the direction of Sergeant Instructor Graley, a transport section under Lieutenant Ridgway,and Maxim Gun Section under Sergeant Range. On Monday morning the work of the camp opened in real earnest. The men paraded in full force at 6.30, with rolled overcoats, for inspection by the colonel. _ .

After breakfast, a parade an shirt sleeve; was ordered and the battalion marched out about four miles and took part in company formation, ecc. The weather broke during the morning to the discomforture of the volunteers. The signallers and ambulance section were practising in the vicinity of camp. In the afternoon, "A" and "I" companies were out firing on the range. The evening was very wet and most of the men very wisely stayed in camp. On Tuesday after breakfast the general inspection was held. The battalion paraded at 9.15 in assembly formation, with great coats and leggings, as it was rain- ing heavily. Colonel Quay Jones, the Brigadier, arrived with his stall and minutely inspected all ranks. In the afternoon, the men were out on the parade ground, and did some very good work skirmishinr under their company officers. Wednesday morning opened very wet and there was no parade before breakfast. The wet weather continued laybut some good work was done in the way of skirmishing by com- panies practically between d h e also a showers semaphore signalling instruction. The latter work is new to all the men in camp except the signalling section,and proved very interesting, the men and n t entering into the drill with zest. The Mounted Infantry company rode out of camp in the afternoon and got through some very interesting work. ACCIDENT TO A WARRINGTON MAN AT PLAY. Yesterday the programme of the South Lancashire Volunteers was unique. They left camp, and took with them field cooking stoves and a day's supply of food, with water cart, 3tc.,for the needs of the battalion The men's dinners were to be prepared in the open wherever they may have happened to be when the halt was sounded. This is excellent practice for the realities of active service. Playing football on Thursday night, one of the War- rington men had the misfortune to break his anale.

SOCIAL SERMONETTES FOR WORKING MEN.
BY JOHN TAYLOR. Author of Search Lights on Land, LnTA:Lr and Social Probleins."
THE DUKE OF DF.VONSAIRE3S ESTATES.

"Whatever may be our opinions as to the disad- vantages to the nation of enormous accumulations of landed estate' it must ba admitted that the Cavendishes have generally acted upon the principle that property has duties as well as 'rights, and they havo more than once rendered valuable service to the popular cause." —IIOWARD EVANS.

If I am to judge by the 'letters of inquiry that come to me, there is a keen and growing interest among my readers on the land question. Our increasing rates and taxes set men thinking about new sources of revenue, and how to compel all classes of the community to con- tribute their share. The landowners come in for a good deal of criticism, and I am asked all sorts of questions about them. One correspondent asks me to show him how the Duke of Devonshire's familyacquired its vast estates. Another wants me to say a word in praise of Mr. TreVelyan's Bill for the taxation of land values, and a third asks in to answer the arguments put forth by those who are opposed to any new taxes being laid on land. It is impossible to answer such questions as these by writing private letters to individual correspondents in different parts of the country, so I am asked to devote one of my articles now and then to these subjects, and then all ray readers will get the benefit of the informa- tion. I will begin by answering the question about the Duke of Devonshire's estates.
1.-THESE ESTATES HAD THEIR ORIGIN IN THE DISSOLUTION OF MONASTERIES.

About three hundred and seventy years ago, William Cavendish, the ancestor of the present Duke of Devon- shire, was a small landowner irr Suffolk. He lived in stirring times, and he knew his way about, and he was always ready when his opportunity came. Henry VIII, was dissolving the monasteries, and plundering the religious houses, and robbing them of their vast estates. William Cavendish managed to get a job as one of the commissioners,to do this bumbailiff's work, and to carry out the evictions, and he did his work so well that he was afterwards appointed Auditor of the Court of Augmentations, and Treasurer of the Chamber of the King. In 1510 the King gave him the lordships and manors of Northame, Childewick, and Cuffley, in Hert- fordshire, which had all been monastic property. Now I am not blaming. William Cavendish for accept- ing this stolen stuff. The robbery of the church had been planned by Henry VIII. and his advisers. It had been sanctioned. by Parliament, and so far as faithful service can commend a man,William Cavendish had as much right to be remembered in these grants as any

other candler. It is well known that the King flung away these church lands as fast as he got them, and any of his para- mours and courtiers could have them for the asking. When these lucky favourites received grants of land in some distant parts of the country that they had never heard of, they were willing to exchange them for other land nearer home, or they would sell them for an old song. William Cavendish was on the spot when these plums were on • the market, and he did a good business in profitable exchanges. Edward VI. had given him estates in Lincoln, Cornwall, and other counties, and these were all Church lands, similar to the Hertfordshire estates. Just before the boy king died, Cavendish "swapped" him all he had got for "divers lands belonging to abbeys, andpriories in Derby, Notts, Stafford,Dorset, Cornwall, Kent, and Essex." Now you can take it from me that William Cavendish never gave something for nothing, and he never " swapped " without getting the best of the bargain. , So by this time he was a great landowner, and wealth and honours were coming to him, and the ball was at his feet. If you ask my opinion about" the glorious reforma- tion in Church and State," that dissolved the monas- teries, and confiscated their lands, I say it was about as honest as highway robbery, or brigandage, or piracy. King Henry VIII. wanted money, and he coerced or dragooned his Parliament into sanctioning the confisca- tion of monastic lands first, and then he attacked the guilds, or trades unions, of those days. He plundered all those that were not rich enough to bribe him, and burhim off, andhe would have eaten up our university lands next, if death had not laid him by the heels, and confiscated him. lI.—THESE ESTATES WERE VASTLY INCREASED BY PRUDENT MARRIAGES.

William Cavendish, the fottnnate founder of the family, married three times, and he managed to catch a wealthy: wife each time. He acted on the principle that it is not wise to marry for money or vast estates, but while you are on the job, you may as well look out for a lady who has got something to bring into the family. His third wife RAS Bess of Hardwicke,a shrewd long- headed Derbyshire widow, and she taught him a thing or two about prudent marriages. She was well off to start with, and she persuaded her brother and her first husband te leave her all their estates, so by the time she married William Cavendish there was money enough to keep their three children. She married twice after the death of Cavendish, and drove a hard bargain with all four of her husbands. She was a champion match- maker for heirs and heiresses. She married the Earl of Shrewsbury. for her fourth husband, and to keep the estates in the family, she made a match between her own son and the earl's daughter, and between the earl's son and heir and her daughter, and all these weddings duly came off, for Bess had a will of her own, and a keen eye to business. The second son of William Cavendish and Bess Hard. wicks succeeded to the estates on the death of his elder brother and then titles and honours began to come into the family. He was created Baron Hardwicke, and held , that title as a compliment to his mother, till he was I created Earl of Devonshire, and sent to the House of Lords. The fourth Earl of Devonshire lived in the stormy I times of King James IL That profligate and foolish I monarch drove his country to revolution, and men had to take sides in the struggle. The Earl of Devonshire ! took the democratic side, and he was one of the nobles who corresponded with William, Prince of Orange, and invited him to comeito this coantry and seize the crown. When William came, he raised his tenantry and armed them to fight for the new monarch. This was a very risky business for him, and he took the chance of losing his estates and his life. If he had put his money on the wrong horse, and James H. had held the throne, he would have been hanged, drawn, and quartered as a traitor, and his estates would have been confiscated to the crown. But William succeeded to the throne, and he recog- nised the courage and devotion of the 'Earl by making him a duke, and Howard Evans says: If ever a duke- dom was fairly won by patriotic and courageous conduct, it was his." Nearly all the Cavendishes have followed the examples of Bess of Hardwicke in making prudent marriages. They did not marry as often as she did, but they took care to marry heiresses, who would bring them vast estates. The fourth Duke made the greatest "catch" in the matrimonial market by marrying the only daughter of the Earl of Burlington and Cork. ['his young lady was sole heiress of the estates of two aristocratic families-- the Cliffords and the Boyles. From the Cliff ords, who had been Earls of Cumberland, she inherited Bolton Abbey, and the manors of Skipton and Barden, Nvith thousands of acres of land in Wharfedale and Airedale, in Yorkshire, in addition to large estates in Cumber- who had been Earls of Cork, slahnedinhFerriotm he Boyles,edtmoretha than twenty thousand acres of land in Ireland, of which Listnore Castle is the centre. She also got from the same family, Chiswick House, near London, and other valuable property in England. So you will agree with me when I say this bride was richly endowed, and she brought houses, and lands, and estates

into the family, that added much to the wealth and dignity of the Cavendishes. Her younger son also made a prudent marriage with the only daughter of the Earl of Northampton, and she succeeded to the large family estates in Sussex at her father's death. rhe Cavendishes have been peculiarly fortunate in their deals with heiresses. James 1., when he was selling Crown lands, granted Furness Abbey to Robert Cecil, Earl of Salisbury, and Cartmel Priory to the Earl of Haddington, one of his Scotch favourites. Both these estates were sold to the Prestons, and carried by another heiress to Sir William Lowther by marriage. This heiress died without issue, and Sir William left the property to his cousin Cavendish. lII.—THESE ESTATES REPRESENT NEARLY

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS
Cricket.

Encouraging progress is being made in the arrange- ments for the West Lancashire Cricket League,and every- thing should be in working order by next season. The I promoters have made an admirable choice in appointing Mr. T. P. Bradshaw hon. secretary. It is almost unnecessary to enlarge upon the keen interest which Mr. Bradshaw takes in various branches of local sport. As secretary of the Warrington and District Football Association League, and he has thrown himself whole- heartedly into the work, and may be relied upon to do his utmost to ensure the success of the new organiza- tion. In Mr.C.W. Emmett, of Earlestown,the league will have an active treasurer. There are still vacancies for several teams, and efforts are being made. to enrol the requisite number of senior clubs.

On Saturday, Warrington made amends for the pre- vious week's defeat by severely trouncing Earlestown. Although two of the regular players—G. H. Übsdell and J. Callon—were absentees, capital substitutes were found in J. -Thompson and Alf Thewlis. The ex- professional was in particularly good form and made 38 not out. The Earlestown eleven was at full strength, and a large assembly of spectators witnessed the match. Batting first, the Warrington men showed that they had quite recovered the excellent form which has gained them such a creditable record, and heavy scoring was the order. When 210 had been compiled, with only 8 wickets down, Mr. Connor thought it safe to declare, and the visitors settled down to their task of dismissing the Earlestown contingent. A weak display by the home team resulted in only 79 being scored. The Warring- zonlans are once more jubilant, and look forward with confidence to to-day's match with Manchester.

A brilliant innings by J. W. Bibby was one of the best features of the match. Batting in vigorous style, he compiled 46, and made no fewer than eight boundary strokes. P. B. Hawtin acquitted himself with great credit, and by dint of cautious play—in striking con- trast to Mr. Bibby's dashing exhibition—ran up 44. Lynes' crisp batting pleased the spectators, and 41 was the outcome. The professional placed nine boundaries, and showed that in the batting as in the bowling depart- Ment he is a power to be reckoned with.

After the tall scoring of the visitors, the Earlestown individual contributions looked small. Only two players attained double figures, T. Miller knocking up 21, and G. Husband being responsible for 11.

E. A. Connor came out with the best bowling analysis. His deliveries were characterised with rare judgment, and he vo.ried the pace with such effect that the bats- men could make little headway. His capture was 5 wickets for 19 runs. Lynes took 3 wickets for 29, and J. W. Bibby one for 27.

Earlestown second proved more formidable opponents, and the Warringtonians had their work cut out in making a draw. Limond was the highest scorer with 33, J. H. Constable (20) being Warrington's most suc- cessful batsman. W. Bennett bowled well, his six wickets costing 42 runs.

Lynes, the popular professional, takes a well-earned benefit to-day, and there should be a good attendance to witness the match with Manchester. All who have followed the doings of the club with interest will admit that Lynes has rendered yeoman service both as a bowler and batsman. This is the last occasion on which War- rington enthusiasts will have an opportunity of giving him a benefit, for, as we have already announced, the professional will figure in the Bacup eleven next season. It is in a large measure owing to his excellent work that the Warrington club has attained such a creditable posi- tion, and I hope the benefit will be a "bumper."

Sankey Wire Mills journeyed to Northfvich, and suffered defeat by 31. Brough (15) was their only player to break the monotony of single figures, whilst R. Hughes (21) gave the best display for the victors. Harper was the destructive agent, capturing seven wickets for 12 runs.

Sankey Wire Mills 2nd eleven after a splendid victory over Peter Walker and Sons 2nd by 140 for 6 wickets to 40 met Mill-lane Ist eleven on Saturday. An exciting game resulted in another win for the Wire Mills by 2 runs. The scores were 72 to 70. For the Wire Mills Hewitt (16), Howard (19) and T. Barrow (9 not out) were the chief scorers. Miles for the losers made the highest score, knocking up 19. Partridge bowled well for the Wire Mills although Bell performed a useful service in terminating a long partnership of two of the Mill-lane batsmen at a time when a Mill-lane victory seemed likely. The Wire Mills 2nd meet Fairfield Ist to-day and have a defeat to avenge.

There was an exciting contest at Grappenhall, the engagement with Stretton and Appleton resulting in a tie. Stretton and Appleton 2nd were beaten by St. Mary's, but as the scores of 45 and 23 indicate, there were no striking performances.

Penketh Friends' School made short work of the " Guardian " printers, the feature of the match being the excellent batting of J. W. Proud, who made 55. The" Guardian" Office team also sustained defeat. St. Paul's, who had a very useful batsman in G. Mason (38) were the conquerors.

Penketh failed to account for Moore at the Cheshire village, the home eleven securing a majority of 33. E. Allen (32) did good service with the bat for the winners, A. Hodgkinson compiling 18 for Penketh.
Latchford Baptists had not much difficulty in dispos- ing, of Moss Side Baptists. Lunt being their top scorer with 31. Cook captured four wickets for six runs.
Bowling.

The attendance at the King— and Queen green on Saturday, to witness the match "Winners v. Rest" was disappointingly small. Those who did put in an appear- ance had the pleasure of witnessing an exciting en- count6r, the "Rest" triumphing by a margin of 19. It was unfortunate that the interest which reached such a high pitch the previous week was not sustained, for it had been hoped to hand over another donation to the Infirmary and District Nursing Association. The pro- ceeds were so small that is doubtful whether they will more than clear expenses.

The first pair on the green—George Ball jun., and John Monks—provided an interesting game. Ball started best, but the players were level at 8 and 9. Then the forge captain had a run of four which placed the issue beyond doubt. Monks got in a double, and Ball following with a single ran out winner by 15-11.

Wu 1 -- The next game between R. Rothwell and George Holbrook was a very close one. At the outset Rothwell carried all before him, and led 11-2. Holbrook had a splendid break of 12, which placed him ahead by 14-11. The three remaining ends were all in Rothwell's favour, and he secured the victory by 15-14.

Another exciting contest was that in which W.Bower- ing figured against W. Hill. The latter scored 7 before his opponent won an end. Bowering was on his mettle, and the contestants were level at 8 and 9. Bowering shot ahead and led 13-12. At the twenty-second end the players were again equal with 14, but Hill sent down the winning wood and triumphed by 15-14.

Tom. Davies and H. Daintith were well matched, aid at 6 and 8 were on equal terms. Davies secured a single and a double, Daintith responding with a run of 6. Davies placed two successive singles, but his opponent was equal to the occasion and won by 15-13.

George Ball, the" Rest" captain, had no difficulty in disposing of W. Mee who could only run up 6. G. Higham was beaten by J. Worsley 15-6, and Herman Williams trounced James Jennings by the same margin.
J. W. Worsley made a good stand against A. Gleave and led at 10-9. From this point Gleave did most of the scoring and was victor by 15-11.

To-day the handicap for employees at works repre- sented in the recent competition will be commenced. The entries up to date are not nearly so numerous as last year,but no doubt the project will be taken up with greater spirit when it has got thoroughly into swing.

The league tourney proceeds apace, and four matches were decided on Saturday. Cemetery had again to admit defeat, their conquerors being Sankey Chapel House. The games were very keenly contested as the margin of 7 points indicates. Bull's Head accounted for Horse and Jockey somewhat easily, but there were very tight games between J. Worsley jun., and James Hardman ; John Swanton and T. Bretherton. In each case the last named player was victorious by the odd chalk.

The Liberal Club tasted the sweets of victory, al- though their odponents—Brooklands—made a bold bid for success. The Liberals had the advantage of playing on their own green, and an out winners by 5 points. At home Brooklands fared much better, and accounted for Penketh Park by the substantial majority of 60.

The following is the league table up to date : p. W. L. For Agst. Pts. Cemetery Horse and Jockey ll ... 6 ••• 5 ...1653 ...1459 ... 12 Bull's Head Chapel House Brooklands Fearnhead Penketh Liberal Club lO ... 3 ... 7 ...1395 _1509 ... 6

The representatives of the Widnes and district league have amply avenged their defeat by the Warringtonians earlier in the season. The match at Halton on Thurs- day evening resulted in a victory for the chemicalopolis trundlers by 87. In the first engagement Warrington gained the victory by 48. •
To-day's league matches are : Bull's Head v. Brooklands. Liberal Club v. Penketh Park. Liberal Club v. Bull's Head.

Death Whilst at Work. William Norman (48), of Factory-lane, was follow- ing his employment at Messrs. Crosfield's works at 12.30 yesterday afternoon when he fell down and e%.- pired. For sometime deceased had suffered front rheumatic fever and had been medically attended. Accident at Warrington Bridge. At 7.20 last evening,Agnes Reynolds, the nine year old daughter of Elizabeth Reynolds, a widow, residing at 5, School-brow, was swinging on the rails near Warrington Bridge when she over-balanced. The tide being out, the girl fell on the mud and stones at the river-side. She was taken to the Infirmary by P.O• Sankey, and Richard Peet, labourer, Howard-street, and it was found that she was suffering from con- cussion of the brain. Music Licences. Mr. Joseph Colbourne, off-licence holder, 101 p Manchester-road, died with painful suddenness on Saturday. The deceased had been ailing for some time, but his condition was not such as to indicate that the end was so near. On Saturday morning he was attending to the general routine of his business when he was suddenly seized with an attack of giddi- ness, and before medical aid arrived,passed away. medical certificate gives the cause of death as syncope- ' Deceaged, who was about 32 years of age, leaves e widow and two children. Cycling. . • The Warrington. Cycling Club carried out a most enjoyable fixture on Saturday. The weather was showery but about a dozen members turned out for Cranage. On reaching this favourite resort to-- adjourned to the Swan Farm where they met mop members of the Manchester Wheelers' organization.. After hearty greetings had been exchanged, a capital tea was served. The adjoining fields were then visited, the Manchester cyclists having brought some cricket. tackle by motor car. A match was arranged, and soon • the eity men were wielding the willow to the deliveries of the Warrington cracks. The . innings realized 63, and then the Warrington contingent embarked upon their task. The shades of night closed' in just a little too early, for when the Warringtoniane had compiled 22 with two wickets down the match had to be concluded. The game had been entered into with spirit and was a most agreeable change from the usual bowls. Warrington was reached at 10.30 after an outing which all voted to have been successful. -- Owing to the threatening weather,there was only a small turnout for Tuesday evening's run. A quick ride • to Hoo Green and back was indulged in, there being no, bowling or" smoker." The first round of the second bowling main was entered upon on Wednesday at Sankey, and there was a good entry and some keen contests. Given suitable weather there should be a great deal of touring this week end. The Warrington C.C. hope to visit Buxton and the Derbyshire Dales, and are" looking forward to an enjoyable time. LIGHTING-UP TIME. To-night Monday 9.8 Tuesday 9.7 Wednesday Thursday Friday Local Success. At Salford Harriers' Sports on Saturday, C. Berrv,o• Warrington, won the mile bicycle handicap holt': the 52 yards mark in 60 1-ssecs. In the half-mile- scratch race he was second to B. Jones, Birmingham- C.C., whose time was lmin. 29 3-ssecs. C. J. Straw, of Warrington, came in fourth in the two, miles invitation race, which was won by A. Shrubb,. South London H., in 9mins. 22 1-5 secs. Angling. • At the monthly meeting of the Latchford Angling Society, held on Wednesday, it was decided to fix the' home match for Saturday, the 13th August. The match will take place in a reach of the Bridgewater Canal which has been rented by the society and which extends from the cottage at Lumb Brook and proceeds as far as Grappenhall. There will also be a match at Northwich: on the 27th August, when valuable prizes will be offered for competition. The arrangements have been left irb' the hands of a committee. During the evening, prizes were distributed to the. value of £4 10s. in connection with the match no 9th. The committee are desirous of strictly r._,,oeving" the reach of the canal which they have rented for the - exclusive use of members of the Latchford Society. There have been a few trespassers in the past, but if any are detected, proceedings will be instituted against them. -- Football: The tragic death by lightning at Barmouth of "Jim' Valentine has given rise to a feeling of sorrow all over the country, and particularly in the North. During his' Jong career "Jim "had played against nearly all the' R.U. Counties, and had four times represented England so that his fame was by no means local. Still he was' certainly best known, admired and respected in South- West Lancashire. As the "Swinton Lion " and " Val "he has struck terror into the hearts of opponents- under both Rugby Union and Northern Union Rules. It. is not mere than a year or so since he led the young "Lions " at V4'ilderspool and I have not to go far bacic before I can recollect him playing in the senior ranks and giving the . Warrington defence endless trouble. Those who saw Valentine at his best have enviable recollections of one of the greatest three-quarter backs who ever donned a jersey. On the field he was invincible, and off it a quieter or genial follow fellow did not wear shoes. "Jim "was a formid- able looking fellow when going for the line, and with his thick close-set brows, determined chin,and headlong stride, he generally inspired rather more than a whole- , some respect. It is particularly saddening to reflect., that after coming through the rigour and hardship °I 27 years' football he should fall on a mountain side, the victim of a lightning flash. I wonder if he WO'S fatalist. He seems to have been singled out by the One, above for a remarkable career and a more remarkable. end! -- Valentine made Swinton a name inseparabla from 0e - history of the game. It is not more than twelve" months ago since he decided to retire definitely; this' at an age when most players have been on the retired list for many years. He was 38 years of age, and of' these, 27 had been devoted to active football. As a stripling of eleven he attracted notice in the Brindle Heath club and when that club amalgam ated with number of others in the district under the name of the Pendleton F.C. he was so good as to be awarded the• reins. A transference to Broughton Rangers in 1883 did' notapparenlly suit him, and he returned to Pendleton, and thence in the same season to Swinton, with which club he never since severed his connection. His captaincy of the club—and here we have in a great measure the secret of Swinton's phenomenal suc-• cess—commenced in the season of 1899 and 1890, and,. with the exception of a break in 1892-93, he remainee the skipper till last season but one. Thus his captaiaa bridged a span of over twelve years. In all matches (county and international games included) since be joined the S' °n on club be scored no fewer than 351 tries, he placed 179 g )als. dropped 21 goals, kicked penalty goals, and two from free kicks. There is n° likelihood of this feat ever being approached,let equalled. In one season alone-1888-9—he ,scored 6u tries, placed 35 goals, and dropped 5 goals. In fa° successive matches he registered 18 tries. Then in 1900-1 he played for Lancashire in nine en; gagemants' in addition to the trial match, scoring the county 18 tries and kicking 13 goals. In the triaL game he scored thrice. In all,he played for the Count.. Palatine on 71 occasions, and his aggregate of scores la these games was 54 tries and 37 goals. He possesseda Lancashire county cap, which bore dates ranging froin 1885 to 1895. Six times did the English Rugby Uni,°° call upon him to represent his country ; four times ne figured in the international games, and twice be received his cap when no matches were played owing dispute between the International Board and the' English Union. In recognition of his unique services to club, count'', and country, Valentine was in 1898 presented with a purse of gold amounting to £350. The 'Swinton einb headed the list with .250, and subscriptions came frora practically every Rugby football centre in the countrY; Last year he was the retipient of another testimoniat, and some handsome presents to mark his definite retira' from the game. An immense concourse of people assembled yesterclar to honour Valentine's memory, and the funeral was f' unique and impressive event. Mr. H. Ashton repl: sented the Warrington Club, which forwarded a hapa some wreath. Football Items. $. Vernon Hampson, Swinton's wing three-quarter, wa on Wednesday transferred to the York Club.
